As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Call upon God, or call upon the Most Merciful; whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾, this is the well-known supplication, and that it is a supplication of request, and it is the occasion of revelation.

They said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to call upon his Lord, saying sometimes: O God, and sometimes: O Most Merciful. So the ignorant among the polytheists thought that he was calling upon two gods, so God revealed this verse."

Ibn ʿAbbās said: "The polytheists heard the Prophet (ﷺ) calling in his prostration: O Most Merciful, O Most Compassionate. They said: This one claims that he calls upon one, but he calls upon two, two by two. So God revealed this verse: Say: Call upon God or call upon the Most Merciful."

It has been said: the supplication here means naming, as in their saying: "I named my son Saʿīd," and "Name him ʿAbd Allāh" and similar. The meaning is: name your Lord God, or name Him the Most Merciful. So the supplication here means naming.

This is the saying of al-Zamakhsharī. What led him to this is His saying: ﴿whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾, for the meaning of "whichever" (ayyan) and its generality here is only the multiplicity of names. The meaning is: whatever name you name Him by from the names of God, whether God or the Most Merciful, to Him belong the most beautiful names, that is, to the named One, exalted is He, belong the most beautiful names. The pronoun in "to Him" refers to the one named. This is what made him take the supplication in this verse to mean naming.

What he said is one of the implications of the meaning intended by supplication in the verse, but it is not its exact intended meaning. Rather, what is intended by supplication is its familiar and consistent meaning in the Qur'an, namely the supplication of request and the supplication of praise. But it contains the meaning of naming, so the intended meaning is not mere naming devoid of worship and request, but naming occurring within supplication of praise and request.

On this meaning, it is correct that "tadʿū" (you call) carries the sense of "tusammū" (you name).

Reflect upon this. The meaning is: whatever you name Him in your praise, your supplication, and your request. And God knows best.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, we used to call upon Him before. Indeed, He is the Good, the Merciful﴾, this is supplication of worship which includes request, out of desire and out of dread.

The meaning is: indeed we used to devote worship sincerely to Him before. By this they deserved that He protect them from the punishment of the scorching wind, not by mere request, which is shared between the one who is saved and others, for God, glorified is He, is asked by whoever is in the heavens and on earth. Success and salvation come only through sincerity in worship, not through mere request and asking.

Likewise is the saying of the youths, the People of the Cave: ﴿Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. We will never call upon any god besides Him﴾, meaning: we will never worship other than Him.

Likewise is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do you call upon Baʿl and leave the best of creators?﴾

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it will be said: Call upon your partners. Then they called upon them, but they did not respond to them, and they saw the punishment, [and wished] that they had been guided﴾, this is from the supplication of request. God, mighty and majestic, rebukes them and disgraces them on the Day of Resurrection by showing them that their partners do not respond to their call. It does not mean "worship them."

It is similar to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the Day He will say: Call upon My partners whom you claimed. Then they will call upon them, but they will not respond to them﴾.

This explanation is useful in the matter of the prayer (ṣalāh): whether it has been transferred from its meaning in the language, so that it became a transferred Islamic technical term (ḥaqīqa sharʿiyya manqūla), used for this act of worship figuratively because of the relation between it and its linguistic meaning, or whether it remains on its linguistic usage with the addition of pillars and rulings to it.

According to what we have established, there is no need for any of that. For the worshipper, from the beginning of his prayer to its end, is never free from supplication, either supplication of worship and praise, or supplication of request and asking, and in both states he is a caller. Thus the prayer has not departed from the reality of supplication. Reflect upon this once you understand it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret﴾ encompasses both kinds of supplication, but it is more evident in the supplication of request, which includes the supplication of worship. For this reason He commanded that it be concealed and made secret.

al-Ḥasan (al-Baṣrī) said: "Between the supplication in secret and the supplication openly there is a difference of seventy times."

The Muslims used to strive in supplication, and no voice of theirs was heard, except a whisper between them and their Lord.

That is because God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret﴾, and because God mentioned a righteous servant and approved of his action, saying: ﴿When he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾.

There are several benefits in concealing the supplication.

The first: it is greater in faith, because its doer knows that God hears his hidden supplication. This is unlike one who says: God hears if we raise our voices, but does not hear if we conceal them.

The second: it is greater in courtesy and reverence. For this reason, one does not address kings or make requests with raised voices; rather, voices are lowered before them, and speech is softened before them to the measure of what they hear. Whoever raises his voice before them is despised. And to God belongs the highest likeness.

So if our Lord hears hidden supplication, it is not proper in courtesy before Him except to lower the voice with it.

The third: it is more eloquent in humility and submission, which is the spirit, the core, and the purpose of supplication. The humble, submissive, and lowly one only asks as a poor, abased person asks when his heart is broken, his limbs are humbled, and his voice is subdued, to the extent that his lowliness, poverty, brokenness, and submission nearly reach the point that his tongue is broken and no longer obeys him in speech. His heart is asking, seeking, and pleading, while his tongue, from the intensity of his abasement, submission, and poverty, is silent. This state does not allow raising the voice in supplication at all.

The fourth: it is more eloquent in sincerity.

The fifth: it is more eloquent in gathering the heart upon God in supplication, for raising the voice scatters it and disperses it. The lower the voice, the more it is conducive to his praise and to concentrating his aim and intention upon the One called, glorified and exalted is He.

The sixth, which is among the wonderful secret subtleties, is that it indicates the nearness of its doer to God, and that because of his nearness to Him and the intensity of his presence, he asks Him a request as one asks the nearest thing to him. So he asks with the request of one intimately speaking to one who is near, not with the request of one calling out to one who is far away.

For this reason, God, exalted is He, praised His servant Zakariyya by saying: ﴿When he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾. So whenever the heart calls to mind God's nearness to it, and that He is nearer to it than any near thing, and it imagines that, it conceals its supplication as much as it can and does not find it possible to raise the voice with it; rather it considers that disapproved. Just as one who addresses a companion who hears his hidden speech, and exaggerates in raising his voice, is reproached for that. And to God belongs the highest likeness, glorified is He.

The Prophet (ﷺ) alluded to this very meaning when he said in the sound hadith, when the Companions raised their voices with takbīr (saying Allahu akbar) while they were with him on a journey: "Be easy on yourselves, for you are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent. You are calling upon One who is Hearing and near, nearer to one of you than the neck of his mount." And God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾.

It has been related that the occasion of its revelation was that the Companions said: "O Messenger of God, is our Lord near so that we may confide to Him, or far so that we may call out to Him?" So God, mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾.

This indicates their guidance to confidential intimate supplication, not to the calling out which is raising the voice, for it was about this that they asked. They were answered that their Lord, blessed and exalted is He, is near, and in calling upon and asking Him, He does not require calling out. Rather one asks with the request of one who is near and intimately addressed, not the request of one who is far and called out to.

This nearness of the caller is a special nearness, not a general nearness to everyone. He is near to his caller and near to his worshipper.

"The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating." (Footnote «١»)

And it is more specific than the nearness of turning in repentance (qurb al-inaba) and the nearness of answering (qurb al-ijaba), which most theologians (mutakallimūn) did not affirm beyond it. Rather, it is a special nearness of the caller and the worshipper, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said, relating from his Lord, blessed and exalted is He: "Whoever draws near to Me a hand's span, I draw near to him an arm's length, and whoever draws near to Me an arm's length, I draw near to him a fathom's length."

This is His nearness to His worshipper. As for His nearness to His caller and His one who asks, it is as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾.

His saying: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret﴾ contains indication and information about this nearness.

As for His nearness, blessed and exalted is He, to His beloved, it is another type, another structure, and another matter, as we have mentioned in the book al-Tuḥfa al-Makkiyya. However, expression falls short of it, and the true meaning of it never settles in the heart; rather, according to the strength or weakness of love, the servant's affirmation of this nearness varies. Beware, then beware, of expressing it in other than this prophetic wording, or having in your heart a meaning other than its sense and intended purpose, lest your foot slip after it was firm. Many people's discernment has weakened in this station, their expression has been poor, and they have fallen into various kinds of excess and ecstatic utterance. And opposite them is one whose veil is thick, who denies the servant's love for his Lord entirely and his nearness to Him, and reduces it to mere created reward, so that the Beloved and the Near is for him nothing but that.

We have mentioned more than a hundred ways of refuting these and those in the book *al-Tuhfa*. The purpose here is the discussion of this verse.

Seventh: it is more conducive to the continuity of seeking and asking, for the tongue does not tire and the limbs do not grow weary. By contrast, when one raises one's voice, the tongue may tire and some of one's faculties may weaken. This is like one who recites and repeats aloud: such a person cannot sustain it for long, unlike one who lowers his voice.

Eighth: concealing supplication is further from obstacles, disturbances, and things that weaken it. When the supplicant conceals his supplication, no one knows of it, so no disturbance or otherwise arises for him. When he voices it, the evil spirits and the wicked satanic ones among jinn and humans become aware of it, and they inevitably disturb him, oppose him, and obstruct him. Even if there were nothing in that except that their attachment to him divides his resolve and weakens the effect of the supplication, that would suffice. Whoever has experience knows this. So when one supplicates secretly and conceals it, he is safe from this harm.

Ninth: the greatest blessing is turning to God, worshipping Him, devoting oneself to Him, and detaching oneself toward Him (*tabattul*). Every blessing has envious ones in proportion to its worth, whether small or great, and there is no blessing greater than this one. The souls of the envious who are cut off are attached to it. There is nothing safer for the one who is envied than concealing his blessing from the envier and not intending to display it to him. Ya'qub said to Yusuf: ﴿Do not relate your vision to your brothers, lest they plot a plot against you. Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy.﴾ How many a person of heart, collectedness, and spiritual state with God has spoken of it and informed others, and outsiders (*aghyar*) stripped it from him, so that he became one who turns his palms in regret. Therefore the knowers and the shaykhs enjoin guarding the secret with God, not letting anyone become aware of it, and keeping it with the utmost secrecy, as one of them recited:

*Whoever they confided in, and he, striving, revealed the secret, they would not trust him with secrets for as long as he lived.*
*They distanced him, so he did not attain their nearness, and they replaced intimacy with him with estrangement.*
*They do not trust one who spreads some part of their secret. Far be it that their affection be like that, far be it.*

The people of God are the greatest in keeping secret their states with God and what God has bestowed upon them of His love, intimacy with Him, and collectedness of heart upon Him, especially the beginner and the traveler (*salik*).

When one of them is firmly established and strong, and the roots of that good tree, whose root is firm and whose branch is in heaven, are fixed in his heart such that he fears no storms, then if he displays his state and condition with God so that he may be emulated and followed, he is not concerned. This is a door of great benefit, known only to its people.

If the supplication commanded to be concealed includes supplication of request, praise, love, and turning toward God, then it is among the greatest treasures, most deserving of concealment and covering from the eyes of the envious. This is a noble and beneficial point.

Tenth: supplication is a mention of the One who is invoked, glorified, and it includes a request from Him and praise of Him through His names and attributes. So it is mention and something more. Just as mention is called supplication because it includes a request, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The best supplication is *al-hamdu lillah* (praise be to God)." So he called "al-hamdu lillah" a supplication, and it is pure praise, because praise includes love and commendation. Love is the highest kind of seeking for the beloved, so the one who praises is seeking his beloved, and he is more entitled to be called a supplicant than one who asks his Lord for some need.

Reflect on this point. When you reflect on it, you will not need what some have said: that mention implicitly seeks bounty even if it does not explicitly ask, so that it is a supplication through what its praise contains of seeking. As Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said in praise of his patron:

*Shall I mention my need, or has your bounty already sufficed me? Your nature is generosity.*
*When a man praises you one day, his praise suffices him from having to seek (your favour).*

According to the method we have mentioned, praise itself includes the greatest request, namely the request of the lover. So it is truly a supplication, and indeed it is more entitled to be called a supplication than other kinds of request that are below it. The point is that each of supplication and mention includes the other and enters into it.

(Section)

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly. Indeed He does not love the transgressors.﴾ (7:55)

It has been said: the meaning is that He does not love transgressors in supplication, such as one who asks for what is not befitting, like the ranks of the prophets and other such things.

Abu Dawud related in his *Sunan*, from the hadith of Hammad ibn Salama, from Sa'id al-Jurayri, from Abu Mu'awiya, that Abd Allah ibn Mughaffal heard his son say: "O God, I ask You for the white palace on the right side of Paradise when I enter it." He said: "My son, ask God for Paradise and seek refuge with Him from the Fire, for I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: 'There will come in this community people who transgress in purification and in supplication.'"

On this basis, transgression in supplication takes several forms. Sometimes it is asking for what one is not permitted to ask, such as aid in forbidden matters. Sometimes it is asking for what God does not do, such as asking Him to make one eternal until the Day of Resurrection, or asking Him to remove from him the necessities of humanity, such as the need for food and drink, or asking Him to inform him of His unseen, or asking Him to make him one of the infallible, or asking Him to grant him a child without a wife or a slave-girl, and similar things whose asking is transgression. Every request that contradicts God's wisdom, or includes a contradiction of His law and command, or includes a contrariness to what He has informed us of, is transgression, which God does not love and neither do His messengers.

Transgression has also been explained as raising the voice in supplication. Ibn Jurayj said: "Among transgression is raising the voice in supplication, calling out loudly, and shouting in supplication." Moreover, the verse is more general than all of that. If transgression in supplication is among what is meant, then it is part of what is meant, and God does not love transgressors in anything, whether supplication or otherwise, as He said: ﴿And do not transgress. Indeed God does not love transgressors.﴾ (2:190)

On this basis, He commanded calling upon Him and worshipping Him, and informed that He does not love the people of transgression, who call upon others along with Him. These are the greatest of transgressors, for the greatest transgression is *shirk* (associating others with God), which is placing worship in other than its proper place. This transgression must be included in His words: ﴿Indeed He does not love the transgressors.﴾

Among transgression is calling upon Him without humility, but with presumption (*idlal*), like one who is self-sufficient in what he has, presuming upon his Lord because of it. This is among the greatest transgressions, and it is contrary to the supplication of the humble, abject, poor, and needy in every respect in all his states. Whoever does not ask with the request of a humble, fearful, needy person is a transgressor.

Among transgression is that you worship Him with what He has not prescribed, and praise Him with what He has not praised Himself with nor permitted. This transgression occurs in supplication of praise and worship, and it is similar to transgression in supplication of asking and request.

On this basis the verse indicates two things. The first is what is beloved to the Lord, blessed and exalted, and pleasing to Him, namely supplication in humility and secrecy. The second is what He dislikes, abhors, and is displeased with, namely transgression. He commanded what God loves and recommended it, and He warned against what He hates and forbade it with the most forceful means of prohibition and warning: that He does not love its doer. And whom God does not love, what good can he attain?

In His words, ﴿Indeed He does not love the transgressors﴾ following His words, ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly,﴾ there is evidence that whoever does not call upon Him humbly and secretly is among the transgressors whom He does not love. So the verse divides people into two kinds: one who calls upon God humbly and secretly, and one who transgresses by abandoning that.

(Section)

His words: ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation.﴾ (7:56)

Most exegetes said: do not corrupt it with sins and by calling to other than obedience to God, after God has reformed it by sending the messengers, explaining the law, and calling to obedience to Him. Worship of other than God, calling to other than Him, and associating others with Him is the greatest corruption on earth. Indeed, the corruption of the earth in reality is only through *shirk* toward Him and opposition to His command. He, exalted, said: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea by what the hands of people have earned﴾ (30:41). Ata said about the verse: "Do not disobey on the earth, lest God withhold the rain and destroy the crops because of your sins." Several of the Salaf said: when the rain is withheld, the animals curse the sinners among the children of Adam and say: "O God, curse them, for because of them the land has become barren and the rain has been withheld."

In sum: *shirk*, calling to other than God, and establishing a worshipped one other than God, or an obeyed and followed one other than the Messenger of God (ﷺ), is the greatest corruption on earth. There is no reform for it, nor for its people, except that God alone is worshipped, and He alone is called upon, not others, and that obedience and following belong to His Messenger alone. Obedience to anyone else is obligatory only when that person commands obedience to the Messenger. If he commands disobedience and opposition to the Messenger's law, then there is no hearing and no obedience to him. For God reformed the earth through His Messenger and His religion, and by commanding His monotheism, and He forbade corrupting it by associating others with Him and opposing His Messenger.

Whoever contemplates the conditions of the world finds that every reform on earth is caused by God's monotheism, His worship, and obedience to His Messenger. And every evil in the world, every trial, calamity, drought, the empowerment of an enemy, and so on, is caused by opposition to His Messenger and calling to other than God and His Messenger.

Whoever reflects on this with true reflection, and contemplates the conditions of the world from its beginning until now, and until God inherits the earth and all who are upon it, and He is the best of inheritors, will find this matter to be so, both in his own self in particular and in others, in general and in detail. There is no power except with God, the Most High, the Mighty.

(Section)

His words: ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation, and call upon Him in fear and hope. Indeed, the mercy of God is near to the doers of good.﴾ (7:56)

He repeated the command to supplicate only because of what He mentioned with it, namely fear and hope. He first commanded calling upon Him humbly and secretly, then commanded that the supplication also be in fear and hope. He separated the two sentences with two sentences: one informative, containing a prohibition, namely His words, ﴿Indeed He does not love the transgressors﴾; and the second imperative, namely His words, ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation.﴾ The two sentences confirm and strengthen the first sentence and emphasize its content. Then, when its establishment was complete and its contrary and contradictory explained, He commanded calling upon Him in fear and hope, and then confirmed that and emphasized its content with an informative sentence, namely His words, ﴿Indeed the mercy of God is near to the doers of good.﴾ So the connection of this sentence to His words, ﴿And call upon Him in fear and hope,﴾ is like the connection of His words, ﴿Indeed He does not love the transgressors,﴾ to His words, ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly.﴾

Since His words, ﴿And call upon Him in fear and hope,﴾ comprise all the stations of faith and excellence (*ihsan*), namely love, fear, and hope, He followed them with: ﴿Indeed the mercy of God is near to the doers of good,﴾ meaning that only one who calls upon Him in fear and hope attains mercy, and so he is a doer of good, and mercy is near to him. For the basis of excellence rests upon these three principles.

Since calling upon Him humbly and secretly is opposed by transgression, which is the failure to be humble and secret, He followed it with: ﴿Indeed He does not love the transgressors.﴾

As for the accusative case of "humbly, secretly, in fear, and in hope": it has been said that it is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), meaning: call upon Him while humble, secret, fearful, and hopeful. This is what al-Suhayli and others preferred. It has also been said that it is an accusative of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*), which is the view of many grammarians. And it has been said that it is an accusative of the verbal noun (*masdar*). On this view there are two estimations. The first is that it is governed by a verb implied from the same root as the verbal noun, meaning: "Be humble toward Him with humility, and hide with hiding." The second is that it is governed by the mentioned verb because it carries the sense of a verbal noun, for the supplicant is humble in seeking the attainment of his object and fearful of its loss, as if he had said: "Be humble with humility."

The correct view is that it is accusative as a circumstantial, the meaning being "toward Him," for the meaning is: "Call upon your Lord, humbly turning toward Him, fearful and hopeful." The verbal noun takes the place of the adjective, as in His words, ﴿But righteousness is [in] one who believes in God﴾ (2:177), and in the expressions "a just man" and "a fasting man." A poet said: "For it is only approach and retreat." This is better than saying "call upon Him humbly and fearful," and more eloquent. What makes it good is that the thing commanded here is twofold: the supplication, described and restricted by a specific attribute, namely the attributes of humility, fear, and hope; so the aim is to restrict the commanded act by that attribute, and to restrict the one described, who is its possessor, by it. So He brought the circumstantial in the form of the verbal noun, since it is fit to be an attribute of the agent and an attribute of the commanded act.

Reflect on this subtle point. When you say, "Remember your Lord humbly," you mean: "Remember Him humbly toward Him, and remember Him with the remembrance of humility." You intend both together. Likewise, when you say, "Call upon Him in hope," you mean: call upon Him with a supplication of hope, and call upon Him hoping for His bounty. Similarly, when you say, "Call upon Him with desire and dread," as in His words, ﴿Indeed they used to hasten to good works, and they would call upon Us with desire and fear﴾ (21:90), and as in His words, ﴿calling upon Us with desire and fear,﴾ and "call upon Him with the supplication of desire and dread."

Reflect on this matter and you will find it to be so. He brought therein the verbal noun, indicating the description of the commanded act by that attribute, and restricting the agent by it, restricting the possessor of the circumstance by the circumstance.

Of what indicates this: you will find that such a construction can serve as an answer to "how?" So if it is said, "How should I call upon Him?" it is answered, "Humbly and secretly." And you will find that the implication of "how?" here is stronger than the implication of "why?" If it were an object of purpose, it would be an answer to "why?", and it would not fit well here. Do you not see that the meaning does not fit that? For it is valid to say, "Why should I call upon Him?" and he answers, "Humbly and secretly." This is clear. It is also not an accusative of the verbal noun specifying the type, which the agent is not restricted by, for the reason we mentioned, namely its fitness as an answer to "how?"

In sum: the verbal-noun status in this matter does not contradict the circumstantial. Rather, bringing the circumstantial here in the form of the verbal noun conveys what the verbal noun conveys, with the added benefit of the circumstantial. It is therefore more complete in meaning, and there is no contradiction between them. And God knows best.

(Section)

God's words: ﴿Indeed the mercy of God is near to the doers of good.﴾

In it there is a clear indication that doing this commanded act is the excellence required of you, and what you seek from God is His mercy, which is near to the doers of good, those who did what they were commanded: calling upon Him in fear and hope. So your goal draws near to you, namely mercy, in accordance with your fulfilment of what He requires of you, namely excellence, which in reality is excellence toward yourselves. For God is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy. If you do good, you do good to yourselves.

His words, ﴿Indeed the mercy of God is near to the doers of good,﴾ carry three kinds of indication: an indication by their explicit wording, an indication by their implication and causal indication (*ta'lil*), and an indication by their implicature (*mafhum*). Their explicit indication is the nearness of mercy to the people of excellence. Their indication by causal implication is that this nearness is deserved through excellence, so excellence is the cause of mercy's nearness to them. And their indication by implicature is the distance of mercy from those who are not doers of good. These are the three indications of this sentence. The people of excellence are singled out for the nearness of mercy because it is a kindness from God, the Most Merciful of the merciful, and His kindness befalls only the people of excellence, for recompense is of the kind of the deed. Just as they did good through their deeds, He does good to them through His mercy. As for one who is not among the people of excellence, since he has distanced himself from excellence, mercy distances itself from him in proportion to his distance, and draws near in proportion to his nearness. Whoever draws near through excellence, God draws near to him through His mercy, and whoever distances himself from excellence, God distances Himself from him through His mercy.

God, glory be to Him, loves the doers of good and hates those who are not among them. Whom God loves, His mercy is the nearest thing to him, and whom He hates, His mercy is the furthest thing from him.

Excellence here is the doing of the commanded act, whether it is excellence toward people or toward oneself. The greatest excellence is faith, monotheism, repentant turning to God, devotion to Him, reliance upon Him, and worshipping God as if you see Him, out of reverence, awe, shyness, love, and fear. This is the station of excellence, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said when Gabriel asked him about excellence, and he said: "That you worship God as if you see Him."

Since this is excellence, God's mercy is near to its possessor, for God shows mercy only to the people of His monotheism who believe in Him. He prescribed His mercy for: ﴿those who fear Him and give *zakat* (obligatory almsgiving), and those who believe in Our verses, and those who follow the Messenger﴾ (7:156). These are the people of mercy, just as they are the doers of good. And as they did good, they are recompensed with excellence. Is the recompense of excellence anything but excellence? That is, is the recompense of one who worships his Lord well anything but that his Lord treats him well? Ibn Abbas said: "Is the recompense of one who says, 'There is no god but God,' and acts by what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought, anything but Paradise?"

Ibn Abi Shaybah and others have related, from the hadith of al-Zubayr ibn 'Adi, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Is the reward of good anything but good?﴾ Then he said: Do you know what your Lord says? They said: Allah and His Messenger know best. He said: He says: Is the reward of one whom I have favoured with monotheism anything but Paradise."

(Section)

As for the report about mercy (rahmah), which is feminine with the tā' marbūṭah, being described by the word "near" (qarīb), which is masculine, there are twelve approaches. We will mention them and explain what in them is sound, what is weak, and what is close to correct.

The first approach: the pattern fa'īl (faʿīl) is of two kinds. One comes in the sense of the active participle (fā'il), such as qadīr (capable), samīʿ (hearing) and ʿalīm (knowing). The other comes in the sense of the passive participle (mafʿūl), such as qatīl (slain) and jarīḥ (wounded), kaff khaḍīb (a dyed hand), ṭarf kaḥīl (a kohl-lined eye) and shaʿr dahīn (oiled hair); all of these have the sense of the passive. When it comes in the sense of the active participle, its analogy is that it takes the tā' with a feminine referent, not with a masculine one, like jamīl/jamīla (beautiful), sharīf/sharīfa (noble), ṣabīḥ/ṣabīḥa (handsome), ṣabī/ṣabiyya (young), malīḥ/malīḥa (comely), ṭawīl/ṭawīla (tall), and the like. When it comes in the sense of the passive, it either accompanies the noun it describes, such as rajul qatīl (a slain man) and imra'ah qatīl (a slain woman), or it stands alone without it. If it accompanies the described noun, the masculine and the feminine are alike in it, as in rajul qatīl and imra'ah qatīl. If it does not accompany the described noun, it takes the feminine form when it applies to a feminine noun, as in qatīlat banī fulān (the slain woman of the Banu so-and-so). From this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion ... and the strangled animal﴾. This is the ruling for fa'īl. The pattern fa'ūl is close to it in form and meaning, since both are alike in measure and in indicating intensity, and both occur in the sense of the active and the passive.

Since fa'īl is lighter, they dispensed with fā'il in the doubled (geminated) roots, such as jalīl (great), ʿazīz (mighty) and dhalīl (humble), out of their dislike for the heaviness of doubling. They would have said jālil, ʿāziz and dhālil, so they used fa'īl with the two identical consonants separated by a silent yā'. They did not use fa'ūl in this case, because fa'īl is lighter than it. Because of its lightness, the pattern fa'īl was also used regularly from the root fa'ula, such as sharīf, ẓarīf (witty), jamīl and nabīl (noble). There is no pattern of fa'ūl that is used regularly. Also because of its lightness, fa'īl occurs more often than fa'ūl among the names of Allah.

Indeed, al-Raḥīm, al-Qadīr, al-Ḥasīb, al-Jalīl, al-Raqīb and their like are more numerous than the words al-Ra'ūf, al-Ghafūr, al-Shakūr, al-Ṣabūr, al-Wadūd and al-ʿAfū, and there are no names beyond these six.

When the resemblance between fa'īl and fa'ūl has been established in what we have mentioned, and since they had specialised fa'ūl in the sense of the active participle by stripping it of the tā' which distinguishes the feminine from the masculine, and had made the masculine form serve for both, they said: rajul ṣabūr and shakūr, and imra'ah ṣabūr and shakūr, and their like. As for ʿadūw and ʿadūwa, that is anomalous. If the tā' is intended to express intensity, it attaches to both masculine and feminine, as in rajul ḥalūla and firūqa (a man who is very forbearing and very much given to parting), and a woman likewise. If fa'ūl has the sense of the passive, the tā' attaches to the feminine, as in ḥalūba and rakūba (a milked-she-camel and a ridden-she-camel).

Having established this, qarīb in the verse is fa'īl in the sense of the active participle, and the intended meaning is not "near" in the sense of qārib (approaching), but the general meaning of the active participle. Its due form would have been with the tā', but they treated it in the manner of fa'īl in the sense of the passive, and did not attach the tā' to it, just as fa'īl in the sense of the passive was treated in the manner of fa'īl in the sense of the active by taking the tā', as they said: khiṣlah ḥamīdah (a praiseworthy trait) and fa'lah dhamīmah (a blameworthy act), in the sense of maḥmūdah and madhmūmah. So they analogised by the tā' in jamīla and sharīfa, and they analogised qarīb to imra'ah qatīl (a slain woman), kaff khaḍīb (a dyed hand) and ʿayn kaḥīl (a kohl-lined eye) in not taking the tā', each of the two categories being analogised to the other.

A parallel to this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿He says: Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾ So ramīm (decayed), which is in the sense of the active participle, was analogised to imra'ah qatīl and its class. This approach is among the strongest paths to safety, and they rely on it. It has been objected to with three objections.

The first: this implies equating the intransitive with the transitive. The fa'īl in the sense of the passive is derived from the transitive verb, while the fa'īl in the sense of the active is derived from the intransitive verb, since that is the usual case with verbs whose middle vowel is ḍamma. So if the ruling of one were applied to the other, that would be an equating of the intransitive and the transitive, and that is impossible.

The second objection: if this is claimed in general, it is false; and if it is claimed only in particular cases, then what is the rule, and what is the distinction between where this usage is permissible and where it is not?

The third objection: the Arabs have used fa'īl in the sense of the passive with the tā', and have stripped it of the tā' in the sense of the active. Jarīr said, lamenting his maternal aunt:

"A fine companion you were, and you were a bow-string [for me] — I was with the call of the wild rocks' stones [i.e. the desert]."

So he stripped qarīn (companion) of the tā' while it is in the sense of the active. And he said:

"May the rain-cloud, which does not cease, water you wherever you have alighted, not one who is missed, with its cool and steady breezes."

So he attached the tā' to faqīdah (one missed), which is fa'īl in the sense of the passive, meaning "not one who is missed" (ghayr mafqūdah). Al-Farazdaq said:

"I treated her for two years, while she was near, I see her and she draws near to me many times and I sip [her]."

And they say: imra'ah fatīn, sarīḥ and harīt (a woman who is delicate/ruined), and they stripped it of the tā', and it is in the sense of the active. They said: imra'ah firūk, halūk, rashūf, anūf and raḍūf, and they stripped them, while they are in the sense of the active, like ṣabūr. They said imra'ah ʿarūb and stripped it also. Then they said imra'ah malūla and firūqa, and attached the tā' to it, while it is also in the sense of the active. The claim that the tā' here is for intensity has no evidence, since you have seen that fa'ūl and fa'īl are both shared in taking the tā' and in lacking it. So the claim that the form without the tā' is original and the form with it is anomalous is answered by a similar claim; and with the response there is the grammatical analogy of attaching the tā' to a feminine noun and stripping it from a masculine one. As for what you (plural) have cited as evidence, the words of the Exalted ﴿who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾, it accords with Arabic analogy: ʿiẓām is the plural of ʿaẓm (bone), which is masculine, but its plural is a broken plural (jam' taksīr), and a broken plural may be treated as a feminine collective. In accordance with this he said wa-hiya ("and it" in the feminine), and did not say wa-huwa. It may also be treated as the singular, and in accordance with this he said ramīm, as one says ʿaẓm ramīm (a decayed bone), although ramīm applies to the masculine both in singular and plural. Jarīr said:

"The family of al-Muhallab, may Allah cut off their root; they have become decayed, with neither root nor branch."

So this is the objection to this approach.

(Section)

The second approach: qarīb in the verse is from the category of interpreting a feminine noun as a masculine one that agrees with it in meaning, like the words of the poet:

"I saw a man among them, sorrowful, as if he were gathering to his flanks a dyed hand."

Here kaff (hand) is feminine, but it is interpreted as meaning "a limb" (ʿuḍw) and "a part" (ṭaraf), so its adjective is masculine. Likewise, raḥmah (mercy) is interpreted as "benevolence" (iḥsān), so its predicate is masculine.

They said: interpreting raḥmah as iḥsān is preferable to interpreting kaff as ʿuḍw, for two reasons. The first: raḥmah is a quality subsisting in the one who shows mercy, while iḥsān is the kindness done to the one shown mercy, and the meaning of nearness in kindness, from the two good qualities, is clearer than it is in mercy.

The second: considering iḥsān through raḥmah, described as near to the benevolent ones, is a counterpart to the benevolence that came from them. When the counterpart is taken into account, the meaning becomes stronger and the wording more forceful, so that it is as if He said: "Indeed Allah's benevolence is near to the people of benevolence," just as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Is the reward of good anything but good?﴾ (55:60). He mentioned qarīb so that it would be understood as an attribute of the masculine, namely iḥsān, and thus the desired counterpart is understood.

They said: among those who interpreted a feminine noun as masculine is what al-Farrā' recited:

"Battles in Muḍar, nine, and in Wā'il there were the tenth."

So he interpreted al-waqā'iʿ (battles), which is feminine, as the masculine "days of war", and so he made the number that goes with it feminine, saying tis'ah (nine). Without this interpretation he would have said tisʿ, since al-waqā'iʿ is feminine.

They said: if it is permissible to interpret a masculine noun as feminine, as in the view of the one who said jā'athu kitābī (my letter came to him), meaning ṣaḥīfatī (my document), and in the words of the poet:

"O rider whose mount is driven, ask the Banu Asad: what is this cry?"

meaning "what is this shout?", and although this takes the root as a branch, then it is more fitting and more appropriate that interpreting a feminine noun as masculine should be permitted, since it takes the branch as a root. This is a sound argument.

This has been objected to with two spurious and unbinding objections.

The first: if it were permissible to interpret a feminine noun as masculine that agrees with it, and the reverse, then one could say: "Zayd spoke to me," and "ʿAmr honoured me," and "Hind spoke to me," and "Zaynab honoured me," interpreting Zayd and ʿAmr as "self" and "body," and interpreting Hind and Zaynab as "person" and "shape." This is false. But this objection is not binding, because they did not claim that this is regular; they claimed only that it is something that may be used, and there is a difference between what is permissible at some times and what is regular, like the nominative of the agent and the accusative of the object. They did not claim it belongs to the second category.

Furthermore, this objection is answered by every case whose usage is permitted by a licence, which is not regular. These cases are too many to be mentioned here, and no grammarian at all denies them. Is this anything but an objection to the rules of Arabic through doubts and contradictions? The people of Arabic pay no attention to any of that. If they had said that every feminine noun may be interpreted as a masculine noun that agrees with it, and the reverse, the refutation would be valid. But they said only that interpreting one as the other is sometimes permissible for a benefit that the interpretation contains, like the benefit we mentioned in interpreting raḥmah as iḥsān.

The second objection: interpreting raḥmah as iḥsān is either taken literally or figuratively, and both are impossible. Raḥmah and iḥsān are different; the existence of one does not require the existence of the other, because raḥmah may exist in full in one who cannot do good, such as a helpless mother and the like. And iḥsān may come from one who has no mercy in his nature, such as a cruel king, who may do good to some of his enemies and others for the sake of his kingdom, although he has no mercy. Once it is clear that one of the two is separable from the other, it is not permissible to apply it to the other, neither literally nor figuratively. As for the literal sense, it is obvious. As for the figurative: its condition is that the figurative meaning come to mind, so that the mind may pass to it; and if it is separated from the literal, it does not come to mind.

This objection is more corrupt than the one before it, and it belongs to the category of obstinacy and contentiousness.

How does this compare with the view of most of the theologians (mutakallimūn) — and perhaps this objector is among them — that there is no meaning of mercy in the sense of an end except pure benevolence? As for the tenderness and compassion that exist among created beings, Allah is not described by them; His mercy is simply His benevolence. Yet we do not accept this view; rather, we affirm for Allah, the Exalted, mercy in its true sense, as He affirmed it for Himself, free and cleared of the particular qualities of created beings, just as we say about all His other attributes: His will, His hearing, His sight, His knowledge, His life and all the attributes of His perfection. We have mentioned this only to show the corruption of this objector's objection to the view of his own leaders and of those who hold the view of the theologians.

Then we say: mercy is never separated from the will for benevolence; it necessarily implies benevolence or the will for it, as a specific implies a general. Just as the existence of the specific without the general is impossible, so too the existence of mercy without benevolence or the will for it is impossible.

As for the case of the helpless mother: although she cannot actually do good, she is benevolent in intention, so her mercy is not separated from her complete will for benevolence, which is accompanied by what she is able to do, whether by prayer, or by giving preference with what she can do, and the like. So the failure of some of the benevolence she cannot perform to be with her mercy does not take her mercy out of its implying the benevolence within her capacity. This is clear. As for the cruel king: if he does good, his benevolence is not mercy. This is because benevolence is more general than mercy, and the more general does not imply the more specific. They did not claim that, so it is not binding upon them.

Furthermore, it may be said that benevolence implies mercy, and what that king did is not benevolence in reality, although its outward form is that of benevolence.

In sum: the obstinacy and contentiousness in this objection are too clear to require one to undertake a refutation and invalidation of it.

(Section)

The third approach: qarīb in the verse belongs to the category of omitting the noun modified and placing the modifier (the genitive) in its position, while keeping in mind the omitted word. It is as if He said: "Indeed the place of mercy is near to the benevolent," then He omitted "place" and gave "mercy" its grammatical case and masculine form. From this is the words of Ḥassān:

"They give to drink from the water of al-Buraiṣ, over them the Barada flows, mixed with the sealed wine."

He said yuṣaffiq with the yā' (masculine), and Barada is feminine, because he meant the water of Barada. From it is the words of the Prophet (ﷺ), when he took gold and silk in his hands and said: "These two are forbidden to the males of my community."

He said ḥarām (in the singular), while the subject is dual, as if he meant: "The use of these two is forbidden."

This approach is very weak, because omitting the noun modified and placing the genitive in its position cannot be asserted in every case; otherwise, the address would be confused, understanding would fail, and the evidences would be rendered useless. For every word of command, prohibition or statement that contains something commanded, forbidden, or reported, it would be possible, on this basis, to posit an omitted noun that removes it from the sphere of command, prohibition, or statement. For example, the one who denies the Qur'anic verse ﴿Pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by mankind﴾ would say that it means "knowledge of the pilgrimage to the House," and ﴿Fasting is prescribed for you﴾ would mean "knowledge of fasting." If this door is opened, discourse is corrupted and evidences are rendered useless. The omitted noun is supposed only where it is determined and the speech is not sound without estimating it, out of necessity, as when one says: "I ate the sheep," meaning "I ate its meat," so omitting the noun here causes no confusion. Likewise if you say: "So-and-so ate the wealth of so-and-so," meaning he consumed his property, the understood meaning is "he ate the fruit of his labour," so omitting the noun here causes no confusion, and there are many similar cases.

The verse ﴿And ask the town﴾ is not an example of this, although most of the usulis (scholars of legal theory) cite it as an example. The word "town" (qaryah) is a name for the inhabitants in a gathered dwelling; the word "town" is used in view of both aspects, like the cup (kaʾs) for what is in it of drink, the bucket (dhanūb) for a bucket full of water, the tray (khiwān) for the food-table when there is food upon it, and their like.

Then, because of their frequent use of this word and its circulation in their speech, they used it sometimes for the inhabitants and sometimes for the dwelling, according to the context and the scope of the discourse. They do this only where there is no ambiguity, no implication and no omission in it.

So consider this point, which has been hidden from the people, despite its clarity.

Given this, His words ﴿Indeed the mercy of Allah is near to the benevolent﴾ contain nothing in the wording that indicates the intention of a place or location at all. So it is not permissible to claim an omitted place; rather, the claim that it is omitted is definitely wrong, because it implies that the speaker intended the omitted word without any proof, neither explicit nor implicit, establishing his intention. So the claim of the one who asserts that He intended it is false.

As for the words "Barada flows": it is likewise not an example of omitting the noun modified. Rather, the poet meant by Barada the river, which is masculine, so he described it with a masculine attribute and said yuṣaffiq (flows). He did not make it masculine on the basis of an omitted noun; rather, he made it masculine because Barada here means the river.

If you say: there must be an omitted noun, because they only give to drink the water of Barada, not the river itself.

I answer: this would be so if it were the poet's meaning, but it does not follow that his claim is correct, namely that he used the masculine yuṣaffiq in consideration of the omitted water. For its masculine form is due only to intending the river, which is masculine, and so it does not support what they claimed.

As for the words of the Prophet (ﷺ), "These two are forbidden": there is a wonderfully subtle secret in using the singular for the predicate, which is to draw attention and indicate that each of the two, on its own, is described as forbidden. If the predicate were dual, there would be no such indication of this meaning. For this reason the predicate was made singular, as if he said: "Each one of these two is forbidden," so the singular predicate indicates the intention of reporting about each one individually.

Reflect on this, for it is among the wonders of the language. This has been explained earlier in this commentary in the question of "kilā and kiltā" (both), and that their saying "kilāhumā qā'im" (both of them are standing) with the singular predicate does not indicate that kilā is singular, as the Basrans hold; rather, it is truly dual. They used the singular predicate only to show that the predication applies to each of the two, standing. We have established this with sufficient explanation.

(Section)

The fourth approach: it is from the category of omitting the described noun and placing the adjective in its position, as if He said: "Indeed the mercy of Allah is a thing near to the benevolent," or "a gentle act near to them," or "a kind act near to them," and the like. Omitting the described noun is common. From this is the words of the poet:

"She wept over his grave, saying: Who will be for me after you, O ʿĀmir?
You left me in the house as one of estrangement; he who has no helper is humbled."

The meaning is: you left me as a person or a human being, in estrangement. Otherwise she would have said: "You left me estrangement." And another:

"Had you, in a day of ease, asked me to part from you, I would not have withheld it, though you are a friend."

He meant: "though you are a person or a human being, a friend."

On this approach Sibawayh based the saying used of a woman: ḥā'iḍ (menstruating), ṭāmith (menstruating) and ṭāliq (divorced). He said: "It is as if they said: a thing that menstruates and a thing that menstruates." This approach is also weak, for three reasons.

The first: omitting the described noun and placing the adjective in its position is good only under two conditions: the adjective must be a specific quality known to belong to that particular described noun and not to anything else.

The second: that the attribute has come to be used predominantly on its own, without the thing it describes, such as *al-barr* (the righteous) and *al-fājir* (the wicked), *al-ʿālim* (the knowing) and *al-jāhil* (the ignorant), *al-muttaqī* (the God-conscious), *al-rasūl* (the messenger) and *al-nabī* (the prophet), and similar words, where the attribute has become customarily used without the noun, so that the noun is scarcely mentioned with it. Such is His saying: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss. And indeed, the wicked will be in the Blazing Fire﴾. And His saying: ﴿Indeed, the God-conscious will be in gardens and springs﴾. And His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and the Muslim women, the believing men and the believing women﴾. And His saying: ﴿And the disbelievers — they are the wrongdoers﴾. This is very frequent in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Arabs. Without this, it is not good to limit oneself to the attribute alone. It is not good to say, "Tall came to me," or "I saw beautiful or ugly," meaning "A tall man came to me," and "I saw a beautiful or ugly man." Nor does one say, "I dwelt near," meaning "in a near place," since the act of dwelling indicates the place.

The second (point): that *shayʾ* (thing) is the most general of the known things, for it includes the necessary and the possible. Therefore there is no added benefit in estimating it or in pronouncing it, by which the speech would be eloquent and articulate, let alone that it would reach the highest levels of eloquence and rhetoric. What eloquence and rhetoric is there in the saying of one who says, of a woman who menstruates (*ḥāʾiḍ*), (*ṭāmith*), and (*ṭāliq*, divorced): "A thing menstruating, a thing *ṭāmith*, a thing divorced"? Even if he declared it openly, the listener would find it repugnant. How, then, can one suppose in the speech an intention that it contains no benefit at all? For being a "thing" is a known, general matter that indicates neither praise nor blame, nor perfection nor deficiency.

Here one must be alert to a matter that cannot be avoided: it is not permissible to interpret the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, merely by the grammatical (*naḥwī*) and inflectional (*iʿrāb*, grammatical parsing) possibility that the structure of the sentence allows, such that the sentence would have some meaning. For most of those who parse the Qur'an have erred in this station. They explain the verse and parse it according to what the structure of that sentence may bear, and from that structure they derive whatever meaning happens to fit. This is a grave error, which convinces the listener that the intended meaning of the Qur'an is other than that. Even if that structure bears this meaning in another context and in other speech, it does not follow that the Qur'an bears it. Such is the saying of some concerning the reading of one who recited ﴿*wa-l-arḥāma*, indeed Allah has been watching over you﴾ with the genitive (*jarr*), that it is an oath (*qasam*). And such is the saying of some concerning His saying: ﴿and obstructing from the way of Allah, and disbelief in Him, and the Sacred Mosque﴾, that *al-masjid* is in the genitive by coordination with the pronoun in *bihi* (in Him). And such is the saying of some concerning His saying: ﴿But those firm in knowledge among them, and the believers, believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, and the establishers of prayer﴾, that *al-muqīmīn* is in the genitive by the *wāw* of oath. The parallels to these are many times more than what we have mentioned, and far weaker. Rather, the Qur'an has a specific usage and known meanings, and it is not fitting to explain it by other than these, nor is it permissible to interpret it contrary to its usage and its established meanings. The relation of its meanings to meanings is like the relation of its words to words, indeed greater. Just as its words are the kings of words, the most majestic and the most eloquent, possessing the highest degree of eloquence which the capacities of all creatures are unable to match, so too its meanings are the most majestic, the greatest, and the most magnificent of meanings. Therefore it is not permissible to explain it by other meanings that are unworthy of it, for other meanings are greater, more majestic, and more magnificent than them.

Thus it is not permissible to read into it meanings that are deficient, merely on the basis of a grammatical or inflectional possibility.

Reflect on this principle and keep it in mind, for you will benefit in recognizing the weakness of many sayings of the exegetes and their falsity, and you will be certain that they are not what the Speaker, Exalted is He, intended by His speech. We shall, if Allah wills, expand on this and explain it at length in discussing the principles of exegesis (*uṣūl al-tafsīr*), for this is one of its principles, indeed the most important of them.

The third aspect: the ta' of *ṭāliq*, *ḥāʾiḍ* and *ṭāmith* is omitted only because there is no need for it. The ta' was introduced to distinguish the masculine from the feminine where confusion might arise. When the attribute is specific to the feminine, there is no confusion, and so there is no need for the ta'. This is the correct view.

This is the view of the Kufan school (*al-madhhab al-Kūfī*).

If you say: "This contradicts the school of Sibawayh."

I say: "So what? Would a discerning person prefer to reject the implication of a sound proof merely because it contradicts the saying of a specific scholar?"

This is the method of bats. As for the people of insight, they never reject a proof and its implication for the sake of a particular opinion, though they are few. There is no doubt that Abu Bishr (may Allah have mercy on him) excelled in this science with the highest stake, won the most distinguished precedence, and took possession from its field of what no other had possessed. He is the one who has prayed in this arena. But that does not mean one must believe that he encompassed all the speech of the Arabs, or that no truth exists except what he said.

How many texts of Sibawayh have been opposed by the majority of his companions, and by its most distinguished? If we were to mention them, the discussion would be long.

And do not forget his saying in the chapter on the attribute resembling the active participle (*al-ṣifa al-mushabbaha*): "I passed by a man *ḥasan* (beautiful) *wajhuhu* (his face)," with *ḥasan* being annexed to *al-wajh* and *al-wajh* to the pronoun, and his opposition to all the Basrans and Kufans in this. Sibawayh (may Allah have mercy on him) is among those whose words are taken and left. As for holding that his saying is correct in everything, that is not so.

If Allah wills, we shall devote a separate book to adjudicating between the Basrans and the Kufans in what they differed on, and explaining the preferred view among them. And success and support are from Allah.

If you say: "It is sufficient to refute what you have chosen concerning *ṭāmith*, *ḥāʾiḍ* and *ṭāliq* from the Kufan school, the saying of Allah: ﴿On the Day you see it, every nursing mother will be distracted from what she nursed﴾."

This is an attribute specific to females, and it has come with the ta'.

I say: "There is no refutation of this school in this, nor any nullification of it, praise be to Allah. For the presence of the ta' here carries a benefit that is not achieved without it, so its use is necessary. That benefit is that *al-murḍiʿa* (the nursing mother) means the one who performs the action of nursing. So the intended meaning is the act, not merely the attribute, and it is not the bare attribute of being one of those who nurse. Had that been intended, it would have said *murḍiʿ* like *ḥāʾiḍ* and *ṭāmith*. Do you not see that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Allah does not accept the prayer of a menstruating woman except with a veil'? The intended meaning there is the one described as belonging to the category of menstruating women, not the one whose blood is flowing. Thus *ḥāʾiḍ* and *murḍiʿ* are general attributes that apply to one who has that attribute, even if it is not actually occurring in her, and they apply to one in whom it actually occurs. The ta' is introduced here to signal that the intended meaning is the one who actually performs nursing, for she is distracted from what she nurses because of the intense terror of the earthquake of the Hour."

And this meaning is reinforced by His saying: ﴿what she nursed﴾.

So it is known that the intended meaning is the nursing mother who is actually nursing, not one who is nursing in potential or readiness. The preference for this school has another place.

(Section)

The fifth approach: that this is from the category of the annexed noun (*al-muḍāf*) acquiring the judgment of the noun it is annexed to, when the first is able to be omitted and dispensed with by the second. Such is the saying of the poet:

*When the news of al-Zubayr came, the walls of Medina and the humble mountains humbled themselves.*

And another said:

*They walked as the spears swayed, their tips swaying, the gentle winds passing over them.*

And another said:

*The insolence of souls, restoring their blessings to them as vengeance, though it has spread and its delusion has lasted.*

So in the first, *al-sūr* (the walls), annexed to *al-madīna* (Medina), is feminine; in the second, *al-marr* (the passing), annexed to *al-riyāḥ* (the winds), is feminine; and in the third, *al-baghy* (insolence), annexed to *al-nufūs* (souls), is feminine, because the annexed-to noun is feminine. Although the masculine is the origin and the feminine is the derivative, the origin is made to follow the derivative. Therefore it is more fitting that a feminine noun be made masculine because it is annexed to a non-feminine noun, for that makes the derivative follow the origin.

From the first category also is the poet's saying:

*And it chokes on the matter that it has spread, as a spear-shaft's chest chokes with blood.*

Here he made *al-ṣadr* (the chest) feminine because it is annexed to *al-qanāh* (the spear-shaft).

One of our companions recited to me, from Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm, on this meaning, with a chain I do not recall:

*Avoid a friend like one you should beware of, the one whose enmity is like ʿAmr between the Arabs and the non-Arabs.*

*For the friend of evil is destroyed, and my witness is as a spear-shaft's chest chokes with blood.*

From this category also is the saying of al-Nābigha:

*Until they sought help from the people of the salt-flats, at dawn, running as their ropes of the leather pads were loosened.*

And from it is the saying of Labīd:

*So he went forward with them, and it was his habit, whenever their feet turned back, ...*

And this approach, although some excellent scholars have accepted it, is not strong. For it is only known to occur in poetry, and in eloquent speech only rarely, like their saying: *dhahabat baʿḍu aṣābiʿihi* (some of his fingers went). What strengthens it here is the close connection between the annexed noun and the annexed-to noun, and that the first is in reality a part of the second. It is as if he said: "A finger and two fingers of his fingers went." But placing the Qur'an upon what is rare, whose opposite is more eloquent, is not easy.

(Section)

The sixth approach: that this is from the category of dispensing with one of the two mentioned in favour of the other, because it is subordinate to it and one of its meanings. When one of them is mentioned, the other is dispensed with because it is understood from it.

Among its instances, according to one of the interpretations, is His saying: ﴿If We willed, We would send down upon them a sign from the heaven, and their necks would remain humbled before it﴾. So the predicate of *al-aʿnāq* (the necks) is dispensed with by the predicate about their owners.

Among its instances, according to one of the interpretations, is His saying: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾. The meaning is: "Allah has more right that they should please Him, and His Messenger likewise." So by restoring the pronoun to Allah, He dispensed with saying "that they should please them both," since pleasing Him is pleasing His Messenger.

Accordingly, the basic form of the verse is: "Indeed Allah is near to the good-doers, and the mercy of Allah is near to the good-doers." Thus the predicate of the omitted noun is dispensed with by the predicate of the mentioned noun, and the clarity of the meaning permits this.

This approach is a fine one when it is clothed in a better expression than this. It is a subtle approach, delicate for understanding, and it is among the secrets of the Qur'an.

What should be expressed by it is: mercy is one of the attributes of the Lord, Blessed and Exalted, and an attribute subsists in the one described and never leaves him, for an attribute does not separate from what it describes. So if mercy is near to the good-doers, the One described, Blessed and Exalted, is more worthy of nearness to them. Indeed, the nearness of His mercy follows from His own nearness, Blessed and Exalted, to the good-doers.

It was mentioned at the beginning of the verse that Allah, Exalted, is near to the people of goodness by rewarding them, and near to those who ask Him by answering them, and we mentioned the evidences for this. Goodness requires the nearness of the Lord to His servant, just as the servant's goodness brings him near to his Lord. Whoever draws near to Him a span, Allah draws near to him a cubit, and whoever draws near to Him a cubit, He draws near to him an arm's length. So the Lord, Blessed and Exalted, is near to the good-doers, and His mercy is near to them; His nearness entails the nearness of His mercy. Therefore the omission of the ta' here is a reminder of this great and sublime benefit: that Allah is near to the good-doers, and this entails both nearnesses, His nearness and the nearness of His mercy. Had it said, "Indeed the mercy of Allah is near to the good-doers," it would not indicate His own nearness to them, because His nearness is more specific than the nearness of His mercy, and the more general does not entail the more specific, unlike His nearness, which, being more specific, entails the more general, namely the nearness of His mercy. So do not belittle this approach, for it has a great standing and includes a wondrous secret of the Book. I do not think the proponent of this approach intended this meaning or was aware of it. He only meant that the report of Allah's nearness to the good-doers suffices in place of reporting the nearness of His mercy to them.

So this is the seventh approach to the verse, which is the preferred one, and it is among the most fitting of what has been said about it.

If you wish, you may say: His nearness, Blessed and Exalted, to the good-doers and the nearness of His mercy to them are mutually entailing; neither can be separated from the other. So if His mercy is near to them, He is also near to them. And when the two meanings are mutually entailing, it is valid to intend each of them. Thus, to explain His nearness, Glorified is He, to the good-doers, is to urge goodness and call souls to it and encourage them to it, providing the greatest share and the most noble and exalted benefit for them absolutely. It is the finest gift a servant can receive: His nearness, Blessed and Exalted, to His servant, which is the ultimate of hopes, the final goal of aspirations, the coolness of eyes, the life of hearts, and the entire happiness of the servant. So in turning from "near" (*qarība*) to "near" (*qarīb*) there is an invitation to goodness and an encouragement of souls toward it, such that none who is left behind after it except one overcome by his own wretchedness. And there is no power except through Allah.

(Section)

The eighth approach: that mercy is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), and verbal nouns, just as they are not dualized or pluralized, should not be feminized. This approach is very weak, for Allah, whenever He mentions mercy, makes it feminine, as in His saying: ﴿And My mercy has encompassed all things, so I will prescribe it for those who are God-conscious﴾, and His saying, related from His Messenger (ﷺ): "Indeed My mercy has overcome or preceded My wrath." Had the omission of the ta' in *raḥma* been because it is a verbal noun, and verbal nouns have no feminine quality, the pronoun referring to it would only be masculine. The same applies to verbal nouns with a ta' such as *qudra* (power), *irāda* (will), *ḥikma* (wisdom), *himma* (aspiration), and their like. The falsity of this shows the falsity of this approach.

(Section)

The ninth approach: that *qarīb* may refer to two things. The first is lineage and kinship, and in this sense one uses the ta': one says "she is a near relative (*qarība*) of mine." The second is nearness of place, and in this sense one omits the ta': one says, "So-and-so sat near me (*qarīban minnī*)," and one does not say "qarība minnī." This is the approach of al-Farrāʾ (may Allah have mercy on him) and a group. But this too is weak, for this applies only when the word *qarīb* is used as an adverb of place (*ẓarf*), in which case it is used without the ta', as he said: "One says: 'The woman sat near me (*qarīban*).'" But when it is a pure noun, it does not apply.

(Section)

The tenth approach: that the feminine of mercy, since it is not a real feminine, permits the omission of the ta', just as one says "the sun rose" (*ṭalaʿa al-shamsu*) and "she rose" (*ṭalaʿat*). This approach too is corrupt. For this applies only when the verb is attributed to an apparent feminine noun. But when it is attributed to a pronoun referring to it, the ta' is necessary, as in your saying: "The sun rose (*ṭalaʿat*)," and you say: "The sun is rising (*ṭāliʿa*)," and you do not say *ṭāliʿ*, because the attribute contains its pronoun, so it is equivalent to the verb in this respect.

(Section)

The eleventh approach: that *qarīb* is a verbal noun, not an attribute, and it is in the position of an opposite, so it is stripped of the ta', because when you describe a feminine noun with a verbal noun, the ta' is not attached to it. Hence you say: "a woman who is *ʿadl*" (just), and you do not say *ʿadla*; "a woman who is *ṣawm*" (fasting), *ṣalāt* (praying), *ṣidq* (truthful), *birr* (dutiful), and similar words.

This approach is among the most corrupt of what has been said about *qarīb*, for its use as a verbal noun is not known at all. It is purely an attribute, and the verbal noun is *qurb*, not *qarīb*.

(Section)

The twelfth approach: that *faʿīl* and *faʿūl* in general are used equally for masculine and feminine, whether the referent is real or not, as Imru' al-Qays said:

*A soft, plump, tender, supple one, like the shoot of the willow that has sprouted.*

*Slender in stature, languid in speech, when she smiles she reveals a row of teeth.*

And he also said:

*Woe to him, if he has fallen, and not the mother of Hashim, nor al-Basbasa, daughter of Yashkur, is near.*

And Jarir said:

*Will life benefit you when Umm ʿAmr is far, neither visiting nor visited?*

And Jarir also said:

*As if we had not fought, O Babithin, had she uncovered her grief, and you are a friend.*

And he also said:

*They called us to passion, then they pledged our hearts with arrows of enemies, and they are friends.*

They said: "Examples of this are numerous." In this approach there is sufficiency from those forced interpretations and suppositions.

This approach too is weak. Among those who rejected it was Abu ʿAbd Allah ibn Malik, who said:

"This view is weak, for its proponent either means that *faʿīl* in this place and elsewhere deserves what *faʿūl* deserves, namely to be applied to masculine and feminine with a single form, or he means that *faʿīl* in this place specifically is to be understood as *faʿūl*. The first is rejected, because the grammarians agree on the obligation of the ta' in *ẓarīfa* (witty), *sharīfa* (noble), and similar words, both in form and in meaning. For this reason, their scholars had to say, concerning His saying: ﴿Your mother was not unchaste (*baghiyyan*)﴾, and His saying: ﴿I was not unchaste (*baghiyyan*)﴾, that the original is *baghawī* on the pattern of *faʿūl*, and therefore the ta' is not attached to it; then it was altered by changing the *wāw* to *yāʾ* and the *ḍamma* to *kasra*, so its form became like that of *faʿīl*. Had *faʿīl* been the original, the ta' would have been attached, and it would have been said: *lam akun baghiyya* (I was not an unchaste woman). The second also is rejected, because *faʿīl* has advantages over *faʿūl* that do not fit it to be subordinate to it. Rather, it is more proper for *faʿūl* to be subordinate to *faʿīl*. Moreover, it implies that *faʿīl* is treated as *faʿūl*, though they differ in form and in meaning. As for form, it is obvious. As for meaning, *qarīb* carries no intensification, for it is applied to anyone who has nearness, however slight. But *faʿūl* must have intensification. Also, what indicates intensification must have a base form without intensification, and then intensification is intended by altering that form, as in *ḍārib* and *ḍarūb* (much-hitting), *ʿālim* and *ʿalīm* (all-knowing). But *qarīb* is not like this, so it carries no intensification.

As for Imru' al-Qays's verse, it is not a proof, for several reasons.

First: it is rare, and rarity has no ruling. It is not accepted as a basis when its forms are few and it does not follow the norm, like *istaḥwadha* (he acquired control), *istawthaqa al-baʿīr* (the camel became secured), *aghyamat al-samāʾ* (the sky became clouded), *aghwara* (he went deep), and *aḥwal* (he squinted). Whatever is like this has no ruling.

Second: he may have meant *qaṭīʿat al-qiyām* (one who cuts off standing), then dropped the ta' for the annexation, for dropping it is permitted according to al-Farrāʾ and others, and on this basis is interpreted His saying: ﴿and the establishment of prayer﴾, meaning *iqāmatuhā* (its establishment), since what is well known in this case is the term *al-iqāma*."

I say "iqam" without an added noun is not used, just as "irad" is not said for "irada" (will) or "iqal" for "iqala" (dismissal), because they made this ta' a substitute for the alif of the ifal form or for its middle radical. The original of iqama is iqwam, so the movement of the middle radical was moved to the first radical, it became an alif, two alifs met, one was deleted, and they brought the ta' as a substitute. So it became obligatory except with a genitive construction (idafa). Its deletion is permitted according to some, by analogy (qiyas), and according to others, by transmitted usage (sama').

Similar to it in obligatoriness is the ta' of 'idda and wizna. Their origins are wa'd and wazn, the waw was deleted, and the ta' was made a substitute for it, so it became obligatory. It may be deleted for idafa, as in the words of the poet:

"Indeed the companions have prepared for separation and departed, and they have failed you the promise of the matter they had promised."

That is, "they have failed you the 'idda (promise) of the matter," so the ta' was deleted.

On this dialect some reciters read: "And had they intended to go out, they would have prepared for it 'uddah (equipment)," with the ha', meaning 'uddatahu (its equipment), so the ta' was deleted.

The third: that fa'il in His words "qatiu al-qiyam" means maf'ul (passive), because the author of al-Muhkam reported that it is said qatha'uhu and aqta'ahu when one silences him, and he is qati' al-qawl (silenced in speech). So qatii, on this reading, means maqtu' (silenced), that is, mubakkit, so deleting the ta' on this interpretation is not contrary to analogy.

And if qatii is taken as built on qata', like sari' from saraa', then its rule would be that the ta' attaches to it when it is applied to the feminine, but it was made similar to fa'il that means maf'ul, and treated accordingly.

This is the completion of twelve approaches to this verse. The soundest of them is the combined approach of the sixth and seventh. The rest are weak, flawed, or merely possible, and the beginner and the imitator do not grasp these subtleties, while the discerning and fair-minded scholar does not miss which of them is strong and which is weak.

Let this be the end of the discussion of the verse, and God knows best.

**Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 7, verses 57–58:**
