Then He mentioned another analogy: that some land is good ground, so when We send down water upon it, it brings forth its vegetation by the permission of its Lord, while other land is wicked and yields its vegetation only meagrely (*nakidan*), meaning sparsely and without benefit. When water is sent down upon this second kind, it does not produce what the good land produces. He, glorified is He, likened the revelation (*al-wahy*) that He sent down from heaven upon the hearts to the water that He sent down upon the earth, in that life is obtained through both. He likened the hearts to the earth, since they are the place of deeds just as the earth is the place of plants. The heart that does not benefit from revelation, does not grow pure through it, and does not believe in it is like the land that does not benefit from rain and produces only a little vegetation with it that is of no use. The heart that believes in revelation, grows pure through it, and acts upon what is in it is like the land that brings forth its vegetation by the rain. So when the believer hears the Qur'an, understands it, and reflects upon it, its effect appears in him. He is likened to the good town that flourishes, becomes fertile, and in which the effect of the rain is excellent, so that it grows every noble pair (*min kulli zawjin karim*). The one who turns away from revelation is the opposite of this. And Allah is the Granter of success.

**(A wonderful benefit)**

*Kull* (كل, "all/each") is a word indicating encompassment of a thing, as if it derives from the words *al-iklil* (crown), *al-kalalah*, and *al-kullah*, which all carry the sense of encircling something. It is a single word in its form but plural in its meaning. Had its meaning not been plural, it would not be permissible to use it to emphasize a plural, because emphasis (*tawkid*) is a repetition of the emphasized element, so it must match it: if the thing is plural, the emphasis is plural, and if it is singular, the emphasis is singular. Its proper construction is to be followed by an indefinite noun that is common within its category, since it demands encompassment. If you attach it to a definite noun, as in your saying *kull ikhwatika dhahib* ("all your brothers are going"), it is poor usage except at the beginning of a sentence. This is because when it is the subject (*mubtada'*) in such a position, its predicate is given in the singular, as a reminder that its original form is to be attached to an indefinite noun, since the indefinite noun is common within the category. It also requires a category that it encompasses. So you may say *kullu wahidin min ikhwatika dhahib* ("each one of your brothers is going"), and the singular predicate indicates the original meaning, which is its attachment to a singular indefinite noun. If you do not make it the subject and attach it to a definite clause, as in *ra'aytu kulla ikhwatika* ("I saw all your brothers") and *darabtu kulla al-qawm* ("I struck all the people"), it does not have the same beauty as what preceded, because you have not attached it to a category, and there is no singular predicate in the sentence that indicates attachment to a category, as in their saying *kulluhum dhahib* ("all of them are going") and *kullu al-qawmi 'aqil* ("all the people are wise"). If you attach it to a category made definite by *al-* (the definite article), as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿So We brought forth thereby fruits of every kind﴾, it is good, because the *al-* here marks the category, not a specific known referent. Were it for a known referent, it would be poor, as when you say *khudh min kulli al-thamarat allati 'indaka* ("take from all the fruits that you have"). This is because, if it is a definite, known clause and you want the sense of encompassment in it, the better course is to keep the sentence in its original form and emphasize the definite noun with *kull*, saying *khudh min al-thamarat allati 'indaka kulliha* ("take from the fruits you have, all of them"). This is because you have not been forced to remove it from emphasis, as you were forced with an indefinite noun when you said *laqitu kulla rajul* ("I met every man"), since an indefinite noun is not emphasized, and it is also common within its category, as already mentioned.

If it is asked: when the two constructions are equal, as in your saying *kull min kulli al-thamarat* and *kull min al-thamarat kulliha*, why is one of the two arrangements specific to the Qur'an in one place and not another?

It is answered: this does not follow, because each of them is eloquent, but there must be a benefit in the specificity.

As for the words of the Exalted ﴿So We brought forth thereby fruits of every kind﴾, the *min* (مِن) here is for specifying the genus (*li-bayan al-jins*), not for partitioning (*lil-tab'idh*), and the prepositional phrase is in the position of the object, not the position of an adverb. What is meant is the fruits themselves, except that He brought forth some of them and inserted *min* to indicate the whole genus. Had He said *akhrajna bihi min al-thamarat kulliha* ("We brought forth thereby from the fruits, all of them"), it would occur to the mind that the prepositional phrase is in the position of an adverb and that the object of *akhrajna* comes afterwards. That would not be suspected with *kull* placed first, because the addressees know that *kull*, when placed first, indicates encompassment of the genus, and when placed after and used as emphasis, it indicates encompassment of the emphasized element specifically, whether that element is a common genus or a known, recognized referent.

As for the words of the Exalted ﴿kulli min kulli al-thamarat﴾ and why it did not say *min al-thamarat kulliha*, the wisdom in it is the same as in the verse before it, with an additional benefit. Before it in the composition the Exalted said ﴿and from the fruits of the palm trees and the grapes﴾. Had He said after it *kuli min al-thamarat kulliha*, the mind would think He meant the fruits mentioned before this, namely "the fruits of the palm trees and the grapes", because the definite article (*al-*) is only understood as referring to what has already been mentioned. So beginning with *kull* was more protective of the meaning, more comprehensive of the genus, more effective in avoiding ambiguity, and more wondrous in the composition. So reflect on it.

When *kull* is detached from its attachment and taken without it, its proper place is to be the beginning of a sentence, and its predicate is to be plural. It must have people mentioned before it, because if no sentence is mentioned before it and it is not attached to a clause, its sense of encompassment is void and it has no meaning. The reason it must have a plural predicate is that it is a noun with the sense of plurality. So you say *kullun dhahibuna* ("all of them are going") when a group has already been mentioned, because you rely on them for meaning, even though you are informing about *kull*. It is like your saying *al-rahtu dhahibun* and *al-nafaru muntaliqun*: *al-rahtu* and *al-nafaru* are singular nouns but carry the sense of the plural. The evidence for what we have explained is the words of the Exalted ﴿and each in an orbit is swimming﴾, ﴿each to Us will be returning﴾, and ﴿and each were wrongdoers﴾.

If *kull* is attached in form to what follows it, you will find its predicate only singular, for the wisdom mentioned earlier, which is that its original form is attached to a singular indefinite noun. So you say *kullu ikhwatika dhahib*, meaning each one of them is going. This is not required when you detach it from the attachment, so you say *kullun dhahibuna*. This is because its reliance, when it is standing alone, is on those mentioned before it and on what has the sense of plurality, whereas its reliance, when attached, is on a singular noun, either explicitly or in implication. Such is the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is answerable for his flock", narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim, where he did not say *ru'a'un wa mas'ulun* (shepherds and answerable). From the same is *kulluhum sayarwi* ("each of them will narrate"), and from the same is the saying of Umar: "Or does each of you have two garments?" where he did not say *tajiduna* (do you find). Similar is the words of the Exalted ﴿Everyone upon it will perish﴾, and the words of the Exalted ﴿all are devoutly obedient to Him﴾, where He used the plural, and the words of the Exalted ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾.

If it is said: the Qur'an has ﴿Each acts according to his manner﴾ and ﴿each denied the messengers﴾, and this contradicts what we have established? It is answered: in these two verses there is an indication that restricts the meaning to this form and not another. As for the words of the Exalted ﴿Say: each acts according to his manner﴾, it is because before it there is mention of two opposing groups, believers and wrongdoers. Had He said *ya'malun* (they act) and given the plural in reporting about them, the sense of difference would be void, so the singular form was more indicative of the intended meaning, as if He were saying: each one, he acts according to his manner. As for the words ﴿each denied the messengers﴾, it is because He mentioned generations and nations and concluded their mention with the people of Tubba'. Had He said *kullu kadhabu* (all denied), and *kull* when singular is relied on for the nearest of the mentioned things to it, the mind would think that the report about the people of Tubba' alone is that they denied the messengers. When He said ﴿each denied﴾, it was known that He meant each group among them, because the singular predicate whenever *kull* occurs indicates this meaning, as already explained. Similar is ﴿each believed in Allah﴾.

As for what we said about *kull* when it is detached from attachment, that its proper place is to be a beginning: what is meant is that it is a beginning about which something is reported, or a beginning in wording that is in the accusative governed by a verb after it, not before it, or in the genitive whose governing preposition is connected to what follows it, as in ﴿and to each God promised the best﴾, and in the words of the poet:

*"With every [remedy] we have treated [it]..."*

It is disliked to put the governing verb before it when it is singular, as in your saying *darabtu kullan* ("I struck each") and *marartu bi-kull* ("I passed by each"). If you say *kullan darabtu* and *bi-kull marartu*, it is not disliked, because placing the governing element before it separates it from the mentioned thing before it in wording. This is because a verbal governor has the front of the sentence, and when you separate it from what precedes it in wording, it has nothing to rely on before it or after it, so that is disliked. But if the governor is conceptual, as in *kullun dhahibuna*, it does not separate it from the mentioned things before it, because it has no existence in wording. So if you say *darabtu Zaydan wa 'Amran wa Khalidan wa shatamtu kullan wa darabtu kullan* ("I struck Zayd, 'Amr, and Khalid, and I insulted each and struck each"), it is not permitted and does not return to a predicate, for the reason we have mentioned.

Once you know this, your saying *kull ikhwatika darabtu* ("I struck all your brothers") whether it is in the nominative or accusative, implies that the striking fell on each one of them. If you say *kull ikhwatika darabani* ("all your brothers struck me"), it also implies that each one of them struck you. If you say *kull ikhwati darabuni* ("all my brothers struck me") and *kull al-qawm ja'uni* ("all the people came to me"), it allows the sense that they were together in the striking and the coming, and it allows that the striking and coming were each individually. This is because you reported about their whole body with a predicate that falls on the whole. This differs from your saying *kull ikhwanika ja'ani* ("each of your brothers came to me"), which is a report about each one of them, and the report about the coming is about all of them. So reflect on the words of the Exalted ﴿Say: each acts according to his manner﴾ and how He made the predicate singular, because it was not intended that they gather in it. And the words of the Exalted ﴿each to Us will be returning﴾ are plural, because the coming was intended as a collective. This is better than the distinction previously mentioned, so reflect on it.

The words of the Exalted ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him﴾ are not an objection to this. Rather, it confirms it and serves as evidence, because the devout obedience (*qunut*) here is the general servitude shared by the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth. It is not restricted to some of them over others, nor to one time over another. It is the servitude of compulsion (*qahr*), so the *qunut* here is the *qunut* of subjugation and humiliation, not the *qunut* of obedience and love. This differs from the words of the Exalted ﴿Everyone upon it will perish﴾, where the predicate is singular because they do not gather in perishing.

Similar is the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "and each of you is answerable for his flock", for God questions each shepherd individually.

Among what came plural because the predicate gathers is the words of the Exalted ﴿each in an orbit is swimming﴾.

Among what came singular because the predicate does not gather is the words of the Exalted ﴿The people of Noah, 'Ad, Pharaoh of the stakes, Thamud, the people of Lot, and the companions of the thicket before them denied; those are the factions. Each one denied the messengers, so My punishment was deserved﴾, where He used the singular because they did not gather in denial.

Similar is in Surah Qaf: ﴿each denied the messengers, so My promise was deserved﴾.

Reflect on how He uncovered this meaning and made it fully clear with the words of the Exalted ﴿and each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone﴾, where He made *atihi* ("will come to Him") singular, since the intention was to indicate that although they all come to Him, each one of them is separate from every companion, relative, or associate, and is alone in his own affair. So it is as if he comes to Him alone, even though he comes with others, because his following of others has ended and he stands independently with regard to himself. In my view this is better than the distinction by attachment and detachment. The distinction by that is the distinction of al-Suhayli, may Allah have mercy on him. So reflect on both distinctions, and you will read the examples and evidences.

**[Section: The Punishment for Sodomy]**

Since the corruption of sodomy (*liwat*, intercourse between men) is among the greatest of corruptions, its punishment in this world and in the Hereafter is among the greatest of punishments.

People have differed over whether it is more severe in punishment than fornication (*zina*), whether fornication is more severe than it, or whether their punishments are equal. There are three views:

The first view, held by Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Ali ibn Abi Talib, Khalid ibn al-Walid, Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, Abdullah ibn Abbas, Khalid ibn Zayd, Abdullah ibn Ma'mar, al-Zuhri, Rabi'a ibn Abi Abd al-Rahman, Malik, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, Imam Ahmad (according to the more authentic of the two reports from him), and al-Shafi'i (according to one of his two opinions), is that its punishment is more severe than the punishment for fornication, and its punishment is execution in all cases, whether the offender is married (*muhsan*) or not.

The second view, held by Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, al-Hasan al-Basri, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Qatada, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i (according to the apparent position of his school), Imam Ahmad (according to his second report), Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad, is that its punishment and the punishment of the fornicator are the same.

The third view, held by al-Hakim and Abu Hanifa, is that its punishment is less than the punishment for fornication, and it is discretionary punishment (*ta'zir*).

They said: Because it is one of the sins for which Allah and His Messenger ﷺ did not prescribe a fixed penalty (*hadd*), so it is subject to discretionary punishment, like eating carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine.

They said: And because it is intercourse in a place that human nature does not desire; rather, Allah Most High has constituted natures to recoil from it, even among beasts. Therefore there is no fixed penalty for it, like intercourse with a female donkey or other animals.

They said: And because it is not called "fornicator" (*zani*) linguistically, legally, or by custom, so it does not enter the texts that establish the penalty for fornicators.

They said: We have observed the principles of the Sharia: when the restraint against a sin is natural, the restraint is considered sufficient and no fixed penalty is needed; and when human nature inclines toward it, the fixed penalty is set in proportion to that inclination. For this reason, fixed penalties were prescribed for fornication, theft, and drinking intoxicants, but not for eating carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine.

They said: The consequence of this principle is that there is no fixed penalty for intercourse with an animal or with a corpse. Allah, glory be to Him, has created human nature to recoil from a man's intercourse with a man like himself, with the greatest recoil, just as He created it to recoil from a man being sought for intercourse; unlike fornication, where the desire is present on both sides.

They said: And because when one of the two parties derives pleasure from the other's form, no fixed penalty is obligatory for him, as when two women rub against each other (*tasahuq*) and each derives pleasure from the other.

The proponents of the first view, who constitute the majority of the Community, and whom more than one scholar reported as a consensus of the Companions, said: There is no sin more corrupt than this corruption, and it is second only to the corruption of disbelief (*kufr*). It may even be greater than the corruption of murder, as we will explain, Allah willing.

They said: Allah Most High did not test any of the worlds with this major sin before the people of Lot, and He punished them with a punishment He did not inflict on anyone else. He combined upon them various kinds of punishments: destruction, overturning their dwellings upon them, causing the earth to swallow them, and pelting them with stones from the sky. He made an example of them with a punishment He did not inflict on any other nation. This was due to the enormity of the corruption of this crime, by which the earth nearly shakes from its sides when it is committed upon it, and the angels flee to the far regions of the heavens and the earth when they witness it, fearing that the punishment will descend upon its people and strike them along with them. The earth cries out to its Lord, blessed and exalted, and the mountains nearly shift from their places.

Killing the one who is sodomized is better for him than having him violated, for when the offender violates him, he kills him with a killing from which life is not hoped, unlike killing him, for he is then an oppressed martyr, and perhaps he will benefit from it in the Hereafter.

They said: The evidence for this is that Allah, glory be to Him, made the punishment for murder subject to the choice of the victim's guardian: if he wishes he may execute, and if he wishes he may pardon. But He made the execution of the sodomite a mandatory fixed penalty, as the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ agreed, and as the clear Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ indicates, which has no contradiction. Indeed, the practice of his Companions and his rightly-guided Caliphs is in accordance with it, may Allah be pleased with them all.

It is established from Khalid ibn al-Walid that he found in one of the outlying areas of the Arabs a man who was being taken in marriage as a woman is taken. So he wrote to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. Abu Bakr consulted the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. Ali ibn Abi Talib was the most emphatic among them in his opinion. He said: "No one does this except a single nation among the nations, and you know what Allah did to them. I think he should be burned with fire." So Abu Bakr wrote to Khalid, and he burned him.

Abdullah ibn Abbas said: "One should look for the highest building in the town, and the sodomite should be thrown from it headfirst, then pursued with stones."

Abdullah ibn Abbas took this penalty from the punishment Allah inflicted on the people of Lot. And Ibn Abbas is the one who narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Whoever you find doing the deed of the people of Lot, kill the doer and the one it is done to."

This was narrated by the compilers of the Sunan, and Ibn Hibban and others authenticated it. Imam Ahmad cited this hadith as evidence, and its chain of transmission meets the criteria of al-Bukhari.

They said: It is also established from him ﷺ that he said: "May Allah curse whoever does the deed of the people of Lot. May Allah curse whoever does the deed of the people of Lot. May Allah curse whoever does the deed of the people of Lot." Yet there is no report from him of cursing the fornicator three times in a single hadith. He cursed a group of major sinners, but he did not exceed one curse with them. He repeated the curse of the sodomites and emphasized it three times.

The Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ agreed upon killing him; not two of them differed about it. Their opinions differed only regarding the manner of his execution. People thought that this was a disagreement among them about his killing, so they reported it as a matter of dispute among the Companions, when among them it is a matter of consensus, not of dispute.

They said: Whoever reflects on the words of Allah, glory be to Him: ﴿And do not approach fornication; indeed, it is an abomination and an evil way﴾ [al-Isra' 17:32],

and His words about sodomy: ﴿Do you commit an abomination that no one in the worlds has committed before you?﴾ [al-A'raf 7:80],

will see the difference between them. He, glory be to Him, used the indefinite form for *fahisha* (abomination) in the case of fornication, meaning it is an abomination among abominations; and He used the definite form for it in the case of sodomy. This indicates that it comprises all the meanings of the term *fahisha*, just as you say: "Zayd is the man" (*Zayd al-rajul*) and "What a man Zayd is" (*ni'ma al-rajul Zayd*). That is: "Do you commit the trait whose vileness is established in the sight of everyone?" Its vileness is so manifest and complete that it needs no mention, such that the term is not applied to anything other than it. This is similar to Pharaoh's words to Moses: ﴿And you did your deed, the deed you did﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:19]. That is: the hideous deed, manifest and known to everyone.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, emphasized the gravity of its abomination by stating that no one in the worlds had committed it before them: ﴿no one in the worlds has committed it before you﴾. Then He increased the emphasis by declaring explicitly what hearts recoil from, what ears turn away from, and what natures shun with the greatest aversion: a man's coming to a man like himself, having intercourse with him as one has intercourse with a female. He said: ﴿Indeed, you approach men﴾ [al-A'raf 7:81].

Then He drew attention to their having no need for it, and that what drives them to it is nothing but mere desire, not the need for which the male inclines toward the female, nor the fulfillment of need and the pleasure of enjoyment, nor the attainment of affection and mercy, by which a woman forgets her parents and remembers her husband, nor the attainment of offspring, which is the preservation of this species, the most noble of creatures, nor the protection of women and the fulfillment of their needs, nor the establishment of the bond of marriage, which is the sister of lineage, nor the men's guardianship over women, nor the emergence from their intercourse of the most beloved of creation to Allah, such as the prophets, the friends of Allah, and the believers, nor the Prophet ﷺ's boasting of his community before the other prophets, nor other benefits of marriage. The corruption in sodomy counterbalances all of that and exceeds it by an amount whose corruption cannot be enumerated, and whose details none knows but Allah.

Then He emphasized the ugliness of this by stating that the sodomites reversed the nature (*fitra*) that Allah created men upon, and inverted the disposition that Allah placed in males, which is desire for females rather than males. So they reversed the matter and inverted the nature and disposition, coming to men with desire in place of women. For this reason, Allah, glory be to Him, overturned their dwellings upon them, making its uppermost part its lowest, and in the same way they were overturned, and they were turned upside down in the punishment onto their heads.

Then He, glory be to Him, emphasized the ugliness of this by judging them as transgressors (*musrifun*), which means exceeding the limit: ﴿Rather, you are a people who transgress﴾ [al-A'raf 7:81].

So reflect: has anything like this, or close to it, come in regard to fornication?

Allah, glory be to Him, further emphasized this against them by His words: ﴿And We saved him from the town that used to commit the vile deeds﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:74].

Then Allah, glory be to Him, emphasized the condemnation against them with two descriptions of utmost ugliness, saying: ﴿Indeed, they were a people of evil, defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:74].

He called them corrupters in the words of their prophet: ﴿My Lord, support me against the corrupting people﴾ [al-Ankabut 29:30].

He called them wrongdoers in the words of the angels to Abraham: ﴿Indeed, we will destroy the people of this town; indeed, its people have been wrongdoers﴾ [al-Ankabut 29:31].

So reflect on who has been punished with such punishments, and whom Allah has condemned with such condemnations.

When His intimate friend Abraham disputed with the angels concerning them, after they had informed him of their destruction, it was said to him: ﴿O Abraham, turn away from this; indeed, the command of your Lord has come, and indeed, a punishment will come to them that cannot be averted﴾ [Hud 11:76].

Reflect on the depravity of the sodomites and the extremity of their rebellion against Allah, when they came to their prophet Lot after hearing that guests had come to him, who were among the most beautiful of human beings in form. The sodomites came to him hurrying. When he saw them, he said to them: ﴿O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you﴾ [Hud 11:78].

He ransomed his guests with his daughters, offering to marry them to them, out of fear for himself and his guests from the severe disgrace. He said: ﴿O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear Allah and do not disgrace me regarding my guests. Is there not among you a single right-minded man?﴾ They replied to him, but with the reply of a tyrannical obstinate one: ﴿You know well that we have no right to your daughters, and you know well what we want﴾ [Hud 11:79].

Then the Prophet of Allah breathed out a sigh, like one afflicted, a breath that came from a distressed heart, and he said: ﴿If only I had power against you, or could take refuge in a strong support﴾. The messengers of Allah relieved him of the reality of the situation, informing him that they were of those who could not be reached, neither could the sodomites reach him through them. So he should not fear them, nor be concerned with them, and should calm himself. They said: ﴿O Lot, indeed we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you﴾. They gave him good news of what they had come with: the promise for him and his people, and the sure threat for them. They said: ﴿So travel with your family in the dark of night, and let none of you look back, except your wife; indeed, she will be struck by what strikes them. Indeed, their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?﴾ [Hud 11:81].

The Prophet of Allah was slow to anticipate the time of their destruction, and said: "I want it sooner than this." The angels said: ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾. By Allah, the time between the destruction of the enemies of Allah and the deliverance of His Prophet and his allies was no more than the time between the pre-dawn meal and the rising of dawn. Suddenly their dwellings were uprooted from their foundations and raised toward the sky, until the angels heard the barking of dogs and the braying of donkeys. Then the decree that cannot be turned back came from the presence of the Majestic Lord to His servant and messenger Gabriel, to overturn them upon them, as He had told in the well-guarded revelation. Then the Mighty and Majestic One said: ﴿So when Our command came, We made its uppermost part its lowest and rained upon it stones of hard clay, layered, marked from your Lord﴾ [Hud 11:82].

He made them a sign for the worlds, an admonition for the God-conscious, and a warning and a precedent for whoever shares their deeds among the criminals. He made their dwellings a road for travelers: ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for those who perceive. And indeed, it is on a road that remains. Indeed, in that is a sign for the believers﴾ [al-Hijr 15:75–77].

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 7, verse 80 (part 2 of 2):

He seized them unawares while they were sleeping, and His punishment came upon them while they were in their intoxication, wandering blindly, and what they had earned did not avail them. So that pleasure turned into pains, and they were punished by it.

Desires that were in life for their people became a torment, and in death they became a torment.

Pleasures passed away, leaving regrets behind; lusts came to an end, leaving wretchedness as their inheritance. They enjoyed a little, and were punished for a long time. They grazed in a pasture of ruin, so He brought upon them a painful punishment. The wine of those lusts intoxicated them, and they did not come to themselves from it except in the abodes of the punished. That heedlessness put them to sleep, and they did not awaken from it except while they were in the dwellings of the perished. So they regretted, by Allah, with the utmost regret, at a time when regret avails nothing, and they wept over what they had sent ahead, shedding blood instead of tears. Had you seen the highest and the lowest of this group, with fire coming out from the openings of their faces and their bodies, while they were among the layers of the Blazing Fire, and they were drinking cups of boiling water instead of delicious drinks, and it was said to them while they were being dragged on their faces: ﴿Taste what you used to earn. Burn in it, so be patient or be not patient; it is all the same for you. You are only being recompensed for what you used to do﴾ [al-Tur: 16].

Allah, glorified is He, has brought close the distance of punishment between this nation and their brethren in deeds, and so He said, warning them that the threat may befall them: ﴿And it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾ [Hud: 83].

O you who marry males, may the good tidings bring you joy; for on the Day when people are resurrected, you will have a reward.

Eat, drink, copulate, and act like Lot, and rejoice; for you have a sigh (zafar) toward the Garden of the red (wine).

Your brethren have prepared the abode before you, and they have said: "Hasten to us, and the good tidings are for you."

Here we are, your predecessors, awaiting you.

The Almighty will gather us in His Great Fire. And do not suppose that those whom you have married

will be absent from you; rather you will see them plainly.

And each of you will curse his companion, and the one who is saddened will suffer in the other world

on account of him. Each of you will be punished by his partner, just as the two of you shared in a pleasure that brings guilt.

[Section: The Remedy for Sodomy]

If it is said: Is there, with all this, a remedy for this incurable disease? And an incantation for this deadly enchantment? And what is the strategy for averting this corruption? Is there a direct path to success? Can one intoxicated with the wine of desire be made to recover? Does the lover still control his heart when passion has reached its core? And for the physician, after that, is there a means of healing him from his core? And if a blamer blames him, he delights in his blame as a remembrance of his beloved; and if a reproacher reproaches him, his reproach spurs him on, and he travels with him on the path of his desire, while the witness of his state calls out upon him with the tongue of his speech:

Desire brought me to a halt where you are, and I have neither one who lags behind it nor one who goes before it.

You humiliated me, and I, striving, humiliated myself; for whoever is humbled by you is not one who is honored.

You resembled my enemies, so I came to love them, since my share from you is like my share from them.

I find blame for your sake sweet, out of love for remembering you; so let the blamers blame me.

And perhaps this is what is meant by the first question, on which the fatwa was sought, and the disease for which a remedy was requested.

It is said: Yes. The answer from the outset is: "Allah, glorified is He, has not sent down any disease except that He has appointed for it a remedy," known by whoever knows it and unknown to whoever does not know it.

The discussion of the remedy for the disease of the heart's attachment to aerial (fleeting) love is in two ways:

The first: cutting off its source before it occurs.

The second: uprooting it after it has descended. Both are easy for whomever Allah facilitates them for, and impossible for whomever Allah does not help, for the reins of affairs are in His hands.

As for the means preventing the occurrence of this disease, there are two matters:

Lowering the gaze, as has preceded, for a glance is a poisoned arrow from the arrows of Iblis, and whoever lets loose his glances, his regrets persist.

The second means preventing the heart's attachment from occurring: occupying the heart with what turns it away from that and comes between it and falling into it. This is either a disquieting fear or an agitating love. Whenever the heart is free of fear of losing something whose loss would harm it more than obtaining this beloved, or fear of obtaining something whose obtaining would harm it more than losing this beloved, or love of what is more beneficial and better for it than this beloved, whose loss would harm it more than the loss of this beloved, it will find no alternative to falling in love with forms.

The explanation of this: the soul does not abandon a beloved except for a higher beloved, or out of fear of a hated thing whose occurrence would harm it more than the loss of this beloved. This requires its possessor two matters; if he lacks them or one of them, he will not benefit himself.

The first: a sound insight by which he distinguishes between the degrees of the loved and the hated, so that he prefers the higher of two loves over the lower, and endures the lesser of two hatreds to be freed from the greater. This is the special quality of intellect, and whoever is opposite to this is not counted as intelligent; rather, cattle may be in a better state than him.

The second: strength of resolve and patience by which he is able to do or abandon this act. Often a man knows the degree of difference, but the weakness of his soul, his aspiration, and his resolve refuse him, on account of his baseness, his greed, the lowliness of his soul, and the meanness of his aspiration, to act upon what benefits him. Such a person does not benefit himself, nor does anyone else benefit from him. Allah, glorified is He, has made leadership in religion impossible except for people of patience and certainty, and He said, the Exalted, and by His word the guided among them are guided: ﴿And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient and were certain of Our signs﴾ [al-Sajdah: 24].

This is the one who benefits by his knowledge, and by whom people benefit; its opposite is not benefited by anyone else. Among people is one who benefits by his knowledge for himself but whom no one else benefits by. The first walks in his light, and people walk in his light; the second, his light has been extinguished, so he walks in darkness and whoever follows him walks in his darkness; and the third walks in his light alone.

(Benefit)

The companions of Ahmad said: "If the Imam sees fit to burn the sodomite with fire, then he may do so when he sees fit, for Khalid ibn al-Walid wrote to Abu Bakr that he had found in some outlying area of the Arabs a man who was mounted as a woman is mounted. So he consulted the companions of the Prophet ﷺ, and Ali ibn Abi Talib, who was the most severe in speech among them, said: 'This sin has not been committed by any nation except one, and Allah did with them what you know. I see that they should be burned with fire.'"

So the opinion of the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ agreed that they should be burned with fire. Abu Bakr wrote to Khalid ibn al-Walid that they should be burned, and then Ibn al-Zubayr burned them, and then Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik burned them.

And Ahmad stated concerning one who reviles the Companions that it has become obligatory upon the ruler to punish him, and the ruler does not have the right to pardon him; rather he should punish him and ask him to repent. If he repents, well and good; otherwise the punishment is repeated upon him.

[Section: Sins Erase Blessing]

Among its punishments is that they erase the blessing of one's life, the blessing of provision, the blessing of knowledge, the blessing of deeds, and the blessing of obedience.

In sum, they erase the blessing of both religion and worldly life. You will not find anyone with less blessing in his life, his religion, and his worldly affairs than one who disobeys Allah. The blessing has been erased from the earth only by the sins of creatures. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been mindful of Allah, We would have opened for them blessings from the heaven and the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 96].

And He the Exalted said: ﴿And [if] they had remained upright on the way, We would have given them abundant water, that We might test them thereby﴾ [al-Jinn: 16-17].

Indeed, a servant may be deprived of provision because of a sin that afflicts him.

And in the hadith: "Indeed, the Holy Spirit (Ruh al-Qudus) breathed into my heart that no soul will die until it has completed its provision. So fear Allah and seek [provision] graciously, for what is with Allah cannot be attained except through obedience to Him. Indeed, Allah has placed ease and joy in contentment and certainty, and has placed distress and grief in doubt and displeasure."

The narration that Ahmad mentioned in the Kitab al-Zuhd has already been cited: "I am Allah. When I am pleased, I bless, and My blessing has no end; and when I am angry, I curse, and My curse reaches the seventh generation of offspring."

The abundance of provision and of deeds is not by their quantity, nor is the length of life by the number of months and years; rather, the abundance of provision and the length of life lie in the blessing within them.

It has already been established that a servant's life ('umr) is the duration of his existence. There is no true life for one who turns away from Allah and occupies himself with other than Him. Indeed, the life of beasts is better than his life, for a human's life is by the life of his heart and spirit. The heart has no life except through knowing its Originator, loving Him, worshipping Him alone, turning to Him in repentance, being at peace through His remembrance, and finding intimacy in His nearness. Whoever loses this life has lost all good, even if he were to be compensated for it with whatever is in this world. Indeed, the entire world is not a compensation for this life. For everything that escapes a servant there is a substitute, but if Allah escapes him, nothing whatsoever can substitute for Him.

How can one who is poor in essence be compensated for the one who is rich in essence, the powerless in essence for the powerful in essence, the dead for the Living who never dies, the created for the Creator, and one who has no existence and nothing of his own essence whatsoever for the One whose sufficiency, life, perfection, existence, and mercy are necessary attributes of His essence? And how can one who does not possess an atom's weight be compensated for the One to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth?

The reason disobedience to Allah causes the erasure of the blessing of provision and of one's term is that Satan is charged with it and with its people. His authority is over them, and their affairs are referred to this register (diwan), its people and its companions. Everything with which Satan is connected and associated loses its blessing. For this reason, the mention of Allah's name has been prescribed at eating, drinking, dressing, riding, and intercourse, because of the blessing in associating Allah's name with them. Mentioning His name drives away Satan, so blessing is obtained without any opposition to it. Everything that is not for Allah has its blessing removed, for the Lord alone is the One who blesses, and all blessing is from Him. Everything attributed to Him is blessed: His speech is blessed, His Messenger is blessed, His believing servant who benefits His creation is blessed, His Sacred House is blessed, and the land of His Shām (Syria), which is the land of blessing, is blessed, for He described it with blessing in six verses of His Book. There is no one blessed except Him alone, and nothing is blessed except what is attributed to Him, meaning attributed to His divinity, His love, and His good pleasure. Otherwise, all existence is attributed to His lordship and creation. Whatever distances itself from Him, whether in substances, statements, or deeds, has no blessing and no good in it. Whatever is closer to Him than that has blessing in proportion to its nearness to Him.

The opposite of blessing is curse. A land that Allah has cursed, a person Allah has cursed, or a deed Allah has cursed is the furthest thing from good and blessing. Whatever is connected to that, bound to it, or has a path to it, has no blessing whatsoever.

Allah cursed His enemy Iblis and made him the furthest of His creatures from Him. Whatever is in his direction receives a share of Allah's curse in proportion to its nearness to him and its connection with him. From here, sins have the greatest effect in erasing the blessing of life, provision, knowledge, and deeds. Every time you disobeyed Allah, or any wealth with which Allah was disobeyed, or any body, status, knowledge, or deed, it belongs to its owner in a way that is not truly his. So he has from his life, wealth, strength, status, knowledge, and deeds only what he used to obey Allah.

For this reason, among people there is one who lives in this abode a hundred years or so, yet his life does not reach twenty years or so in reality. Likewise, among them is one who owns heaps of gold and silver, yet his wealth in reality does not reach a thousand dirhams or so. The same applies to status and knowledge.

In al-Tirmidhi, from him (ﷺ): "The world is cursed, and what is in it is cursed, except the remembrance of Allah and what accompanies it, or a scholar or a student."

In another report: "The world is cursed, and what is in it is cursed, except what is for Allah." This is what alone contains blessing. And Allah is the One sought for help.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 7, verse 99:

Even if a servant reaches the highest level of obedience, it is not fitting for him to be free of this caution (al-hadhar). The best of His creation and the chosen among His servants feared it. Shu'ayb (ﷺ), when his people said to him, ﴿O Shu'ayb, we will surely expel you and those who believed with you from our town, or you will return to our religion.﴾ He said, ﴿Even though we are unwilling? We would have invented a lie against Allah if we returned to your religion after Allah has saved us from it.﴾ up to his words ﴿In Allah we have put our trust.﴾ [al-A'raf: 88-89], he referred the matter to the will and knowledge of Allah, out of good manners toward Allah, recognition of the right of lordship (rububiyyah), and standing within the limit of servanthood (ubudiyyah). Likewise Ibrahim (ﷺ) said to his people, when they frightened him with their gods, ﴿And I do not fear what you associate with Him, unless my Lord wills something. My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge.﴾ [al-An'am: 80], so he referred the matter to the will and knowledge of Allah. Allah the Exalted has also said, ﴿Do they feel secure from the plan of Allah? None feels secure from the plan of Allah except the losing people.﴾ [al-A'raf: 99].

The early scholars (al-salaf) differed on whether it is disliked for a servant to say in his supplication: "O Allah, do not make me feel secure from Your plan (makr)?"

Some of the salaf used to supplicate with this, and their intent was: do not abandon me, so that I feel secure from Your plan and do not fear it. Mutarrif ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Shikhkhir disliked it.

Imam Ahmad said: 'Abd al-Wahhab related to us from Ishaq, from Mutarrif, that he disliked saying: "O Allah, do not make me forget Your remembrance, and do not make me feel secure from Your plan." Rather he would say: "O Allah, do not make me forget Your remembrance, and I seek refuge in You from feeling secure from Your plan, until You are the one who makes me secure."

In summary: whoever is left to himself has been subjected to a plan against him.

Imam Ahmad said: Abu Sa'id, a client of the Banu Hashim, related to us; al-Salt ibn Tarif al-Mi'wali related to us; Ghaylan ibn Jarir related to us, from Mutarrif, who said: "I found this human being placed between Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and Satan. If Allah the Exalted knows good in his heart, He draws him to Himself; and if He does not know good in him, He leaves him to himself. Whoever is left to himself has perished."

Ja'far ibn Sulayman said: Thabit related to us, from Mutarrif, who said: "If my heart were taken out and placed in this left hand, and good were brought and placed in this right hand, and then I were brought close to the other, I could not insert anything into my heart until Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, places it."

Among what shows that joy is one of the causes of (divine) plotting, when it is not accompanied by fear, is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the doors of every thing until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and they were then in despair.﴾ [al-An'am: 44]

And the people of Qarun said to him, ﴿Do not exult; indeed, Allah does not love the exultant.﴾ [al-Qasas: 76]. So joy, whenever it is in Allah and in what Allah has bestowed, accompanied by fear and caution, does not harm its possessor; and whenever it is devoid of that, it inevitably harms him.

Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 7, verse 143:

Allah, glorified and exalted, has told us about the one among the people of the earth who had the greatest knowledge of Him in his time, namely His interlocutor (kalim), His confidant (najiy) and His chosen one (safiy), that he asked his Lord, exalted is He, to let him look upon Him. His Lord, blessed and exalted, said to him: ﴿You will not see Me, but look at the mountain; if it remains firm in its place, then you will see Me.﴾ But when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust (dakk).

The evidence from this verse is in several respects:

The first: It is not to be supposed of the interlocutor of the Most Merciful and His noble messenger that he would ask his Lord for something impermissible for Him, rather for what is among the most false of falsehoods and the greatest of impossibilities. According to the philosophers (furukh al-Yunan), the Sabians and the Pharaonists, it is on a par with asking Him to eat, drink, sleep and the like, from which Allah is exalted. So how strange it is that the followers of the Sabians, the Magians and the idol-worshipping polytheists, and the offshoots of the Jahmiyya and the Pharaonists, should become more knowledgeable about Allah, exalted is He, than Musa ibn Imran, and about what is impossible for Him and what is necessary for Him, and more emphatic in declaring Him free of imperfection than he was!

The second aspect: Allah, glorified and exalted, did not reject his request. Had it been impossible, He would have rejected it. For this reason, when Ibrahim the Friend (Khalil) asked his Lord, blessed and exalted, to show him how He gives life to the dead, He did not reject it. When 'Isa ibn Maryam asked his Lord to send down a table (ma'idah) from heaven, He did not reject his request. But when Nuh asked his Lord to save his son, He rejected his request and said: ﴿I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant.﴾ ﴿He said: My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge; and unless You forgive me and have mercy on me, I will be among the losers.﴾

The third aspect: He answered him with His saying ﴿You will not see Me﴾, and did not say "You cannot see Me," nor "I am not to be seen," nor "My seeing is not permissible."

The difference between the two answers is evident to whoever reflects upon it.

This indicates that He, glorified and exalted, can be seen, but that Musa's faculties could not bear seeing Him in this world, because of the weakness of human strength in it to see Him, exalted is He, as the following makes clear.

The fourth aspect, which is His saying ﴿But look at the mountain; if it remains firm in its place, then you will see Me﴾: He informed him that the mountain, despite its strength and solidity, cannot remain firm when He manifests Himself to it in this world, so how about frail man, who was created from weakness?

The fifth aspect: Allah, glorified and exalted, is capable of making the mountain remain firm in its place. This is not impossible in His power; rather it is possible. He has made seeing Him contingent upon it. Had seeing Him been impossible in its very essence, He would not have made it contingent upon something possible in itself. And had seeing been impossible, it would be akin to saying: "If the mountain remains firm, then I will eat, drink and sleep." Thus, by your reckoning, the two matters are equal.

The sixth aspect: His saying, glorified and exalted, ﴿When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust﴾. This is among the clearest proofs of the permissibility of seeing Him, blessed and exalted. For if it is permissible for Him to manifest Himself to the mountain, which is inanimate, having neither reward nor punishment, how could it be impossible for Him to manifest Himself to His prophets, messengers and friends in the abode of their honour, and show them Himself? Thus Allah, glorified and exalted, informed Musa that if the mountain could not remain firm at His seeing in this world, then human beings are weaker.

The seventh aspect: His Lord, glorified and exalted, has spoken to him directly, addressed him, conversed with him in private and called to him. Whoever is permitted to speak and to be spoken to, and to have his addressee hear his speech directly without an intermediary, seeing Him is all the more permissible. For this reason, denying the seeing is not complete except by denying the speaking. These sects have combined the denial of both matters: they deny that He speaks to anyone or that anyone sees Him. This is why Musa, peace be upon him, asked Him to be seen, and He made him hear His speech. The prophet of Allah knew the permissibility of seeing Him from the occurrence of His addressing him and speaking to him; He did not inform him of its impossibility, but showed him that what he asked for, he could not bear, just as the mountain did not remain firm at His manifestation. As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You will not see Me﴾, it indicates only negation in the future, and does not indicate perpetual negation, even if it were qualified by eternity (ta'bid), so how much more so when it is unqualified? He, exalted is He, says: ﴿But they will never wish for it (the death), ever﴾, together with His saying: ﴿And they will call out: O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us!﴾

Consider the state of Moses, the one who spoke with God (al-Kalim), and the trials and tribulations (fitan) that befell him from his birth until the end of his affair, until God spoke to him directly (takliman), brought him near to Himself, wrote the Torah for him with His own hand, and raised him up to the highest of the heavens. And God overlooked from him what He would not overlook from anyone else. He threw the Tablets upon the ground until they shattered; he seized the beard of the Prophet of God, Harun (Aaron), and dragged him toward himself; he slapped the face of the Angel of Death so that he gouged out his eye; and on the night of the Isra' (Night Journey) he disputed with his Lord concerning the affair of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and his Lord loved him for all of that. Nothing fell from him in the eyes of God, nor did his station with Him diminish; rather, he is the honoured one (al-wajih) before God, the one brought near. Had it not been for his earlier virtues (sawabiq), his bearing of hardships and great trials for the sake of God, and his enduring of the severe affair between Pharaoh and his people, and then the Children of Israel and the harm they inflicted on him, and his patience with them for the sake of God, that would not have been the case.

Then consider the state of the Messiah (al-Masih), his patience with his people, his forbearance for the sake of God, and what he endured from them, until God raised him up to Himself, purified him from those who disbelieved, took vengeance on his enemies, scattered them throughout the land, tore them to every shred, and stripped them of their kingdom and their pride until the end of time.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 7, verse 155:

Allah's words, ﴿And Musa chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time﴾, mean: he chose from among them. With this, the answer is given to the question raised by the Qadariyyah, who say: regarding disbelief and acts of disobedience, are they occurring by Allah's choice or without His choice? If you say they occur by His choice, then everything chosen is pleased with, chosen and beloved, so they would be pleasing and beloved to Him. And if you say they occur without His choice, then they did not occur by His will and choice.

The answer to this is to say: What do you mean by "choice" (al-ikhtiyar) in the general sense in the terminology of the theologians (al-mutakallimun), which is will and volition (al-mashi'ah and al-iradah)?

Or do you mean by it the specific choice found in the Qur'an, the Sunnah and the speech of the Arabs?

If you mean the first, then they occur by His choice in this sense, but it is not permissible to apply that term to them, because the word ikhtiyar contains the meaning of selection and love. Rather, it is said that they occur by His will and power. And if you mean by choice its meaning in the Qur'an and the language of the Arabs, then they do not occur by His choice in this sense, although they occur by His will.

If it is said: Do you say that they occur by His will (iradah) or do you not apply that term?

It is said: The word iradah (will) in the Book of Allah is of two kinds: a universal, cosmic will (iradah kawniyyah), encompassing all creatures, such as His words: ﴿Doer of what He wills﴾, and His words: ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town﴾, and His words: ﴿If Allah intends to lead you astray﴾, and similar examples; and a religious, prescriptive will (iradah diniyyah amriyyah), whose intended object is not necessarily realized, such as His words: ﴿Allah intends for you ease﴾, and His words: ﴿And Allah intends to accept your repentance﴾. Thus it is willed in the first sense and not willed in the second sense.

Likewise, if it is asked: Do they occur by His permission or not?

Permission (al-idhn) is also of two kinds: cosmic, such as His words: ﴿And they will not harm anyone thereby except by the permission of Allah﴾, and religious, prescriptive, such as His words: ﴿Has Allah permitted you?﴾ and His words: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against because they have been wronged﴾.

The word ikhtiyar is derived from khayr (good), which is the opposite of sharr (evil). Since the fundamental nature of a living being is that it wills what benefits it and what is good, will was called ikhtiyar. This implies that will as choice does not prefer one kind over another except by a factor that inclined the agent toward that kind.

The point is that knowledge is mentioned alongside specifications, as in the words of Allah: ﴿And We chose them with knowledge over the worlds﴾.

There is no disagreement among people that the meaning is "with knowledge from Us that they are people of choice," so the phrase is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: We chose them knowing them and their circumstances, and what their choosing requires from the time of their creation.

He (glorified is He) mentioned their being chosen and the wisdom in His choosing them, and He mentioned His knowledge, which indicates the places of His wisdom and His choice.

(Benefit)

The original usage of "ikhtara" (to choose) is that it takes a prepositional particle, because it implies extracting something from something. It came elided in His words: ﴿And Musa chose from his people﴾, because the verb includes the meaning of an intransitive verb, as if he sifted his people, distinguished them, tested them, and similar. Hence, and Allah knows best, the preposition was dropped, as in "amartuka al-khayr" (I bade you the good), meaning I obligated you and charged you, since command is obligation and charge. From this also: "tamurrun al-diyar" (you pass by the abodes), meaning you cross over and pass them; and "rahibtuka al-diyar" (the abodes made you spacious), meaning they widened for you.

(Another Benefit)

In the pattern of "ikhtara", the usual practice is to front the prepositional phrase and delay the direct object that is not introduced by a preposition. So you say "ikhtara min al-rijal Zaydan" (he chose Zayd from among the men), and it is permissible to delay it. But when you drop the particle, it is not good to delay what was originally governed by the preposition, so it is ugly to say "ikhtara Zaydan al-rijal" and "ikhtara 'ashratan al-rijal" (meaning: from the men), because it creates the impression that the prepositional phrase is an adjective of "ashrah" and not in the position of the second object. Also, "al-rijal" is definite, so it deserves to be fronted for emphasis, as is required when a prepositional phrase that is a predicate of an indefinite noun is fronted, as in "fi al-dar rajul" (there is a man in the house), since the prepositional phrase is definite and is in effect the topic. So when you drop the preposition, there is no alternative to fronting the noun that was formerly governed, as in "ikhtara al-rijal 'ashratan". The wisdom in this is that the meaning which prompted dropping the preposition is a non-verbal meaning, so it could only bear the dropping of the preposition when it was attached to and close to the verb. A second point: when a small number chosen from a larger one is something divisible, and it is followed by the verb "ikhtara", it may be understood that it is also chosen from among it, because whatever is divisible may be chosen and may be chosen from. So they required the delay and fronted the noun from which the choice is made, which was more fitting for that reason. If it is something indivisible, such as Zayd and 'Amr, it may be permitted, though rarely, in speech, as in the poet's verse:

"And among us is the one whom men were chosen for generosity."

This is not like your saying "ikhtara faraso al-khayl" (he chose a horse of the horses), because "faras" is a generic noun and may be divided like that, and one may choose from it. "Zayd," insofar as he is a body, is divisible, and insofar as he is a proper name for a specific thing, is not divisible. So reflect on this point.

(Question) What did Musa intend by his words: ﴿Had You willed, You could have destroyed them before and me﴾ [al-A'raf: 155]?

Various views have been given on this:

Al-Suddi said: When they died, Musa stood weeping and saying: O Lord, what shall I say to the Children of Israel when I come to them and You have destroyed their best?

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: I chose from them seventy men, the best of the best; shall I return to them with not a single man of them with me? What then will they believe me about, or entrust me with, after this?

On this view, the meaning is: Had You willed, You could have destroyed them before our departure, so that the Children of Israel would witness it and not accuse me.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: Had You willed, You could have destroyed them before You tested them with what made the quake obligatory for them.

I say: All of these circle around the intended meaning.

What appears to me, and Allah knows best His intent and the intent of His Prophet, is that this is a plea by Musa, peace be upon him, to his Lord, and an appeal to Him by His pardon of them earlier, when their people worshipped the calf and they did not denounce them.

Musa says: Something has already occurred from them that calls for their destruction, yet with this Your pardon and forgiveness embraced them, and You did not destroy them. So let what embraced them before embrace them today.

This is like one whose master seized him for a crime, saying: Had You willed, You could have taken me before this for something even greater than this offense, but Your pardon first embraced me, so let it embrace me today.

Then the Prophet of Allah said: ﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾

Ibn al-Anbari and others said: This is an interrogative in the sense of denial, meaning: You do not do that.

"The foolish" here means the worshippers of the calf.

Al-Farra' said: Musa thought they were destroyed for their people's taking the calf, so he said: ﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾ [al-A'raf: 155].

Their destruction was in fact due to their saying: ﴿Show us Allah openly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 55].

Then he said: ﴿It is none other than Your trial﴾.

This is part of the appeal: that is, it is nothing but Your testing and Your trial of Your servants. You tested them and examined them, so the matter is entirely Yours and in Your hand; none can remove it but You, just as none but You tested and examined them. So we take refuge in You from You, and we flee from You to You.

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on Surah 7, verse 157 (part 1 of 4):

God has called the burdensome obligations "shackles" in His words: ﴿And He relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾.

He likened them to shackles because of their severity and difficulty. Al-Hasan (al-Hasan al-Basri) said: "They are the hardships that were in worship, such as cutting off the place of urine, killing oneself as repentance, cutting off the sinning limbs, and tracing the veins out of the flesh."

Ibn Qutaybah said: "They are God's prohibition, may He be exalted, upon them of many things that He permitted for the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ). He made them shackles because prohibition restrains as a shackle restrains the hand."

(Section)

If those who deny divine wisdom with respect to the Lord, and who hold that goodness and badness are not innate (fitrī), say that the "good" (al-ma'ruf) means only what He commands, so that it becomes good only by command, and the "bad" (al-munkar) means only what He forbids, so that it becomes bad only by prohibition, then what meaning remains in His words, exalted is He: ﴿He commands them with what is good and forbids them from what is bad﴾?

And what is the outcome of that beyond saying: He commands them with what He commands them, and forbids them from what He forbids them?

This is a statement that the speech of ordinary intelligent people is too exalted to contain, let alone the speech of the Lord of the worlds.

Does the verse indicate anything other than that He commanded them with what is good, which reason recognizes and innate nature (fitrah) affirms as good, so He commanded them with what is good in itself to every sound intellect? And He forbade them from what is bad in human dispositions and intellects, such that when His command and prohibition are presented to a sound intellect, it accepts them with the greatest acceptance and bears witness to their goodness, as one of the Bedouins said when he was asked:
"How did you know that he is the Messenger of God?" He said: "He never commanded a thing, but the intellect said: 'Would that he had forbidden it.' Nor did he forbid a thing, but it said: 'Would that he had commanded it.'"

This Bedouin knew God, His religion, and His Messenger better than those people. His intellect and innate nature affirmed the goodness of what he commanded and the badness of what he forbade, until it became, for him, one of the signs of his prophethood and the proofs of his messengership.

But if the basis of its being good or bad were the bare command, there would be no evidence in it, and one would have to seek evidence for it from elsewhere.

Whoever follows that false path cannot establish the soundness of his prophethood by the very content of his call and his religion.

It is known that the religion he brought and the community to which he called are among the greatest proofs of his truthfulness and the signs of his prophethood. Whoever affirms for it existential attributes that make it good and acceptable to intellects, and affirms for its opposite attributes that make it bad and repugnant to intellect, has closed the door on himself to establishing its truth by the call itself, making the call something to be proven rather than a proof.

Among what shows the soundness of this is His saying: ﴿And He makes lawful for them the good things and makes unlawful for them the foul things﴾. This is explicit that the lawful was good before it was made lawful, and that the foul was foul before it was made unlawful.

The goodness of this and the foulness of that were not derived from the very act of making lawful and unlawful, for two reasons.

The first: this is one of the signs of his prophethood, by which God argued against the People of the Book, saying: ﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel, who commands them with what is good, forbids them from what is bad, makes lawful for them the good things, makes unlawful for them the foul things, and relieves them of their burden﴾. If the goodness and foulness were derived only from the making lawful and unlawful, there would be no evidence in it, since it would amount to saying: He makes lawful what He makes lawful, and makes unlawful for them what He makes unlawful.

This is also false, because it has no benefit. This is the second reason.

Thus it is established that He made lawful what was good in itself before the making lawful, and by making it lawful He clothed it with another goodness, so its source of goodness became both together.

Reflect upon this point with the utmost reflection, and it will reveal to you the secrets of the Shariah and show you its excellence, its perfection, its splendor, and its majesty. It is impossible, in the wisdom of the Most Wise of judges, that it should be contrary to what it was revealed with. God is exalted above that, as He is exalted above all that is unfitting for Him.

(Section)

The questioner said: "It is well known among you, from the Book and the Sunnah, that your Prophet is written with them in the Torah and the Gospel, but they erased him from both because of leadership and food. Reason finds this problematic. Did they all agree to erase his name from the revealed books of their Lord, east and west, south and north? This is a matter that reason finds more problematic than their denial with their tongues, because it is possible to retract what they said with their tongues, but retracting what they erased is far less likely."

The answer: This question is based on a corrupt understanding, namely that the Muslims believe that the explicit name of the Prophet (ﷺ), which is Muhammad in Arabic, is mentioned in the Torah and the Gospel, the two books that contain the two Shariahs. And the Muslims believe that the Jews and Christians in all regions of the earth erased that name and dropped it entirely from the churches, and coordinated this with one another, near and far, east and west. No scholar among the scholars of the Muslims has said this, nor has God, may He be exalted, informed of it in His Book concerning them, nor has His Messenger, nor has He rebuked them with it at any time, nor has any of the Companions said it, nor the imams after them, nor the scholars of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis), nor those concerned with the reports and histories of the nations. And even if it is supposed that some of the common Muslims said it, intending to support the Messenger, it has been said: "An ignorant friend harms more than an intelligent enemy."

These people only came into error from a lack of understanding of the Qur'an, and they thought that His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel, who commands them with what is good and forbids them from what is bad﴾ indicates the specific name in Arabic in the Torah and the Gospel in particular, and that this was never found at all. So there are three stages.

The first: The Lord, may He be exalted, only informed that His Messenger is written with them, meaning the information about him, his description, his place of emergence, and his attributes. He did not inform that the explicit Arabic name is mentioned with them in the Torah and the Gospel. This is found in the two books, as we will mention their wording, God willing. This is more eloquent than mentioning him merely by his name, because the name may be shared, so that identification and distinction are not achieved. Anyone who wishes to be called by this name may claim that he is he, and he can do so. The reference is only to the bare name, and no clarification, identification, or guidance is achieved by it. This is unlike mentioning him by his description, his attributes, his signs, his call, the attributes of his community, the time of his emergence, and the like. This specifies him, distinguishes him, and confines his type to his person. This amount is mentioned in the Torah, the Gospel, and other prophecies that are in the hands of the People of the Book, as we will mention. The following points indicate this.

The first point: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was the most eager of people to have him believed and followed, and to establish the proof against whoever opposed him and denied his prophethood, especially the people of knowledge and the Book. Arguing against them with what they know to be false is something no intelligent person would do. It is like someone saying to a man: "The sign of my truthfulness is that you are so-and-so, son of so-and-so, and your description is such-and-such, and you know such-and-such," when the matter is not so but the opposite. This does not proceed from anyone who has a grain of intelligence, and no one would accept him in that, and no one would follow him. Rather, all intelligent people would flee from believing and following him, and custom makes it impossible for them to remain silent about criticizing him, refuting him, and denouncing his words.

It is known by necessity that Muhammad, son of Abdullah (ﷺ), may He increase him in honor, prayers, and peace, proclaimed openly among these two nations, which are the most knowledgeable of nations on earth before his mission, that his mention, his description, and his attributes are precisely with them in their books. He recited this to them night and day, secretly and openly, in every gathering and every assembly, calling them to it, meaning to believe in him and to affirm him. Some of them believed in him and affirmed him, and reported what was in their books of his description, attributes, and mention, as will pass before you, God willing.

The utmost a denying rejecter can say is: "This description is true, but you are not the one meant by it; rather it is another prophet." This is the most stubbornness he can muster, and this stubbornness does not help him except to expose his shame and reveal his disgrace through lying and slander. The attributes, descriptions, and signs mentioned among them fit him exactly, step for step, so that whoever knows them and sees him does not doubt that he is the one they describe, as Salman knew him, and as Heraclius knew him by those signs that he asked Abu Sufyan about, which matched what he had. So he said: "If what you say is true, he is a prophet, and he will rule what is beneath these feet of mine."

Likewise those we have already mentioned from the rabbis and monks, who recognized him by his description and attributes as they recognize their own sons. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recognize him as they recognize their sons, and indeed a party of them conceal the truth while they know﴾.

And He said in another place: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recognize him as they recognize their sons. Those who have lost themselves, they do not believe﴾.

It is known that this recognition is only by the description and attributes written with them, which fit him, as one of the believers among them said: "By God, one of us knows him better than he knows his own son. Indeed one of us goes out from his wife's presence and does not know what will happen after him."

For this reason God, may He be exalted, praised those among them who knew the truth and did not shrink from following it, saying: ﴿You will surely find the most intense of people in enmity toward those who believe to be the Jews and those who associate partners, and you will surely find the nearest of them in affection toward those who believe to be those who say: "We are Christians." That is because among them are priests and monks, and because they are not arrogant. And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they have recognized. They say: "Our Lord, we have believed, so register us among the witnesses. And why should we not believe in God and in what has come to us of the truth, while we aspire that our Lord will admit us among the righteous people?" So God rewarded them for what they said with gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever, and that is the reward of the doers of good. But those who disbelieved and denied Our signs, those are the companions of Hellfire﴾.

Ibn Abbas said: "When the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) were present before the Negus (al-Najashi) and recited the Qur'an, the priests and monks heard it, and their tears streamed forth because of the truth they recognized. So God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿That is because among them are priests and monks, and because they are not arrogant﴾."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "The Negus sent eighty men from the best of his companions to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). He recited the Qur'an to them, and they wept and softened. They said: 'By God, we recognize that it is the truth.' So they accepted Islam and went back to the Negus and informed him, and he accepted Islam. God, may He be exalted, revealed concerning them: ﴿And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger﴾, the verses."

Al-Suddi said: "They were twelve men, seven of the priests and five of the monks. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited the Qur'an to them, they wept and said: 'Our Lord, we have believed in what You have revealed and followed the Messenger, so register us among the witnesses.'"

Ibn Abbas said: "They are Muhammad and his Ummah, and they are the righteous people whom they hoped God would admit them among." The point is that these people recognized that he is the Messenger of God by the description that they had. So they could not restrain their eyes from weeping, nor their hearts from hastening to belief. A parallel to this is His saying, glorified and exalted: ﴿Say: "Believe in it or do not believe. Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it, when it is recited to them, fall down on their faces in prostration, and they say: 'Exalted is our Lord; indeed the promise of our Lord has been fulfilled.' And they fall down on their faces weeping, and it increases them in humility"﴾.

The imam of the people of tafsir, Mujahid, said: "They are a people from among the People of the Book who, when they heard the Qur'an, fell down prostrate and said: ﴿Exalted is our Lord; indeed the promise of our Lord has been fulfilled﴾."

God, may He be exalted and majestic, had promised through the tongues of His prophets and messengers that He would send, at the end of time, a prophet of great station, whose religion would prevail over all religions, whose call would spread throughout the regions of the earth, and at whose head of community the Hour would be established.

The People of the Book are unanimous that God promised them this Prophet. So the fortunate among them recognized the truth and believed in it and followed it, and the wretched said: "We are awaiting him, and he has not yet been sent as a messenger." When these people heard the Qur'an from the Messenger, they recognized that he was the promised Messenger, so they fell down in prostration to God, out of faith in Him and His Messenger, and in affirmation of His promise, which He had fulfilled. They saw it with their own eyes, and they said: "Exalted is our Lord; indeed the promise of our Lord has been fulfilled."

Yunus ibn Bukayr mentioned, from Salama ibn Abd Yasu', from his father, from his grandfather. Yunus said, and he had been a Christian before he embraced Islam: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote to the people of Najran: "In the name of the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. From Muhammad the Prophet, the Messenger of Allah, to the Bishop (usquf) of Najran and the people of Najran: (Peace be upon you.) I praise before you the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. To proceed: I call you to the worship of Allah instead of the worship of men, and I call you to the guardianship of Allah instead of the guardianship of men. If you refuse, then pay the jizya (poll tax). If you refuse, then I have declared war upon you. Peace."

When the letter reached the Bishop and he read it, he was struck with dread and became greatly afraid.
