Likewise is the hadith of al-Maqburī, from Abū Hurayra, may God be pleased with him, traced to the Prophet, which has preceded, and others among the hadiths in which: "God brought forth the offspring of Ādam from his back, showed them to him, and placed the people of happiness in His right handful and the people of wretchedness in the other handful."

As for the reports in which He made them speak, called them to witness, and addressed them, they are between mawqūf and marfūʿ reports whose chains are not sound, like the hadith of Muslim ibn Yasār and the hadith of Hishām ibn Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām. In the chain of the latter are Baqiyya ibn al-Walīd and Rāshid ibn Saʿd, about both of whom there is criticism, and Qatāda al-Naṣrī, who is unknown (*majhūl*).

In sum: the reports about the bringing forth of the offspring from the back of Ādam and their being in the two handfuls are numerous, and there is no way to reject or deny them. It is enough that they reached the *tābiʿūn* (the successors); how much more so the companions? Such matters are not said by opinion and conjecture. But what the sound among these reports indicates is the affirmation of divine decree (*qadar*): that God knew what would be before it was, and knew the wretched and the happy among the offspring of Ādam. Whether what He brought out and Ādam saw were their likenesses or their very persons, the matter is the same. As for their speech, there is nothing in any of the hadiths on which proof is established, nor does the Qur'an indicate it. For the Qur'an says concerning it: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Ādam from their loins their offspring﴾. So it mentions taking from the loins of the children of Ādam, not from the very back of Ādam. And "their offspring" encompasses all whom they begot, however many. As He says in the rest of the verse: ﴿Or lest you say, "Only our fathers associated others with God before, and we were offspring after them"﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 173]. And He, exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, God chose Ādam and Nūḥ and the family of Ibrāhīm and the family of ʿImrān over the worlds — offspring, some of them from others﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 33–34]. And He says: ﴿The offspring of those We carried with Nūḥ﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 3]. And He says: ﴿And from his offspring, Dāwūd and Sulaymān and Ayyūb and Yūsuf and Mūsā and Hārūn﴾ [al-Anʿām: 84]. So the term "offspring" (*dhurriyya*) includes adults.

As for His saying: ﴿And had them bear witness concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes"﴾ — a person's bearing witness against himself in the Qur'an is intended to mean his acknowledgment. Whoever acknowledges a right owed by him has borne witness to it against himself.

The Almighty said: ﴿Be steadfast in upholding justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves or your parents and close relatives﴾ [al-Nisa larger: 135]. The jurists (fuqaha') likewise used this verse as evidence for the validity of confession (iqrar).

In the hadith of Ma'iz ibn Malik: "When he testified against himself four times," meaning that he confessed four times.

He also said: ﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah while they testify against themselves with disbelief﴾ [al-Tawbah: 17]. They were acknowledging what amounts to disbelief, and this acknowledgment was their testimony against themselves.

From the same usage is His saying: ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you, relating to you My verses and warning you of the meeting of this your Day? They said, "We testify against ourselves." The worldly life deceived them, and they testified against themselves that they had been disbelievers﴾ [al-An'am: 130]. Their testimony against themselves is their confession, and it is the rendering of testimony against themselves.

The expression "So-and-so testified" (shahida fulan) and "he made someone a witness to it" (ashhada bihi) can mean bearing testimony (tahammul al-shahadah), that is, receiving it, and it can mean giving testimony (ada' al-shahadah), that is, delivering it.

The first meaning is like His saying: ﴿And call to witness two just men from among you﴾ [al-Talaq: 2].

The second is like His saying: ﴿Be steadfast in upholding justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa: 135].

As for His saying: ﴿And He made them witnesses concerning themselves﴾, it is not the case, in this second sense, that He caused them to receive testimony about themselves and deliver it at another time. In such contexts He, glorified is He, only makes a person witness against another, as in the story of Adam, when He made the angels witnesses against him, and as in the testimony of the angels and the testimony of the bodily parts (jawarih) against their owners. For this reason some exegetes said that the meaning is "He made some of them witnesses against others." However, this expression, wherever it occurs in the Qur'an, means only a person's testimony against himself, in the sense of delivering testimony against himself.

Their saying ﴿Yes, we testify﴾ is their acknowledgment that He is their Lord. Whoever reports a matter concerning himself has testified to it against himself. Their words ﴿Yes, we testify﴾ mean: "You are our Lord." This is an acknowledgment by them of His lordship over them, and of their being made witnesses against themselves to what they acknowledged. His saying "He made them witnesses" implies that He is the One who made them witnesses against themselves that He is their Lord. This making-to-witness involves their acknowledging that they were taken from the loins of their fathers. This taking, which is known and witnessed and about which there is no doubt, is the extraction of the sperm from the loins of the fathers and its descent into the wombs of the mothers. But the mothers are not mentioned here, as in His saying: ﴿Or you should say, "Only our fathers associated others with Allah before us, and we were offspring after them"﴾ [al-A'raf: 173]. They were following the religion of their fathers, not the religion of their mothers, as they said: ﴿We found our fathers upon a community﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22]. For this reason He said: ﴿Even if I brought you better guidance than what you found your fathers upon?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 24].

So He, glorified is He, is saying: Remember when they were taken from the loins of the fathers, and they were created, and when they were born they were upon the fitrah (innate natural disposition), acknowledging the Creator and testifying against themselves that Allah is their Lord. This acknowledgment is a proof for Allah against them on the Day of Resurrection. So He mentions His taking them and His making them witnesses against themselves, for He, glorified is He, created and proportioned, and decreed and guided. Their being taken involves their creation, and the making-to-witness involves His guidance of them to this acknowledgment. He said "He made them witnesses," that is, He made them witnesses. This making-to-witness is among the necessary attributes of the human being, and every human being has been made by Allah to acknowledge His lordship and to be a witness against himself that he is created and that Allah is his Creator. This is a matter of necessary knowledge (ilm darurI) for the children of Adam, and no created being is free of it. It is something they were innately constituted with, so it is a necessary knowledge for them, and no one can deny it.

Then He said after that: "Lest you say" (an taqulu), that is, out of aversion to your saying, or so that you do not say: ﴿Indeed we were unaware of this﴾, that is, unaware of this acknowledgment of Allah's lordship and of our own servitude. For they were not unaware of this. Rather, this was among the necessary knowledges binding upon them, which no human being has ever been free of. This is unlike many knowledges that may be necessary, but many children of Adam may neglect them, such as knowledge of numbers and calculation and other things. For when these are conceived, they become necessary knowledges, yet many people are unaware of them.

As for acknowledging the Creator, it is a necessary knowledge binding upon the human being, and no one is so unaware of it that he does not know it. Rather, he must have known it, even if it is supposed that he forgot it. For this reason, reminding people of it is called tadhkir (reminder), since it is a reminder of innate necessary knowledges, though the servant may forget them, as He said: ﴿And do not be like those who forgot Allah, so He made them forget themselves﴾ [al-Hashr: 19]. In the authentic hadith: "Allah will say to the disbeliever: 'Today I forget you as you forgot Me.'"

Then He said: ﴿Or you should say, "Only our fathers associated others with Allah before us, and we were offspring after them. Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?"﴾ [al-A'raf: 173]. Thus He, glorified is He, mentioned for them two arguments which this making-to-witness repels. The first: that they say ﴿Indeed we were unaware of this﴾. He clarified that this is an innate, necessary knowledge which every human must know. This involves Allah's proof in refuting ta'til (the denial of the Creator), and that affirming the Maker is necessary innate knowledge, and it is a proof against the denial of the Creator.

The second: that they say ﴿Only our fathers associated others with Allah before us, and we were offspring after them. Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?﴾ [al-A'raf: 173]. Those fathers were polytheists, that is: "Will You punish us for the sins of others?" For even if it were supposed that they did not know that Allah is their Lord, and found their fathers to be polytheists, and they were their offspring after them, the natural custom would require a man to follow his father even in crafts, dwellings, clothing and food, since the father is the one who raised him. For this reason, his parents would make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian. When this is the requirement of custom and nature, and there was nothing in their fitrah and intellects that contradicted it, they would say: "We are excused, and our fathers were the ones who associated others with Allah, and we were their offspring after them, and we had nothing to show us their error." But when there was in their fitrah what they testified to, namely that Allah alone is their Lord, there was with them what would demonstrate the falsehood of this polytheism, namely the tawhid which they testified to against themselves.

So when they argue by the natural custom of following fathers, the proof against them is the natural, active fitrah which precedes this newly arisen custom. The fitrah that requires Islam precedes the upbringing they cite as an argument. This implies that the very intellect by which they recognize tawhid is itself a proof against shirk, and that this does not require a messenger, since He made what precedes it a proof against them without this. This does not contradict His saying: ﴿And We would never punish until We send a messenger﴾ [al-Isra: 15], since the messenger calls to tawhid, but the fitrah is a rational evidence by which the existence of the Maker is known. The mere fact of a message was not what constituted the proof against them. Thus this testimony against themselves, which includes their acknowledgment that Allah is their Lord, and their knowledge of this, is a matter necessarily binding on all children of Adam, by which Allah's proof is established in confirming His messengers. So no one can say on the Day of Resurrection, "I was unaware of this," nor that the sin was upon my polytheist father rather than me, because he knew that Allah is his Lord with no partner. Hence he was not excused for denial of the Creator (ta'til) or for associating others with Him. Rather, what he committed deserves punishment.

Then Allah, glorified is He, out of the perfection of His mercy and beneficence, does not punish anyone except after sending a messenger to him, even though he commits what deserves blame and punishment. Allah has two proofs over His servant, which He has prepared for him, and He does not punish him except after both have been established:

The first: what He innately constituted him with, and created him with, of acknowledging that He is his Lord, his Sovereign, and his Originator, and His right over him is binding.

The second: the sending of His messengers to him with the detailed explanation of this, its confirmation, and its completion. Thus the witness of the fitrah and of the sacred law (shir'ah) stands against him, and he acknowledges against himself that he was a disbeliever, as He said: ﴿And they testified against themselves that they had been disbelievers﴾ [al-An'am: 130]. So He did not carry out judgment against them except after confession and two witnesses, and this is the utmost justice.

Thus Allah, glorified is He, likened the one to whom He gave His Book and taught the knowledge that He withheld from others, but who abandoned acting upon it, followed his desires, and preferred the displeasure of Allah over His pleasure, his worldly life over his Hereafter, and the created over the Creator, to the dog. It is among the most wicked of animals, the lowest in rank, and the basest in self. Its aspiration does not extend beyond its belly, and of all animals it is the most greedy and the most harmful. From its greed, it does not walk except with its snout to the ground, sniffing and smelling, out of greed and avidity. It keeps sniffing its rear in preference to the rest of its body. When you throw a stone at it, it returns to bite it, out of its excessive craving. It is among the most abject of animals, the most willing to bear humiliation, and the most content with base things. Rotting, foul carrion is dearer to it than fresh meat, and dung is dearer to it than sweets. When it finds a carcass sufficient for a hundred dogs, it does not leave a single dog to take any of it without snarling at it and overpowering it, because of its greed, stinginess, and avidity. Among the strangest of its behaviour and greed is that when it sees a person in shabby appearance, with base clothing and a wretched state, it barks at him and attacks him, as though it imagines he shares with it and competes with it for its food. But when it sees a person of good appearance, fine clothing, and high standing, it lowers its snout to the ground, humbles itself to him, and does not raise its head to him.

Regarding the likening of the one who prefers the world and its immediate gains over Allah and the Last Abode, despite his full knowledge of the dog in its state of panting, there is a wondrous secret. It is that this person, whose condition is what Allah mentioned, of "detachment from His signs" and "following his desire," is only so because of the intensity of his longing for the world, due to his heart being severed from Allah and the Last Abode. Thus he is intensely eager for it, and his eagerness is like the eagerness of the dog, which is constant in its state of agitation and neglect. "Lahaf" (intense longing) and "lahath" (panting) are twin brothers in wording and meaning.

Ibn Jurayj said: "The dog is one whose heart is severed; it has no heart. If you attack it, it pants; if you leave it, it pants. So it is like the one who abandons guidance, who has no heart; rather, his heart is severed." I say: his meaning by the severing of its heart is that it has no heart that would drive it to patience and to refraining from panting. Likewise, the one who has been detached from the signs of Allah has no heart left that would drive him to patience regarding the world and to refrain from longing for it. So this one longs for the world due to his lack of patience with it, and that one pants due to his lack of patience with water. The dog is among the least patient of animals regarding water; when it is thirsty, it eats the dust out of thirst, though it has patience for hunger. In every case, it is among the most panting of animals: it pants standing, sitting, walking, and stationary. This is because of its intense greed. The heat of greed in its liver necessitates its constant panting. Likewise, the intensity of greed and the heat of desire in the heart of its counterpart necessitate his constant longing. If you direct admonition and advice to him, he longs; and if you leave him and do not admonish him, he longs. Mujahid said: "This is the likeness of the one who was given the Book but did not act upon it."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "If you bear wisdom upon him, he does not bear it; and if you leave him, he is not guided to any good. He is like the dog: if it is lying down, it pants, and if it is driven away, it pants." Al-Hasan said: "He is the hypocrite who does not remain firm upon the truth, whether he is invited or not, whether he is admonished or not, like the dog that pants whether it is chased or left alone." 'Ata' said: "It barks whether you attack it or do not attack it." Abu Muhammad Ibn Qutayba said: "Everything pants only from exhaustion or thirst, except the dog, which pants in a state of fatigue, in a state of rest, in a state of health, in a state of sickness, and in thirst." So Allah struck this as a likeness for the one who denied His signs, and said: if you admonish him, he is astray, and if you leave him, he is astray, like the dog: if you drive it away, it pants, and if you leave it in its state, it pants. A parallel to this is His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they will not follow you; it is the same for you whether you call them or you remain silent﴾ [al-A'raf: 193].

(Benefit)
Reflect on what wisdom and meaning are in this parable. Among them is His saying: ﴿We gave him Our signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 175]. He, glorified is He, informed that it is He who gave him His signs, for they are a blessing, and Allah is the One who bestowed them upon him. So He attributed them to Himself. Then He said: ﴿but he detached himself from them﴾ [al-A'raf: 175], meaning he came out of them as a snake sheds its skin, separating from them as a skin separates from the flesh when it is stripped away. He did not say "We stripped him from them," because it was he who brought about his detachment from them by following his desire.

Among them is His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿so Satan pursued him﴾ [al-A'raf: 175], meaning he overtook him and reached him, as He said about the people of Pharaoh: ﴿So they pursued them at sunrise﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 60]. He had been protected and guarded by the signs of Allah, shielded on his side by them from Satan, who could take from him nothing except through heedlessness and a sudden snatch. But when he detached himself from the signs of Allah, Satan seized him as a lion seizes its prey. So he became one of the misguided, who act contrary to their knowledge, who know the truth yet act against it, like the scholars of evil.

Among them is that He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Had We willed, We would have raised him thereby﴾ [al-A'raf: 176]. He informed that elevation in His sight is not by mere knowledge, for this man was among the scholars. Rather, it is by following the truth, preferring it, and seeking the pleasure of Allah.

All of this is about one of the most knowledgeable people of his time, yet Allah did not raise him by his knowledge, nor did it benefit him. We seek refuge in Allah from knowledge that does not benefit. He, glorified is He, informed that it is He who raises His servant, when He wills, by means of the knowledge He has given him. If Allah does not raise him, he is lowered, and no one raises his head by it at all. The Abaser and the Exalter, glorified is He, has lowered him and not raised him. The meaning is: had We willed, We would have favoured him, honoured him, and raised his rank and station through the signs that We had given him. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Had We willed, We would have raised him by acting upon them." Another group said: the pronoun in His saying ﴿We would have raised him﴾ refers to disbelief, and the meaning is: had We willed, We would have lifted disbelief from him through what was with him of Our signs. Mujahid and 'Ata' said: "We would have lifted disbelief from him through faith and protected him." This meaning is true, but the first is the intended meaning of the verse, while this is one of its necessary implications. It has already been mentioned that the early scholars (al-salaf) often draw attention to a necessary implication of the verse's meaning, so that the one who hears may suppose that this is what is intended by it.

As for His saying: ﴿but he inclined to the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 176], Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "He settled upon the earth (rakana ila al-ard)." Mujahid said: "He settled down (sakana)." Muqatil said: "He was content with the world." Abu 'Ubayda said: "He clung to it and lingered." The one who "akhlada" (inclines persistently) among men is the one who slows his walk; and among animals, it is the one whose front teeth remain until his molars come out. Al-Zajjaj said: "Khalada and akhlada: its root is from khulud, which is permanence and endurance. It is said: so-and-so akhlada in the place when he stayed in it." Malik ibn Nuwayra said:

"Among the sons of a tribe from the tribes of Malik,
and 'Amr ibn Yarbu', they stayed and inclined persistently."

I say: From this is His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿There will circulate among them youths made eternal﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 17], meaning they have been created for permanence; therefore they do not change and do not grow old, but remain at one age forever. It was said: they are those adorned with earrings and wearing bracelets on their wrists. The proponents of this view explained the word by one of its necessary implications, which is a sign of being fixed at that age. So there is no contradiction between the two statements.

As for His saying: ﴿and he followed his desire﴾ [al-A'raf: 176], al-Kalbi said: "He followed the lowest matters and left the highest." Abu Waraq said: "He chose the world over the Hereafter." 'Ata' said: "He desired the world and obeyed his Satan." Ibn Duraid said: "His desire was with the people," meaning those who fought Moses and his people. Yaman said: "He followed his wife, because she was the one who drove him to what he did."

If it is said: the adversative "but" (lakinna) requires that after it there be an affirmation of what was negated before it, or a negation of what was affirmed, as you say: "Had I willed, I would have given him, but I did not give him," or "Had I willed I would not have done such-and-such, but I did it." So the adversative would require: "Had We willed, We would have raised him by them, but We did not will, or We did not raise him." How then does He use the adversative with His saying ﴿but he inclined to the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 176] after His saying ﴿Had We willed, We would have raised him thereby﴾ [al-A'raf: 176]? It is said: this is speech in which the meaning is considered rather than the wording, and it is diverted from observing the words to the meanings. The content of His saying ﴿Had We willed, We would have raised him thereby﴾ is that he did not undertake the causes that would have required his elevation through the signs: preferring Allah and His pleasure over his desire. Rather, he preferred the world, inclined to the earth, and followed his desire.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "The meaning is: had he adhered to Our signs, We would have raised him by them. He mentioned the will, but what is meant is what is consequent upon it and caused by it, as if it were said: had he adhered to them, We would have raised him by them. Do you not see His saying ﴿but he inclined﴾, where the adversative corrects the will by his inclining, which is his own act? So ﴿had We willed﴾ must mean what is his act." If the speech were according to its apparent meaning, it would have to be said: "Had We willed, We would have raised him, but We did not will." This is a feature of his speech that we recognize from a Qadari who denies the general will of Allah, who strains to make the speech of Allah Mu'tazili and Qadari. Where is His saying ﴿Had We willed﴾ in relation to his saying "had he adhered to them"? Moreover, if adherence to them depends on the will of Allah, which is the truth, then his foundation collapses.

And his saying: "The will of Allah is consequent upon his adherence to the signs" is among the most corrupt and invalid speech. Rather, his adherence to His signs is consequent upon the will of Allah. The will of Allah, glorified is He, is the followed, not the follower; it is the cause, not the caused; it is the necessitating and determining, not the determined. What Allah wills must exist, and what He does not will cannot exist.

(Another benefit)
His saying: ﴿And recite to them the news of the one to whom We gave Our signs, but he detached himself from them, so Satan pursued him, and he became one of the misguided. Had We willed, We would have raised him thereby﴾.

Reflect on His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿We gave him Our signs﴾. He informed that this was attained for him only by the Lord's giving to him, not by his own acquisition. Then He said: ﴿but he detached himself from them﴾, and He did not say "We stripped him," but attributed the detachment to him. He expressed his disavowal of them by the word "detachment," which indicates his complete abandonment of them, and this is the condition of the disbeliever. As for the believer, even if he disobeys Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, he does not completely detach himself from faith. Then He said: ﴿so Satan pursued him﴾ and did not say "so he followed him," for "pursued" (atba'ahu) indicates that he overtook him and reached him, as Allah said: ﴿So they pursued them﴾, meaning they caught up with them and reached them. Then He said: ﴿Had We willed, We would have raised him thereby﴾. In this is evidence that mere knowledge does not raise its possessor. This man, Allah, glorified is He, informed, was given His signs, yet He did not raise him by them. So elevation through knowledge is a degree beyond mere learning it. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, informed of the cause that prevented him from being raised by them, saying: ﴿but he inclined to the earth and followed his desire﴾. His saying ﴿inclined to the earth﴾ means he settled into it and descended by his nature into it, so his soul was earthly and lowly, not heavenly and lofty. According to how much the servant inclines to the earth, he descends from the heavens. Sahl said: "Allah divided the limbs from desire; for each limb He allotted a share of it. When a limb inclines toward desire, its harm returns to the heart. The soul has seven heavenly veils and seven earthly veils. Whenever the servant buries his soul in the earth, layer by layer, his heart ascends, heaven by heaven. When he buries the soul beneath the soil, the heart reaches the Throne." Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the likeness of the one who follows his desire: like the dog, which does not cease panting in both states, whether it is left alone or attacked. Thus is this one: panting does not leave him, whether he is desirous of the world or fearful of it.

The purpose is that this sura, from its beginning to its end, is about the condition of the people of desire and lusts, and what their affair came to. Love and desire are the root of every affliction.

[Section: Disobedience makes its doer one of the lowly]

Among its punishments is that it makes its doer one of the lowly, after he had been prepared to be among the exalted. Allah created His creation in two categories: the exalted and the lowly. He made the 'Illiyyin the abode of the exalted, and the lowest of the lowest the abode of the lowly. He made the people of His obedience the highest in this world and the Hereafter, and the people of His disobedience the lowest in this world and the Hereafter, just as He made the people of His obedience the most honoured of His creation before Him, and the people of His disobedience the most despised of His creation before Him. He made honour for these, and humiliation and abasement for those, as in the Musnad of Ahmad, from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "I was sent with the sword before the Hour, and my provision has been placed under the shade of my spear, and humiliation and abasement have been placed upon whoever opposes my command."

Whenever a servant commits an act of disobedience, he descends one degree, and he continues descending until he becomes among the lowest. Whenever he performs an act of obedience, he rises one degree by it, and he continues rising until he becomes among the highest.

It may happen that during the days of a servant's life he experiences both ascent in one respect and descent in another. Whichever of the two predominates over him, he belongs to its people. Thus, one who ascends a hundred degrees and descends one degree is not like one whose situation is the reverse.

However, a great error arises here for souls: a servant may descend a descent so far that it is farther than the distance between the East and the West, and farther than the distance between the heaven and the earth. Then his ascent of a thousand degrees does not compensate for this single descent. This is as in the authentic (sahih) report from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said:

"Indeed, a servant may utter a single word, giving it no thought, and it throws him into the Fire farther than the distance between the East and the West."

So what ascent can balance this descent? Descent is something necessary for a human being. However, among people there is one whose descent is into heedlessness (ghaflah). When such a person awakens from his heedlessness, he returns to his degree, or to one higher than it, according to the degree of his awakening.

Among them is one whose descent is into something permissible (mubah), without intending by it to seek help for obedience. When such a person returns to obedience, he may return to his degree, or may not reach it, or may rise above it. He may return with a higher resolve than before, or with a weaker resolve, or his resolve may return as it was.

Among them is one whose descent is into an act of disobedience, whether minor or major. Such a person, in returning to his degree, needs sincere repentance (tawbah nasuh) and true turning back (inabah).

People have differed as to whether, after repentance, he returns to the degree he was in. Those who hold that repentance erases the effect of the sin and makes its existence like its non-existence, so that it is as though it had never been, say that he returns. Those who hold that repentance's effect is only in dropping the punishment say that he does not return to the degree that he missed, and he does not reach it.

They said: The explanation of this is that during the time in which he disobeyed, he was prepared, by his occupation with obedience in the past, for another ascent and elevation carried by his previous deeds. This is like a man who earns each day by the whole of his wealth, which he possesses; and whenever the wealth multiplies, the profit multiplies. So during the time of disobedience, he has lost an elevation and a profit that his deeds would have carried. When he resumes work, he resumes ascent from a descent, whereas before that he was ascending from the lowest point to the highest, and between the two states there is a great gap.

They said: The likeness of this is two men who climb two ladders with no end, and they are equal. One of them descends to a lower step, even by a single step, and then resumes climbing. The one who did not descend will inevitably be above him.

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah (may Allah have mercy on him) judged between the two groups with an acceptable judgment. He said:

"The verified position is that among those who repent there is one who returns to a degree higher than his former degree, and among them there is one who returns to the likeness of his former degree, and among them there is one who does not reach his former degree."

I say: This depends on the strength and completeness of the repentance, and on what the sin has produced in the servant of humility, lowliness, turning back, caution, fear of Allah, and weeping out of awe of Allah. These matters may grow strong, until the penitent returns to a degree higher than his former degree, and becomes after repentance better than he was before the sin. For such a person, the sin may be a mercy in his case, for it removed from him the disease of self-admiration, freed him from confidence in himself and from relying upon his deeds, placed the cheek of his humble supplication and his lowliness and brokenness upon the threshold of the door of his Lord and Master, made him know his worth, made him witness his poverty and his need for his Master's preservation of him, for His pardon of him and His forgiveness of him. It drove out of his heart the pride of obedience, broke his nose from being proud of it, boasting by it, or seeing himself as better than others because of it. It made him stand before his Lord in the station of sinful wrongdoers, head bowed before his Lord, ashamed, fearful of Him, anxious, belittling his obedience, magnifying his disobedience, knowing himself by deficiency and blame. His Lord is singular in perfection, praise and fidelity, as it has been said:

"Allah has reserved fidelity and praise for Himself, and has turned blame away from the man."

So whatever blessing from Allah reaches him, he regards it as too great for himself, sees himself as falling short of it, and does not consider himself worthy of it. And whatever calamity or trial reaches him, he sees himself as worthy of something greater than it, and sees his Master as having been good to him, in that He did not punish him according to the measure of his offence, nor a part of it, nor even the smallest fraction of it.

For what he deserves of punishment, the firm mountains could not bear, let alone this weak and incapable servant. Indeed, though a sin may be small, confronting the Great, of whom nothing is greater, the Mighty, of whom nothing is mightier, the Majestic, of whom none is more majestic or more beautiful, the Benefactor who bestows all kinds of blessings, subtle and great, is among the most ugly, most grievous, and most shameful of matters. Confronting the noble, the honored, and the lords of people with such a thing is judged ugly by everyone, believer and unbeliever alike.

The basest of people and the most lacking in manliness is one who confronts them with vices. So how about the Great of the heavens and the earth, the King of the heavens and the earth, and the God of the people of the heavens and the earth? Had His mercy not preceded His wrath, and His forgiveness not preceded His punishment, the earth would have been crushed upon whoever confronted Him with what is not fitting to confront Him with. Had it not been for His forbearance and His forgiveness, the heavens and the earth would have been shaken by the disobedience of the servants. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease; and if they should cease, none could hold them after Him. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving﴾ [Fatir: 41].

So reflect on how this verse ends with two of His names: "the Forbearing" (al-Halim) and "the Forgiving" (al-Ghafur). See how beneath that you find that were it not for His forbearance toward the offenders and His forgiveness of the disobedient, the heavens and the earth would not remain firm.

Allah, glorified is He, has also informed us about the disbelief of some of His servants, that: ﴿The heavens are about to be torn apart from it, and the earth split open, and the mountains fall down in ruin﴾ [Maryam: 90].

Allah, glorified is He, expelled the two parents from Paradise because of a single sin which they committed, in which they opposed His prohibition. He cursed Iblis, drove him away, and expelled him from the dominion of the heavens and the earth because of a single sin which he committed, in which he opposed His command. As for us, we are the foolish folk, as it has been said:

"We pile sins upon sins, and hope for the stations of the Gardens, for the one of lasting bliss."

"We certainly know that He expelled the two parents from His supreme dominion because of a single sin."

The purpose is that after repentance a servant may become better than he was before the sin and higher in degree. But the sin may also weaken his resolve, enfeeble his determination, and sicken his heart, so the medicine of repentance cannot restore him to his original health, and he does not return to his degree. Yet the sickness may also be removed, so that health returns as it was, and he returns to the like of his former deeds, and so returns to his degree.

All of this applies when his descent was into an act of disobedience. If his descent was into something that harms the very root of his faith, such as doubts, skepticism, and hypocrisy, then that is a descent for which no ascent is hoped for its doer, except by renewing his Islam.

Thus Allah, glorified is He, likened the one to whom He gave His Book and taught the knowledge that He withheld from others, but who abandoned acting upon it, followed his desires, and preferred the displeasure of Allah over His pleasure, his worldly life over his Hereafter, and the created over the Creator, to the dog. It is among the most wicked of animals, the lowest in rank, and the basest in self. Its aspiration does not extend beyond its belly, and of all animals it is the most greedy and the most harmful. From its greed, it does not walk except with its snout to the ground, sniffing and smelling, out of greed and avidity. It keeps sniffing its rear in preference to the rest of its body. When you throw a stone at it, it returns to bite it, out of its excessive craving. It is among the most abject of animals, the most willing to bear humiliation, and the most content with base things. Rotting, foul carrion is dearer to it than fresh meat, and dung is dearer to it than sweets. When it finds a carcass sufficient for a hundred dogs, it does not leave a single dog to take any of it without snarling at it and overpowering it, because of its greed, stinginess, and avidity. Among the strangest of its behaviour and greed is that when it sees a person in shabby appearance, with base clothing and a wretched state, it barks at him and attacks him, as though it imagines he shares with it and competes with it for its food. But when it sees a person of good appearance, fine clothing, and high standing, it lowers its snout to the ground, humbles itself to him, and does not raise its head to him.

Regarding the likening of the one who prefers the world and its immediate gains over Allah and the Last Abode, despite his full knowledge of the dog in its state of panting, there is a wondrous secret. It is that this person, whose condition is what Allah mentioned, of "detachment from His signs" and "following his desire," is only so because of the intensity of his longing for the world, due to his heart being severed from Allah and the Last Abode. Thus he is intensely eager for it, and his eagerness is like the eagerness of the dog, which is constant in its state of agitation and neglect. "Lahaf" (intense longing) and "lahath" (panting) are twin brothers in wording and meaning.

Ibn Jurayj said: "The dog is one whose heart is severed; it has no heart. If you attack it, it pants; if you leave it, it pants. So it is like the one who abandons guidance, who has no heart; rather, his heart is severed." I say: his meaning by the severing of its heart is that it has no heart that would drive it to patience and to refraining from panting. Likewise, the one who has been detached from the signs of Allah has no heart left that would drive him to patience regarding the world and to refrain from longing for it. So this one longs for the world due to his lack of patience with it, and that one pants due to his lack of patience with water. The dog is among the least patient of animals regarding water; when it is thirsty, it eats the dust out of thirst, though it has patience for hunger. In every case, it is among the most panting of animals: it pants standing, sitting, walking, and stationary. This is because of its intense greed. The heat of greed in its liver necessitates its constant panting. Likewise, the intensity of greed and the heat of desire in the heart of its counterpart necessitate his constant longing. If you direct admonition and advice to him, he longs; and if you leave him and do not admonish him, he longs. Mujahid said: "This is the likeness of the one who was given the Book but did not act upon it."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "If you bear wisdom upon him, he does not bear it; and if you leave him, he is not guided to any good. He is like the dog: if it is lying down, it pants, and if it is driven away, it pants." Al-Hasan said: "He is the hypocrite who does not remain firm upon the truth, whether he is invited or not, whether he is admonished or not, like the dog that pants whether it is chased or left alone." 'Ata' said: "It barks whether you attack it or do not attack it." Abu Muhammad Ibn Qutayba said: "Everything pants only from exhaustion or thirst, except the dog, which pants in a state of fatigue, in a state of rest, in a state of health, in a state of sickness, and in thirst." So Allah struck this as a likeness for the one who denied His signs, and said: if you admonish him, he is astray, and if you leave him, he is astray, like the dog: if you drive it away, it pants, and if you leave it in its state, it pants. A parallel to this is His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they will not follow you; it is the same for you whether you call them or you remain silent﴾ [al-A'raf: 193].

(Benefit)
Reflect on what wisdom and meaning are in this parable. Among them is His saying: ﴿We gave him Our signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 175]. He, glorified is He, informed that it is He who gave him His signs, for they are a blessing, and Allah is the One who bestowed them upon him. So He attributed them to Himself. Then He said: ﴿but he detached himself from them﴾ [al-A'raf: 175], meaning he came out of them as a snake sheds its skin, separating from them as a skin separates from the flesh when it is stripped away. He did not say "We stripped him from them," because it was he who brought about his detachment from them by following his desire.

Among them is His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿so Satan pursued him﴾ [al-A'raf: 175], meaning he overtook him and reached him, as He said about the people of Pharaoh: ﴿So they pursued them at sunrise﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 60]. He had been protected and guarded by the signs of Allah, shielded on his side by them from Satan, who could take from him nothing except through heedlessness and a sudden snatch. But when he detached himself from the signs of Allah, Satan seized him as a lion seizes its prey. So he became one of the misguided, who act contrary to their knowledge, who know the truth yet act against it, like the scholars of evil.

Among them is that He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Had We willed, We would have raised him thereby﴾ [al-A'raf: 176]. He informed that elevation in His sight is not by mere knowledge, for this man was among the scholars. Rather, it is by following the truth, preferring it, and seeking the pleasure of Allah.

All of this is about one of the most knowledgeable people of his time, yet Allah did not raise him by his knowledge, nor did it benefit him. We seek refuge in Allah from knowledge that does not benefit. He, glorified is He, informed that it is He who raises His servant, when He wills, by means of the knowledge He has given him. If Allah does not raise him, he is lowered, and no one raises his head by it at all. The Abaser and the Exalter, glorified is He, has lowered him and not raised him. The meaning is: had We willed, We would have favoured him, honoured him, and raised his rank and station through the signs that We had given him. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Had We willed, We would have raised him by acting upon them." Another group said: the pronoun in His saying ﴿We would have raised him﴾ refers to disbelief, and the meaning is: had We willed, We would have lifted disbelief from him through what was with him of Our signs. Mujahid and 'Ata' said: "We would have lifted disbelief from him through faith and protected him." This meaning is true, but the first is the intended meaning of the verse, while this is one of its necessary implications. It has already been mentioned that the early scholars (al-salaf) often draw attention to a necessary implication of the verse's meaning, so that the one who hears may suppose that this is what is intended by it.

As for His saying: ﴿but he inclined to the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 176], Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "He settled upon the earth (rakana ila al-ard)." Mujahid said: "He settled down (sakana)." Muqatil said: "He was content with the world." Abu 'Ubayda said: "He clung to it and lingered." The one who "akhlada" (inclines persistently) among men is the one who slows his walk; and among animals, it is the one whose front teeth remain until his molars come out. Al-Zajjaj said: "Khalada and akhlada: its root is from khulud, which is permanence and endurance. It is said: so-and-so akhlada in the place when he stayed in it." Malik ibn Nuwayra said:

"Among the sons of a tribe from the tribes of Malik,
and 'Amr ibn Yarbu', they stayed and inclined persistently."

I say: From this is His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿There will circulate among them youths made eternal﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 17], meaning they have been created for permanence; therefore they do not change and do not grow old, but remain at one age forever. It was said: they are those adorned with earrings and wearing bracelets on their wrists. The proponents of this view explained the word by one of its necessary implications, which is a sign of being fixed at that age. So there is no contradiction between the two statements.

As for His saying: ﴿and he followed his desire﴾ [al-A'raf: 176], al-Kalbi said: "He followed the lowest matters and left the highest." Abu Waraq said: "He chose the world over the Hereafter." 'Ata' said: "He desired the world and obeyed his Satan." Ibn Duraid said: "His desire was with the people," meaning those who fought Moses and his people. Yaman said: "He followed his wife, because she was the one who drove him to what he did."

If it is said: the adversative "but" (lakinna) requires that after it there be an affirmation of what was negated before it, or a negation of what was affirmed, as you say: "Had I willed, I would have given him, but I did not give him," or "Had I willed I would not have done such-and-such, but I did it." So the adversative would require: "Had We willed, We would have raised him by them, but We did not will, or We did not raise him." How then does He use the adversative with His saying ﴿but he inclined to the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 176] after His saying ﴿Had We willed, We would have raised him thereby﴾ [al-A'raf: 176]? It is said: this is speech in which the meaning is considered rather than the wording, and it is diverted from observing the words to the meanings. The content of His saying ﴿Had We willed, We would have raised him thereby﴾ is that he did not undertake the causes that would have required his elevation through the signs: preferring Allah and His pleasure over his desire. Rather, he preferred the world, inclined to the earth, and followed his desire.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "The meaning is: had he adhered to Our signs, We would have raised him by them. He mentioned the will, but what is meant is what is consequent upon it and caused by it, as if it were said: had he adhered to them, We would have raised him by them. Do you not see His saying ﴿but he inclined﴾, where the adversative corrects the will by his inclining, which is his own act? So ﴿had We willed﴾ must mean what is his act." If the speech were according to its apparent meaning, it would have to be said: "Had We willed, We would have raised him, but We did not will." This is a feature of his speech that we recognize from a Qadari who denies the general will of Allah, who strains to make the speech of Allah Mu'tazili and Qadari. Where is His saying ﴿Had We willed﴾ in relation to his saying "had he adhered to them"? Moreover, if adherence to them depends on the will of Allah, which is the truth, then his foundation collapses.

And his saying: "The will of Allah is consequent upon his adherence to the signs" is among the most corrupt and invalid speech. Rather, his adherence to His signs is consequent upon the will of Allah. The will of Allah, glorified is He, is the followed, not the follower; it is the cause, not the caused; it is the necessitating and determining, not the determined. What Allah wills must exist, and what He does not will cannot exist.

(Another benefit)
His saying: ﴿And recite to them the news of the one to whom We gave Our signs, but he detached himself from them, so Satan pursued him, and he became one of the misguided. Had We willed, We would have raised him thereby﴾.

Reflect on His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿We gave him Our signs﴾. He informed that this was attained for him only by the Lord's giving to him, not by his own acquisition. Then He said: ﴿but he detached himself from them﴾, and He did not say "We stripped him," but attributed the detachment to him. He expressed his disavowal of them by the word "detachment," which indicates his complete abandonment of them, and this is the condition of the disbeliever. As for the believer, even if he disobeys Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, he does not completely detach himself from faith. Then He said: ﴿so Satan pursued him﴾ and did not say "so he followed him," for "pursued" (atba'ahu) indicates that he overtook him and reached him, as Allah said: ﴿So they pursued them﴾, meaning they caught up with them and reached them. Then He said: ﴿Had We willed, We would have raised him thereby﴾. In this is evidence that mere knowledge does not raise its possessor. This man, Allah, glorified is He, informed, was given His signs, yet He did not raise him by them. So elevation through knowledge is a degree beyond mere learning it. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, informed of the cause that prevented him from being raised by them, saying: ﴿but he inclined to the earth and followed his desire﴾. His saying ﴿inclined to the earth﴾ means he settled into it and descended by his nature into it, so his soul was earthly and lowly, not heavenly and lofty. According to how much the servant inclines to the earth, he descends from the heavens. Sahl said: "Allah divided the limbs from desire; for each limb He allotted a share of it. When a limb inclines toward desire, its harm returns to the heart. The soul has seven heavenly veils and seven earthly veils. Whenever the servant buries his soul in the earth, layer by layer, his heart ascends, heaven by heaven. When he buries the soul beneath the soil, the heart reaches the Throne." Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the likeness of the one who follows his desire: like the dog, which does not cease panting in both states, whether it is left alone or attacked. Thus is this one: panting does not leave him, whether he is desirous of the world or fearful of it.

The purpose is that this sura, from its beginning to its end, is about the condition of the people of desire and lusts, and what their affair came to. Love and desire are the root of every affliction.

[Section: Disobedience makes its doer one of the lowly]

Among its punishments is that it makes its doer one of the lowly, after he had been prepared to be among the exalted. Allah created His creation in two categories: the exalted and the lowly. He made the 'Illiyyin the abode of the exalted, and the lowest of the lowest the abode of the lowly. He made the people of His obedience the highest in this world and the Hereafter, and the people of His disobedience the lowest in this world and the Hereafter, just as He made the people of His obedience the most honoured of His creation before Him, and the people of His disobedience the most despised of His creation before Him. He made honour for these, and humiliation and abasement for those, as in the Musnad of Ahmad, from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "I was sent with the sword before the Hour, and my provision has been placed under the shade of my spear, and humiliation and abasement have been placed upon whoever opposes my command."

It may happen that during the days of a servant's life he experiences both ascent in one respect and descent in another. Whichever of the two predominates over him, he belongs to its people. Thus, one who ascends a hundred degrees and descends one degree is not like one whose situation is the reverse.

However, a great error arises here for souls: a servant may descend a descent so far that it is farther than the distance between the East and the West, and farther than the distance between the heaven and the earth. Then his ascent of a thousand degrees does not compensate for this single descent. This is as in the authentic (sahih) report from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said:

"Indeed, a servant may utter a single word, giving it no thought, and it throws him into the Fire farther than the distance between the East and the West."

So what ascent can balance this descent? Descent is something necessary for a human being. However, among people there is one whose descent is into heedlessness (ghaflah). When such a person awakens from his heedlessness, he returns to his degree, or to one higher than it, according to the degree of his awakening.

Among them is one whose descent is into something permissible (mubah), without intending by it to seek help for obedience. When such a person returns to obedience, he may return to his degree, or may not reach it, or may rise above it. He may return with a higher resolve than before, or with a weaker resolve, or his resolve may return as it was.

Among them is one whose descent is into an act of disobedience, whether minor or major. Such a person, in returning to his degree, needs sincere repentance (tawbah nasuh) and true turning back (inabah).

People have differed as to whether, after repentance, he returns to the degree he was in. Those who hold that repentance erases the effect of the sin and makes its existence like its non-existence, so that it is as though it had never been, say that he returns. Those who hold that repentance's effect is only in dropping the punishment say that he does not return to the degree that he missed, and he does not reach it.

They said: The explanation of this is that during the time in which he disobeyed, he was prepared, by his occupation with obedience in the past, for another ascent and elevation carried by his previous deeds. This is like a man who earns each day by the whole of his wealth, which he possesses; and whenever the wealth multiplies, the profit multiplies. When he resumes work, he resumes ascent from a descent, whereas before that he was ascending from the lowest point to the highest, and between the two states there is a great gap.

These matters may grow strong, until the penitent returns to a degree higher than his former degree, and becomes after repentance better than he was before the sin. For such a person, the sin may be a mercy in his case, for it removed from him the disease of self-admiration, freed him from confidence in himself and from relying upon his deeds, placed the cheek of his humble supplication and his lowliness and brokenness upon the threshold of the door of his Lord and Master, made him know his worth, made him witness his poverty and his need for his Master's preservation of him, for His pardon of him and His forgiveness of him. It made him stand before his Lord in the station of sinful wrongdoers, head bowed before his Lord, ashamed, fearful of Him, anxious, belittling his obedience, magnifying his disobedience, knowing himself by deficiency and blame. His Lord is singular in perfection, praise and fidelity, as it has been said:

"Allah has reserved fidelity and praise for Himself, and has turned blame away from the man."

So whatever blessing from Allah reaches him, he regards it as too great for himself, sees himself as falling short of it, and does not consider himself worthy of it. And whatever calamity or trial reaches him, he sees himself as worthy of something greater than it, and sees his Master as having been good to him, in that He did not punish him according to the measure of his offence, nor a part of it, nor even the smallest fraction of it.

The basest of people and the most lacking in manliness is one who confronts them with vices. So how about the Great of the heavens and the earth, the King of the heavens and the earth, and the God of the people of the heavens and the earth? Had His mercy not preceded His wrath, and His forgiveness not preceded His punishment, the earth would have been crushed upon whoever confronted Him with what is not fitting to confront Him with. Had it not been for His forbearance and His forgiveness, the heavens and the earth would have been shaken by the disobedience of the servants. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease; and if they should cease, none could hold them after Him. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving﴾ [Fatir: 41].

So reflect on how this verse ends with two of His names: "the Forbearing" (al-Halim) and "the Forgiving" (al-Ghafur). See how beneath that you find that were it not for His forbearance toward the offenders and His forgiveness of the disobedient, the heavens and the earth would not remain firm.
