Allah, glorified is He, expelled the two parents from Paradise because of a single sin which they committed, in which they opposed His prohibition. He cursed Iblis, drove him away, and expelled him from the dominion of the heavens and the earth because of a single sin which he committed, in which he opposed His command. As for us, we are the foolish folk, as it has been said:

"We pile sins upon sins, and hope for the stations of the Gardens, for the one of lasting bliss."

"We certainly know that He expelled the two parents from His supreme dominion because of a single sin."

The purpose is that after repentance a servant may become better than he was before the sin and higher in degree. But the sin may also weaken his resolve, enfeeble his determination, and sicken his heart, so the medicine of repentance cannot restore him to his original health, and he does not return to his degree. Yet the sickness may also be removed, so that health returns as it was, and he returns to the like of his former deeds, and so returns to his degree.

All of this applies when his descent was into an act of disobedience. If his descent was into something that harms the very root of his faith, such as doubts, skepticism, and hypocrisy, then that is a descent for which no ascent is hoped for its doer, except by renewing his Islam.

**Question:** If it is said, then, is the Name (al-ism) according to you the Named (al-musamma) or other than it?

**Answer:** People have often erred on this matter and failed to grasp the truth of it. The word "name" is sometimes used to mean the Named itself, and sometimes to mean the expression that indicates it. When you say, "God said such-and-such," "God istawa (established Himself) upon His Throne," "God hears and sees," or "God created," the word refers to the Named Himself. When you say, "Allah is an Arabic name, and al-Rahman is an Arabic name, and al-Rahman is one of God's names, and al-Rahman has the form fa'lan, and al-Rahman is derived from mercy (rahma)," and so on, then "name" here refers to the Named.

It should not be said that the name is "other than" the Named, because the word "other" (ghayr) is ambiguous. If by "otherness" one means that the expression is different from the meaning, then this is true. But if one means that God, glorified is He, existed without a name until He gave Himself a name when He created, or until His creatures named Him with names of their own making, then this is among the greatest errors and deviations.

His saying in the hadith, "You named Yourself with it" (sammayta bihi nafsaka), and not "You created it for Yourself" or "Your creation named You with it," is evidence that He, glorified is He, spoke that name and named Himself with it, just as He named Himself in His Books, which He truly spoke, by His Names. His saying, "or You have kept it hidden with You in the knowledge of the unseen," is evidence that His Names are more than ninety-nine, and that He has Names and Attributes which He has kept hidden in the knowledge of the unseen with Himself, which no one else knows. On this basis, His saying, "Indeed God has ninety-nine names; whoever enumerates them enters Paradise," does not negate that He has other names. The statement is a single whole, meaning that He has names described by this quality, just as one says, "So-and-so has a hundred slaves whom he has prepared for trade, and a hundred horses which he has prepared for jihad."

This is the view of the majority (al-jumhur), but Ibn Hazm opposed them and claimed that His Names are confined to this number. The hadith shows that seeking nearness to Him through His Names and Attributes is more beloved to Him and more beneficial to the servant than seeking nearness to Him through His creatures. The same applies to the other hadiths, such as the hadith of the Greatest Name (al-ism al-a'zam): "O God, I ask You, because all praise is Yours; there is no god but You, the Bestower, the Originator of the heavens and the earth, O Possessor of Majesty and Honour, O Living, O Self-Subsisting." And in another hadith: "I ask You by my testifying that You are God, there is no god but You, the One, the Eternal Refuge, who has not begotten nor been begotten, and to whom no one is equal." And in another hadith: "O God, I ask You by Your knowledge of the unseen and Your power over creation."

All of these are sound hadiths, narrated by Ibn Hibban, Imam Ahmad, and al-Hakim.

This is the verification of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To God belong the most beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them﴾.

**[Chapter: The Eighth Station, the Station of the Names and Attributes]**

This is among the most exalted of the stations, higher and broader than what precedes it.

What leads one to this station is knowing how existence, in creation and command, is connected to the Most Beautiful Names and the Lofty Attributes, and how it is bound to them, even if the world with what is in it is only some of their effects and requirements.

This is among the most noble and excellent forms of knowledge. Each of His Names, glorified is He, has a specific attribute, for His Names are attributes of praise and perfection. Each attribute has a requirement and an act, either intransitive (lazim) or transitive (muta'addi). That act has a connection to an object which is among its necessities. This applies to His creation and His command, His reward and His punishment; all of this is the effect and requirement of the Most Beautiful Names.

It is impossible to suspend (ta'til) His Names from their attributes and meanings, or to suspend the attributes from what they require and call for of acts, or to suspend the acts from the objects acted upon. Just as it is impossible to suspend His object of action from His acts, or His acts from His attributes, or His attributes from His Names, or His Names and attributes from His essence.

Since His attributes are attributes of perfection, His acts are wisdoms and benefits, and His Names are most beautiful, then supposing their suspension from their requirements is impossible for Him. For this reason He denounces whoever suspends Him from His command and prohibition, His reward and punishment, and He states that by this they attribute to Him what is unfitting for Him and what He is exalted above. That such a judgment is an evil judgment from the one who makes it. And whoever attributes this to Him has not measured Him by His true measure nor magnified Him as He deserves. As He, exalted is He, said concerning those who deny prophethood, the sending of messengers, and the revelation of books: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure when they said, "God has not sent down anything upon a human being"﴾ [al-An'am: 91]. And He said concerning those who deny the Return, reward, and punishment: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure, while the earth entirely will be His grip on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded in His right hand﴾ [al-Zumar: 67]. And He said concerning those who permit that He would equate between opposites, such as the righteous and the wicked, the believers and the disbelievers: ﴿Do those who commit evil deeds think that We will make them like those who believe and do righteous deeds, equal in their living and their dying? Evil is what they judge﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 21]. So He informed that this is an evil judgment, unfitting for Him, which His Names and Attributes repudiate. And He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us? Exalted is God, the King, the Truth; there is no god but Him, Lord of the Noble Throne﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115], concerning this assumption and supposition, which His Names and Attributes repudiate.

Similar examples in the Qur'an are numerous, in which He negates of Himself what contradicts the requirement of His Names and Attributes, since that would entail suspending them from their perfection and their requirements.

So His Name al-Hamid (the Praiseworthy), al-Majid (the Glorious) prevents a human being from being left neglected, idle, suspended, not commanded and not forbidden, neither rewarded nor punished. Likewise His Name al-Hakim (the Wise) refuses that. Likewise His Name al-Malik (the King) and His Name al-Hayy (the Living) prevent Him from being suspended from action, for the reality of life is action; every living being is active. His being Creator and Self-Subsisting (al-Qayyum) is among the requirements of His life and its demands. His Name al-Sami' (the All-Hearing), al-Basir (the All-Seeing) requires something heard and something seen. His Name al-Khaliq (the Creator) requires a created thing; likewise al-Raziq (the Provider). His Name al-Malik requires a dominion, governance, management, giving and withholding, benevolence and justice, reward and punishment. The names al-Barr (the Benevolent), al-Muhsin (the Benefactor), al-Mu'ti (the Giver), al-Mannan (the Bountiful), and similar names require their effects and their requirements.

Having understood this: among His Names, glorified is He, are al-Ghaffar (the Forgiving), al-Tawwab (the Accepter of Repentance), al-'Afuww (the Pardoner). These Names necessarily have objects of their action: there must be a transgression that is forgiven, a repentance that is accepted, and offences that are pardoned. His Name al-Hakim necessarily has an object in which His judgment appears, for the requirement of these Names for their effects is like the requirement of the names al-Khaliq, al-Raziq, al-Mu'ti, and al-Mani' (the Withholder), with regard to the created being, the provided-for, the given, and the withheld. All these Names are most beautiful.

The Lord, exalted is He, loves His essence, His attributes, and His Names. So He is the Pardoner who loves pardon; He loves forgiveness; He loves repentance; and He rejoices at the repentance of His servant when he turns to Him with the greatest joy that can occur to the mind.

The measure of what He forgives, pardons from its doer, forbears from, accepts repentance for, and overlooks is from the requirement of His Names and Attributes. The attainment of what He loves and is pleased with from that, and what He praises Himself with, and what the people of His heavens and the people of His earth praise Him with, is among the requirements of His perfection and the demand of His praise.

He, glorified is He, is the Praiseworthy, the Glorious, and His praise and His glory require their effects. Among their effects are the forgiveness of slips, the remission of stumbles, the pardon of misdeeds, and the overlooking of offences, together with complete capacity to exact the right. He has knowledge of the offence and the measure of its punishment; so His forbearance is after His knowledge, His pardon is after His power, and His forgiveness is from the perfection of His might and wisdom. As the Messiah (ﷺ) said: ﴿If You punish them, they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 118]. That is, Your forgiveness comes from the perfection of Your power and wisdom. You are not like one who forgives out of weakness or overlooks out of ignorance of the value of the right; rather, You are All-Knowing of Your right, capable of exacting it, and Wise in its enforcement.

Whoever contemplates the operation of the effects of the Names and Attributes in the world and in the command will realise that the source of the decree of these offences by the servants, and their ordainment, is from the perfection of the Names, Attributes, and Acts. And their ultimate ends are likewise the requirement of His praise and His glory, just as they are the requirement of His lordship and His divinity.

So in all that He decrees and ordains there is perfect wisdom, manifest signs, disclosures to His servants of His Names and Attributes, and a call to them to love Him, remember Him, thank Him, and worship Him by His Most Beautiful Names. For every Name has a specific form of worship (ta'abbud) proper to it, in knowledge, recognition, and state. The most perfect of people in servitude ('ubudiyyah) is the one who worships by all the Names and Attributes that human beings can perceive. The servitude of one Name does not veil him from the servitude of another Name, unlike one whom the worship of the Name al-Qadir (the Powerful) veils from worshipping the Name al-Halim al-Rahim (the Forbearing, the Merciful), or whom the servitude of the Name al-Mu'ti (the Giver) veils from the servitude of the Name al-Mani' (the Withholder), or whom the servitude of the Names al-Rahim, al-'Afuww, and al-Ghafur veils from the Name al-Muntaqim (the Avenger), or whom the worship by the names of affection, goodness, kindness, and benevolence veils from the names of justice, majesty (al-jabarut), greatness, and pride, and similar things.

This is the path of the perfected among the wayfarers to God (al-sa'irin ila Allah). It is a path derived from the core of the Qur'an. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿To God belong the most beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them﴾ [al-A'raf: 180]. Calling upon Him by them encompasses the supplication of request (du'a' al-mas'alah), the supplication of praise (du'a' al-thana'), and the supplication of worship (du'a' al-ta'abbud). He, glorified is He, calls His servants to know Him by His Names and Attributes, to praise Him by them, and to take their share of servitude to them.

He, glorified is He, loves what the requirements of His Names and Attributes demand.

So He is the Knowing who loves every knowing person; the Generous who loves every generous person; the Odd (witr) who loves oddness; the Beautiful who loves beauty; the Pardoner who loves pardon and its people; the Modest who loves modesty and its people; the Righteous (barr) who loves the righteous; the Grateful (shakur) who loves the grateful; the Patient (sabur) who loves the patient; the Forbearing (halim) who loves those of forbearance. So because of His love, glorified is He, for repentance, forgiveness, pardon, and forgiveness of offence, He created those whom He forgives, accepts repentance from, and pardons; and He ordained over them what requires the occurrence of what is hateful and detestable to Him, so that there may follow what He loves and is pleased with. Thus His permitting it is like the permitting of hateful causes which lead to what is beloved.

> Perhaps what the servants find hateful
> is the cause of what they love, and a similar cause.

Causes, together with their effects, are of four kinds: a beloved cause leading to a beloved result; a hateful cause leading to a beloved result. These two kinds are the basis of His decrees and ordinances, glorified is He, in relation to what He loves and what He dislikes.

The third: a hateful cause leading to a hateful result. The fourth: a beloved cause leading to a hateful result. These two kinds are impossible with respect to Him, glorified is He, because the intended ends of His decree and ordinance, for the sake of which He created what He created and decreed what He decreed, can only be beloved and pleasing to the Lord. The causes that lead to them are divided into what is beloved to Him and what is hateful to Him.

So acts of obedience and monotheism (tawhid) are causes beloved to Him, leading to beneficence and to the reward which is also beloved to Him. Polytheism (shirk) and sins are causes He abhors, leading to justice which is beloved to Him. Although grace (fadl) is more beloved to Him than justice ('adl), the combination of justice and grace is more beloved to Him than the isolation of either from the other, because in them is the perfection of sovereignty and praise, the variety of commendation, and the perfection of power.

If it is said: it would have been possible for this beloved outcome to occur without the mediation of what is hateful.

It is said: this is a false question, because the existence of the necessitated thing without its necessary consequence is impossible. What is supposed in the mind to exist is something other than this beloved object of the Lord. The mind's judgment about it that it is beloved to the Lord is a judgment without knowledge; indeed it may be detested by the Lord, exalted is He, because it contradicts His wisdom. So when the mind judges that it is beloved to Him, that is an attribution to Him of what is not fitting for Him, and He is exalted above it.

So let the discerning person give this point its due reflection, for it is a place where feet slip and minds go astray. If those who do not know refrained from speech, disagreement would be far less.

This station is too great to be encompassed by a book or to be fully expressed in a discourse. We have only pointed to it with the slightest allusion, through which one may catch a glimpse of what lies behind it. God is the Granter of success and the Helper.

**(A Précis of Great Benefit)**

What is predicated as an attribute or a predicate of the Lord, blessed and exalted is He, is of several kinds:

First: what refers to the essence itself, such as your saying "essence" (dhat), "existent" (mawjud), and "thing" (shay').

Second: what refers to qualities that are meanings (sifat ma'nawiyyah), such as the All-Knowing (al-'Alim), the All-Powerful (al-Qadir), and the All-Hearing (al-Sami').

Third: what refers to His acts, such as the Creator (al-Khaliq) and the Provider (al-Razzaq).

Fourth: what refers to pure transcendence (tanzih mahd), and it must include an affirmative element, since there is no perfection in pure non-existence, such as al-Quddus (the Holy) and al-Salam (the Source of Peace).

**The Fifth:** Most people do not mention this type, which is a name that indicates a number of attributes without being restricted to one particular attribute. Rather, it indicates its meaning as a whole and not a single meaning, such as *al-Majid* (the Glorious), *al-'Azim* (the Great), and *al-Samad* (the Eternal Refuge). *Al-Majid* refers to one who is described by many attributes of perfection, and the word itself indicates this, since it is coined for vastness, abundance, and increase. From it come *istamjada al-markh* (the plant of *markh* grew abundantly) and *amjada al-naqa 'alafan* (he made the she-camel's fodder abundant). From it also comes ﴿Lord of the Throne, the Glorious﴾, used as an attribute of the Throne because of its vastness, greatness, and nobility. Consider how this name is linked to the request for blessings upon God's Messenger (ﷺ), as we have been taught, because it stands in the context of seeking more and of expressing the vastness, abundance, and permanence of giving. So in this request one uses a name that suits it, just as you say: "Forgive me and have mercy upon me, You are the Forgiving, the Merciful," and it would not be fitting to say, "You are the Hearing, the Seeing." Thus it returns to the one through whom one seeks nearness by His names and attributes, and this is among the closest and most beloved means of seeking nearness to Him. Among this is the hadith in the *Musnad* and at-Tirmidhi: "Persist in saying: O Possessor of Majesty and Honor" (*Alizzu bi-ya dhal-jalali wal-ikram*). And among it is: "O Allah, I ask You, because to You belongs all praise, there is no god but You, the Bestower, the Originator of the heavens and the earth, O Possessor of Majesty and Honor." This is a request to Him and a seeking of nearness to Him by praising Him and by stating that there is no god but Him, the Bestower. It is a seeking of nearness to Him through His names and attributes, and how worthy this is of being answered, and how great its standing is with the One who is asked. This is a great gate of *tawhid* (the affirmation of God's oneness), to which we have only alluded briefly, and it is opened to whom God grants insight. Explaining the great divine name *al-Samad* is also part of this.

Let us return to the purpose, which is describing Him with a name that includes many attributes. *Al-'Azim* is one who is described by many attributes of perfection. Likewise *al-Samad*. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the Lord (*sayyid*) who is perfect in his lordship. Ibn Wa'il said: it is the Lord whose lordship has reached its end. 'Ikrimah said: it is the one above whom there is no one. Likewise al-Zajjaj said: it is the one to whom lordship ultimately belongs, so everything turns to Him in need. Ibn al-Anbari said: "There is no disagreement among the linguists that *al-Samad* is the lord above whom there is no one, the one to whom people turn in their needs and affairs." Its derivation indicates this, for it comes from gathering and intention, the one toward whom intentions converge, and in whom the attributes of lordship are gathered. This is its original meaning in the language, as one poet said:

*"Has the messenger of death brought word of the best of the Banu Asad,*
*of 'Amr ibn Yarbu', and of the lord *al-Samad*?"*

The Arabs call their nobles *al-Samad* because the intentions of those who seek them converge upon them, and the attributes of lordship are gathered in them.

**The Sixth:** An attribute that arises from the combination of one name or attribute with another, which is an additional measure beyond each one individually, such as *al-Ghani al-Hamid* (the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy), *al-'Afuw al-Qadir* (the Pardoner, the Capable), *al-Hamid al-Majid* (the Praiseworthy, the Glorious), and so on. This applies to most of the paired attributes and joined names in the Qur'an. Self-sufficiency is an attribute of perfection, and praiseworthiness is likewise. The combination of self-sufficiency with praiseworthiness is another perfection. So He has praise for His self-sufficiency, praise for His praiseworthiness, and praise for the combination of the two. Likewise *al-'Afuw al-Qadir*, *al-Hamid al-Majid*, and *al-'Aziz al-Hakim* (the Mighty, the Wise). Reflect upon this.

Indeed, it is among the most noble of knowledge to apply negative attributes to the names of Allah, the Exalted. As for purely negative attributes, they do not enter into His attributes, unless they include an affirmation, such as *al-Ahad* (the One), which includes His singularity in lordship and divinity, and *al-Salam* (the Free from all defects), which includes His freedom from every deficiency that contradicts His perfection. Likewise, informing about Him through negations is because they include an affirmation, as in His saying: ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾, which includes the perfection of His life and self-subsistence. Likewise His saying: ﴿And no weariness touched Us﴾ includes the perfection of His power. Likewise His saying: ﴿And not an atom's weight escapes your Lord﴾ includes the perfection of His knowledge. Likewise His saying: ﴿He neither begets nor is He begotten﴾ includes the perfection of His self-sufficiency and independence. Likewise His saying: ﴿Nor is there any equal to Him﴾ includes His singularity in His perfection and that He has no like. Likewise His saying: ﴿No vision can grasp Him﴾ includes His greatness, and that He is exalted above being encompassed in a way that could be enclosed. This applies throughout everything He has described Himself with through negations. Several matters must be known here.

First: What falls under informing about Him is broader than what falls under His names and attributes, such as "thing," "existent," and "self-subsistent," for one informs about Him with them, but they are not among His Most Beautiful Names or His Highest Attributes.

Second: When an attribute is divided into perfection and deficiency, it does not enter His names in its absolute form. Rather, only its perfect form is applied to Him. Examples are *al-Murid* (the Willing), *al-Fa'il* (the Doer), and *al-Sani'* (the Maker). These terms do not enter His names. This is why whoever calls Him *al-Sani'* in absolute terms has erred. Rather, He is *al-Fa'\'al* (the one who does what He wills). Will, action, and making are divided, so He only applied to Himself from these what is most perfect in action and report.

Third: It does not follow that when one informs about Him by a restricted action, a general name must be derived from it for Him. Some later scholars erred in this, making among His Most Beautiful Names *al-Mudill* (the Misleader), *al-Fatin* (the Tempter), and *al-Makir* (the Schemer). Exalted is Allah above such statements. These names were applied to Him only in specific, particular acts, so it is not permissible to name Him by their unrestricted forms. And Allah knows best.

Fourth: His Most Beautiful Names, the Mighty and Majestic, are both proper names and descriptive attributes. Describing Him with them does not contradict their being proper names, unlike the attributes of created beings, which contradict their being proper names, because their attributes are shared, so the proper name that belongs exclusively to one is opposed to them. This is not so with His attributes.

Fifth: One of His names has several indications: it indicates the essence and the attribute by direct correspondence, and it indicates one of them by inclusion, and the other attribute by necessary implication.

Sixth: His Most Beautiful Names have two considerations: one in terms of the essence and one in terms of the attributes. By the first consideration they are synonymous, and by the second they are distinct.

Seventh: What is applied to Him in the domain of names and attributes is by revelation (*tawqifi*), but what is applied to Him in the domain of information need not be by revelation, such as "eternal," "thing," "existent," and "self-subsistent." This is the decisive resolution of the question of whether His names are fixed by revelation or whether it is permissible to apply to Him some names that revelation did not report.

Eighth: When a name is applied to Him, it is permissible to derive from it the verbal noun and the verb, and to inform about Him with them, as verb and verbal noun. For example, *al-Sami' al-Basir al-Qadir* (the Hearing, the Seeing, the Capable): from them one applies hearing, sight, and power, and one informs about Him with verbs from these, as in ﴿Allah has indeed heard﴾ and ﴿So We measured, and excellent were the measurers﴾. This is if the verb is transitive. If it is intransitive, one does not inform about Him with it, as with *al-Hayy* (the Living). Rather, one applies the name and the verbal noun but not the verb, so one does not say "He lives" (*hayya*).

Ninth: The actions of the Lord, blessed and exalted, proceed from His names and attributes, while the names of created beings proceed from their actions. The Lord, blessed and exalted, acts out of His perfection, while the created being is perfected by his actions. Names are derived for the created being after he has been perfected by action. The Lord has always been perfect, so His actions proceed from His perfection, since He is perfect in His essence and attributes. So His actions proceed from His perfection. He was perfect and so He acted, while the created being acted and so became perfect with the perfection suitable to him.

Tenth: Enumerating the Most Beautiful Names and knowing them is the foundation for knowing every knowable thing. For the knowables apart from Him are either creations of His, or commands, which are either knowledge of what He created or knowledge of what He legislated. The source of creation and command proceeds from His Most Beautiful Names, and they are bound to them in the way that what is required is bound to what requires it. So the whole matter proceeds from His Most Beautiful Names. This is all good, and does not depart from the benefit of the servants, from compassion and mercy toward them, and from kindness to them by perfecting them in what He commanded them and forbade them. So all His command is benefit, wisdom, gentleness, and kindness, since its source is His Most Beautiful Names. His entire action does not depart from justice, wisdom, benefit, and mercy, since its source is His Most Beautiful Names. So there is no inconsistency in His creation, no futility, and He did not create His creation in vain, nor aimlessly, nor idly. Just as every existent other than Him exists by His bringing it into being, so the existence of whatever is other than Him follows His existence, as the created effect follows its creator. Likewise, knowledge of His names is the foundation for knowledge of everything other than Him. Knowledge of His names and enumerating them is the foundation for all knowledge. Whoever enumerates His names as is fitting for a created being has enumerated all knowledge, since enumerating His names is the foundation for enumerating every knowable thing, because the knowables proceed from them and are bound to them. Reflect on how creation and command proceed from His knowledge and wisdom, the Exalted. For this reason you will not find in them any defect or inconsistency, because the defect that occurs in what a servant commands or does is either due to his ignorance of it or to his lack of wisdom. But the Lord, the Exalted, is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise, so no defect, inconsistency, or contradiction reaches His action or His command.

Eleventh: All His names are most beautiful, and there is no name among them other than this at all. It has been said before that some of His names are applied to Him by consideration of action, such as *al-Khaliq* (the Creator), *al-Raziq* (the Provider), *al-Muhyi* (the Giver of Life), and *al-Mumit* (the Causer of Death). This indicates that all His actions are pure goodness with no evil in them. For if He had done evil, a name would have been derived from it for Him, and not all His names would be most beautiful, and this is false. So evil is not attributed to Him. Just as it does not enter His attributes or touch His essence, it does not enter His actions. So evil does not belong to Him; it is not attributed to Him as an action or as an attribute. Rather, it enters what is made, which is distinct from Him, and there is a difference between the action and the thing made. Evil subsists in His creation, which is separate from Him, not in His action, which is His action. Reflect upon this, for it has been obscure to many theologians (*mutakallimun*), whose feet have slipped and whose understanding has gone astray in it, while God guided the people of truth to what they differed about by His permission, and God guides whom He wills to a straight path.

**The Twelfth:** On explaining the levels of enumerating His names, by which whoever enumerates them enters Paradise. This is the pivot of happiness and the axis of salvation and success.

*The first level:* enumerating their words and number.
*The second level:* understanding their meanings and what they signify.
*The third level:* calling upon Him by them, as He said: ﴿To Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them﴾. This has two parts. One is calling in praise and worship, and the second is calling in request and asking. So one does not praise Him except by His Most Beautiful Names and His Highest Attributes, and likewise one does not ask except by them. So one does not say "O Existent," "O Thing," or "O Essence, forgive me and have mercy upon me." Rather, in every request one asks by a name that is suitable to that request, so the petitioner is seeking nearness to Him through that name. Whoever reflects on the supplications of the prophets, especially their seal and leader (ﷺ), will find them in agreement with this. This expression is better than the expression of one who says "he takes on the character of God's names," for that is not a precise expression, and it is derived from the saying of the philosophers about "assimilating to God as far as one can." Better than it is the expression of Abu al-Hakam ibn Burhan, which is "worship" (*ta'abbud*), and better than that is the expression that agrees with the Qur'an, which is supplication that includes worship and request. So its levels are four. The most strongly rejected is the expression of the philosophers, which is "assimilation" (*tashabbuh*). Better than it is the expression of one who said "taking on character" (*takhalluq*). Better than it is the expression of one who said "worship" (*ta'abbud*). The best of all is supplication (*du'a'*), which is the wording of the Qur'an.

**The Thirteenth:** The theologians have differed about the names that are applied both to God and to servants, such as *al-Hayy* (the Living), *al-Sami'* (the Hearing), *al-Basir* (the Seeing), *al-'Alim* (the Knowing), *al-Qadir* (the Capable), *al-Malik* (the King), and the like. One group of theologians said they are literal in the servant and figurative in the Lord. This is the view of the extreme Jahmiyya (followers of Jahm ibn Safwan), and it is the most corrupt and most deficient of views. The second is the opposite: they are literal in the Lord and figurative in the servant. This is the view of Abu al-'Abbas al-Nashi'. The third: they are literal in both. This is the view of the people of the Sunna (*Ahl al-Sunna*), and it is the correct view. The difference of the two realities in them does not remove them from being literal in both. The Lord has of them what suits His majesty, and the servant has of them what suits him. This is not the place to examine the sources of these views, to refute their falsehoods, and to affirm their truths, for the purpose is to point out matters that should be known in this domain. If the aim were to expand on them, it would require two or more volumes.

**The Fourteenth:** A name and attribute of this kind has three considerations: a consideration in itself, setting aside its being restricted to the Lord, blessed and exalted, or to the servant; a consideration of it as referred to the Lord and specific to Him; and a consideration of it as referred to the servant and restricted to him. What is necessarily tied to the name by its essence and reality is established for both the Lord and the servant. The Lord has of it what suits His perfection, and the servant has of it what suits him. An example is the name *al-Sami'* (the Hearing), which necessarily entails perceiving what is heard, and *al-Basir* (the Seeing), which necessarily entails seeing what is seen, and *al-'Alim* (the Knowing), *al-Qadir* (the Capable), and the rest of the names. For the condition for correctly applying them is that their meanings and realities be present in the one described by them. So what is necessarily tied to these names by their essence, affirming it for the Lord, blessed and exalted, is not objectionable in any way. Rather, it is established for Him in a way in which His creatures do not resemble Him and do not share with Him. Whoever negates it from Him because it is applied to a created being has deviated from His names and denied the attributes of His perfection. Whoever affirms it for Him in a way that resembles His creatures has likened Him to His creatures, and whoever likens God to His creatures has disbelieved. Whoever affirms it for Him in a way that does not resemble His creatures, but as is fitting to His majesty and greatness, has been freed from the filth of likening and the blood of negation. This is the way of the people of the Sunna.

What is necessarily tied to an attribute because it is referred to the servant must be negated from God, as life in the servant necessarily involves sleep, drowsiness, need for nourishment, and the like. Likewise, what is necessarily tied to his will, such as the movement of his soul to obtain what benefits him and to repel what harms him. Likewise, what is necessarily tied to his height, such as his need for what is above him, his being carried, dependent, or encompassed. All this must be negated from the Holy, the Free from all defects, blessed and exalted.

What is necessarily tied to an attribute because of its being specific to God, the Exalted, is never affirmed for a created being in any way. Such as His knowledge, which necessarily entails eternity, necessity, and encompassing every knowable thing, and His power, will, and the rest of His attributes. For what is specific to Him among them cannot be affirmed for a created being. When you comprehend this rule, understanding it as it should be understood, you will be saved from the two calamities that are the root of the theologians' affliction: the calamity of negation (*ta'til*) and the calamity of likening (*tashbih*). For when you fulfill this station of understanding in its due measure, you affirm for God the Most Beautiful Names and the Highest Attributes in truth. You are saved from negation and you deny for them the specific properties of created beings and their resemblance to them, and so you are saved from likening. So reflect on this point, and make it your refuge to which you return in this domain. And God is the granter of success to what is right.

**The Fifteenth:** When an attribute subsists in a described subject, four matters necessarily follow from it: two verbal and two conceptual. The two verbal are affirmative and negative. The affirmative is that the described subject is derived a name from it and is informed about by it. The negative is that its ruling does not return to another and is not a report about another. This is a great rule in knowing the names and attributes, so let us mention one example, which is the attribute of speech. When it subsists in a locus, it becomes the speaking of that one, and not of the one in whom it does not subsist. It is reported about him by it, and its ruling returns to him and not to another. So one says: he spoke, commanded, forbade, called out, conversed in secret, reported, addressed, spoke, and made speak, and the like. These rulings are impossible for another, so by these rulings and names one infers that the attribute subsists in him, and that its negation from another is because it does not subsist in that other. This is the foundation of the Sunna, by which they refuted the Mu'tazila and the Jahmiyya, and it is among the soundest principles in both its affirmation and its negation.

**The Sixteenth:** The Most Beautiful Names cannot be confined by any limit or restricted to any number. For God, the Exalted, has names and attributes that He has kept to Himself in the knowledge of the unseen with Him, which no near angel nor sent prophet knows. As in the authentic hadith: "I ask You by every name that is Yours, by which You named Yourself, or which You revealed in Your Book, or which You kept to Yourself in the knowledge of the unseen with You." It is authentic according to the more likely view. So He divided His names into three categories: a category by which He named Himself and made it manifest to whom He willed among His angels or others, and He did not reveal it in His Book; a category which He revealed in His Book and by which He made Himself known to His servants; and a category which He kept to Himself in the knowledge of His unseen, so none of His creation has been given knowledge of it. For this reason He said "kept to Myself," meaning that He alone knows it. The meaning is not that He alone names Himself by it, because this exclusivity holds for the names which Allah revealed in His Book.

From this is the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of intercession: "Then He will open to me praises of Him with which I cannot praise Him now." Narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim. Those praises fulfill His names and attributes.

And among it is his saying: "I cannot enumerate Your praise; You are as You have praised Yourself." Narrated by Muslim, Abu Dawud, and others.

As for his saying (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah has ninety-nine names; whoever enumerates them enters Paradise." Narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim. The statement is a single unit, and his saying "whoever enumerates them enters Paradise" is a description, not a future report. The meaning is that He has many names, and the characteristic of them is that whoever enumerates them enters Paradise. This does not negate that He has other names beyond them, just as you say, "So-and-so has a hundred slaves, whom he has prepared for jihad." This does not negate that he has other slaves besides them, prepared for other than jihad. There is no disagreement among the scholars on this.

Seventeenth: His names, may He be exalted, include some that are applied to Him singly and also paired with others, and this is the majority of His names. Such are al-Qadir (the All-Powerful), al-Sami' (the All-Hearing), al-Basir (the All-Seeing), al-'Aziz (the Mighty), and al-Hakim (the Wise). It is permissible to call upon Him with these singly or paired with others, so you say: "O Mighty, O Forbearing, O Forgiving, O Merciful," and to mention each name separately. Likewise in praising Him and speaking of Him, it is permissible to use them singly or in combination.

Among them are names that are not applied to Him on their own, but only together with their opposites, such as al-Mani' (the Withholder), al-Darr (the Harmer), and al-Muntaqim (the Avenger). It is not permissible to mention these separately from their opposites, for they are paired with al-Mu'ti (the Giver), al-Nafi' (the Benefactor), and al-'Afu (the Pardoner). So He is al-Mu'ti, al-Mani', al-Darr, al-Nafi', al-Muntaqim, al-'Afu, al-Mu'izz (the Exalter), al-Mudhill (the Abaser). Perfection lies in pairing each of these names with its opposite, because what is meant is that He alone holds lordship and governs His creation and disposes of them by giving and withholding, benefiting and harming, pardoning and avenging. As for praising Him solely by withholding, avenging, or harming, this is not permissible. These paired names function like a single name, whose parts cannot be separated from one another. Although they are many, they operate as one name. For this reason they never came singly and were never applied to Him except in pairs. Know this. If you said, "O Abaser, O Harmer, O Withholder," and reported this about Him, you would not be praising Him or extolling Him until you mentioned their opposites.

Eighteenth: Attributes are of three types: attributes of perfection, attributes of deficiency, and attributes that imply neither perfection nor deficiency. Although hypothetical division may suggest a fourth type, namely that which is perfection in one respect and deficiency in another, the Lord, exalted is He, is exempt from the three types and is described by the first. His attributes are all pure perfection. He is described by attributes in their most complete form and possesses the most complete perfection. Likewise, His names that indicate His attributes are the most beautiful and most complete names. There is no name more beautiful than them, nothing else can take their place, and nothing else conveys their meaning. Explaining one of these names by another is not a pure synonym-based definition but is an approximation for the sake of clarification. Once you understand this, for each attribute of perfection He has the most beautiful name, the most complete and perfect in meaning, and the furthest and most free from any trace of defect or deficiency. So from the attribute of comprehension, He has al-'Alim (the All-Knowing) and al-Khabir (the All-Aware), rather than al-'Aqil (the Intelligent) or al-Faqih (the Discerning). From the attribute of hearing and seeing, He has al-Sami' and al-Basir, rather than al-Sami' (the Listener) or al-Basir (the Seer) or al-Nazir (the Observer). From the attributes of goodness, He has al-Barr (the Benevolent), al-Rahim (the Merciful), and al-Wadud (the Loving), rather than al-Rafiq (the Gentle), al-Shafiq (the Compassionate), and similar names. Likewise al-'Ali (the Most High) and al-'Azim (the Mighty), rather than al-Rafi' (the Exalted) or al-Sharif (the Noble). Likewise al-Karim (the Generous), rather than al-Sakhi (the Bountiful). Al-Khaliq (the Creator), al-Bari' (the Originator), and al-Musawwir (the Fashioner), rather than al-Fa'il (the Doer) or al-Sani' (the Maker) or al-Mushkil (the Shaper). Al-Ghafur (the Forgiving) and al-'Afu (the Pardoner), rather than al-Safuh (the Forbearing) or al-Satir (the Concealer). Likewise, all His other names, He applies to Himself the most complete and most beautiful of them, and those that nothing else can substitute for. Reflect on this: His names are the most beautiful names, just as His attributes are the most perfect attributes. So do not deviate from what He named Himself to something else, just as you must not go beyond what He described Himself with, and what His Messenger described Him with, to what the deniers and the negators describe Him with.

Nineteenth: Among His beautiful names are some that indicate several attributes, and that name encompasses all of them in the same way that a name indicating a single attribute encompasses it, as explained earlier. Such are His names al-'Azim (the Magnificent), al-Majid (the Glorious), and al-Samad (the Eternal Refuge). Ibn 'Abbas said, as narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim in his tafsir: "al-Samad: the Lord who has perfected His lordship; al-Sharif: the one who has perfected His nobility; al-'Azim: the one who has perfected His greatness; al-Halim: the one who has perfected His forbearance; al-'Alim: the one who has perfected His knowledge; al-Hakim: the one who has perfected His wisdom; and He is the one who has perfected the kinds of His nobility and lordship; He is Allah, subhanahu." Its chain is weak. These are His attributes, which befit none but Him: ﴿He has no equal, and nothing is like Him. Glory be to Allah, the One, the Subduer.﴾ This is his wording. This is something hidden from many who have undertaken to explain the Most Beautiful Names. They explained the name without its full meaning, and thereby diminished it without knowing it. Whoever has not comprehensively grasped this has wronged the Greatest Name and reduced its meaning. So reflect on it.

Twentieth: This encompasses all the aspects mentioned above, and it is knowing the deviation (ilhad) regarding His names, so that one does not fall into it. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And to Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them, and leave those who deviate concerning His names. They will be recompensed for what they used to do.﴾

Ilhad concerning His names is diverting them, along with their realities and meanings, from the truth established for them. It is derived from inclination, as its root L-H-D indicates. From it comes al-lahd, the cleft in the side of a grave that inclines away from the middle. From it also comes al-mulhid fi al-din, one who inclines from truth to falsehood. Ibn al-Sikkit said: "al-Mulhid is one who inclines away from truth, introducing into it what is not part of it." From it also comes al-multahad, which is of this form. The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And you will never find, besides Him, a refuge (multahad)﴾ mean a place to which you turn, flee, seek shelter, and make supplication, inclining to it away from anything else. The Arabs say: "Fulan iltahada ila Fulan" when he turned toward him.

Once this is understood, ilhad concerning the names of Allah, the Exalted, has several types. The first: naming idols by them, such as their naming al-Lat from al-Ilah (the Deity) and al-'Uzza from al-'Aziz (the Mighty), and their calling the idol a god. This is true ilhad, for they diverted His names to their idols and false gods. The second: naming Him by what does not befit His majesty, such as the Christians calling Him Father, or the philosophers calling Him an originator by His essence or an efficient cause by nature, and similar things. The third: describing Him with what He is exalted and sanctified above of deficiencies, such as the words of the most wicked of the Jews that He is poor, their saying that He rested after creating His creation, and their saying: ﴿The hand of Allah is chained﴾, and similar things which constitute ilhad concerning His names and attributes.

The fourth: nullifying the names of their meanings and denying their realities, such as the statement of the Jahmiyya and their followers that they are mere words that include no attributes or meanings. They apply to Him the names al-Sami' (the All-Hearing), al-Basir (the All-Seeing), al-Hayy (the Living), al-Rahim (the Merciful), al-Mutakallim (the Speaker), and al-Murid (the Willer), yet they say He has no life, no hearing, no sight, no speech, and no will subsisting in Him. This is among the greatest ilhad concerning them, rationally, legally, linguistically, and by innate nature. It is the counterpart of the ilhad of the polytheists, for those gave His names and attributes to their deities, while these stripped Him of the attributes of His perfection, denied them, and nullified them. Both are deviators concerning His names. Then the Jahmiyya and their offshoots differ in this ilhad: among them are the extreme, the moderate, and the unfortunate. Whoever denies anything of what Allah described Himself with, or what His Messenger described Him with, has committed ilhad in that matter. Let him take little or much of it.

The fifth: likening His attributes to the attributes of His creatures, exalted is Allah far above what the likeners say. This ilhad stands opposite the ilhad of the nullifiers. Those denied His attributes of perfection and rejected them, while these likened them to the attributes of His creatures. Thus ilhad unites them, though its paths diverge among them. Allah has absolved the followers of His Messenger and his heirs who uphold his Sunnah from all of this. They did not describe Him except with what He described Himself with, did not deny His attributes, did not liken them to the attributes of His creatures, and did not divert them from what was revealed to him, in wording or in meaning. Rather, they affirmed for Him names and attributes and denied Him any resemblance to created things. Thus their affirmation was free from likening, and their glorification free from nullification. This is unlike one who likened Him until it was as if he worshipped an idol, or nullified Him until it was as if he worshipped only nothingness. Ahl al-Sunnah are the middle path among sects, just as the Muslims are the middle path among religions. They kindle the lamps of their knowledge from: ﴿a blessed olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it; light upon light; Allah guides to His light whom He wills.﴾ So we ask Allah, the Exalted, to guide us to His light, to make easy for us the way to reach His pleasure and follow His Messenger. Indeed He is near and responsive.

These are twenty benefits, added to the principle with which we began concerning the categories of what the Lord, blessed and exalted, is described by. So hold fast to knowing and observing them. Then explain the Most Beautiful Names if you find a comprehending heart, an articulate tongue, and a receptive place; otherwise silence is more fitting for you, for the majesty of Lordship is greater and more glorious than what occurs to the mind or what speech can express: ﴿And above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows.﴾ until knowledge ends with the One who encompasses all things in knowledge.

May Allah, by His grace, help us to compose the explanation of the Most Beautiful Names, observing in it the rules of these principles, free from ilhad concerning His names and from nullifying His attributes. He is the Bestower of grace, and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.

The single soul and its mate are Adam and Eve, and the two of them who "made for Him partners in what He gave them" are the idolaters among their offspring. Do not turn to other interpretations, such as the claim that Adam and Eve had children who died, so Iblis came to them and said, "If you wish your child to live, name him Abd al-Harith," and they did so. Allah, exalted is He, chose Adam and guided him, so he would not associate partners with Him after that.

(Section)

[The Cause of Passionate Love]

Passionate love ('ishq) is composed of two things: admiration for the beloved, and desire to attain him. When either of these is absent, passionate love is absent. The cause of passionate love has baffled many intelligent people, and some of them spoke about it in words that are better left unmentioned in favour of what is correct.

We say: The wisdom of Allah, exalted is He, in His creation and command has been established upon the occurrence of harmony and affinity between similar things, and upon a thing's being naturally drawn to what agrees with it and is of its kind, and fleeing from what opposes it and naturally recoiling from it. The secret of mixing and connection in the upper and lower worlds is nothing other than resemblance, likeness and agreement, and the secret of separation and disconnection is nothing other than the absence of likeness and resemblance. Upon this creation and command stand. Like is inclined toward like and returns to it, and opposite flees from its opposite and recoils from it. Allah, the Exalted, has said: ﴿He it is who created you from a single soul and made from it its mate that he might find tranquility in her﴾ [al-A'raf: 189]. So He, glorified is He, made the reason for a man's tranquility with his wife to be that she is of his kind and essence. Thus the reason for the aforementioned tranquility, which is love, is that she is from him. This shows that the cause is not beauty of form, nor agreement in purpose and will, nor in character and guidance, though these too are among the causes of tranquility and affection.

It is established in the Sahih (the authentic collection) from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Souls are assembled troops; those among them that recognise one another become attuned, and those among them that are strangers to one another become estranged." In Musnad al-Imam Ahmad and others, concerning the occasion of this hadith: a woman in Makkah used to make people laugh, then she came to Madinah and stayed with a woman who also made people laugh, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Souls are assembled troops," and the hadith continues.

Allah's law is established that the ruling on a thing is the ruling on its like. His law never distinguishes between two alike, nor combines two opposites. Whoever thinks otherwise either has little knowledge of the Shari'ah, or falls short in recognising sameness and difference, or attributes to His law what He has not sent down any authority for, and it is rather from the opinions of men. By His wisdom and justice His creation and His law became manifest, and by justice and balance creation and law stand: equality between two alike, and distinction between two different.

Just as this is established in this world, so it is on the Day of Resurrection. Allah, the Exalted, has said: ﴿Gather those who did wrong and their companions, and what they used to worship besides Allah, and lead them to the path of Hellfire﴾ [al-Saffat: 22].

'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), and after him the Imam Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him), said: "Their companions (azwajahum) are their likes and their counterparts."

And Allah, the Exalted, has said: ﴿And when the souls are paired﴾ [al-Takwir: 7], meaning: He joins every person of deeds with his like and counterpart. So He joins those who loved one another for Allah's sake in Paradise, and joins those who loved one another in obedience to Satan in the Fire. A person is with whom he loves, whether he wishes it or not. In al-Mustadrak of al-Hakim and others, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "A person does not love a people without being gathered with them."

Summing up: this kind of analogy (qiyas) in the Qur'an comes only as something rejected and blamed. Among its examples is the Exalted One's saying: ﴿Indeed, those you invoke besides Allah are servants like you. So call upon them, and let them respond to you, if you are truthful. Do they have feet by which they walk? Or do they have hands by which they strike? Or do they have eyes by which they see? Or do they have ears by which they hear? Say: Call your partners [to help you], then plot against me and give me no respite.﴾

Here Allah, glorified is He, made clear that these idols are mere forms and images, empty of the attributes of divinity; that the meaning which is required (for worship) is absent from them; and that, even if they were called upon, they would not respond. They are images devoid of the qualities and meanings that would call for their worship. He reinforced this affirmation with His saying: ﴿Do they have feet by which they walk? Or do they have hands by which they strike? Or do they have eyes by which they see? Or do they have ears by which they hear?﴾ That is, all the limbs these idols possess, which your hands have carved, are merely lifeless forms, void of their realities and attributes. For the meaning intended and specific to the foot is walking, and this is absent in this foot; the meaning specific to the hand is striking, and this is absent in this hand; what is intended by the eye is seeing, and this is absent in this eye; and from the ear is hearing, and this is absent in it. The forms in all of this are established and existent, yet all of them are empty and void of attributes and meanings. Thus their existence and non-existence are equal. All of this refutes the analogy of resemblance (qiyas al-shabah) that is devoid of the effective cause ('illah mu'aththirah) and of the attribute that necessitates the ruling (hukm). And Allah knows best.

Among its interpretations, according to one of the two readings, is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you see them looking at you, yet they do not see﴾ (7:198). For they would look at the form of the Prophet ﷺ with the outward senses, but they did not perceive the reality of his prophethood and its meaning with the inward sense, which is the sight of the heart.

The second opinion is that the pronoun refers to the idols. Concerning this there are two views.

The first is that it is figurative, meaning: as if they were looking at you, while they have no eyes with which to see you.

The second is that what is meant is facing: the Arabs say, "My house looks at your house," meaning it faces it.

He had gathered for him the noble qualities of character in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Take what is easy and forgive, enjoin what is right, and turn away from the ignorant.﴾ [al-A'raf: 199]

Ja'far ibn Muhammad said: "Allah commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) with the noble qualities of character. There is no verse in the Qur'an more comprehensive of the noble qualities of character than this verse." It has been mentioned that when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Jibril: "What is this?" He said: "I do not know until I ask." So he asked, then returned to him and said: "Allah commands you that you join ties with the one who cuts you off, give to the one who withholds from you, and pardon the one who wronged you."

There is no doubt that the one who is obeyed has three states with the people:

The first: commanding them and forbidding them in what is in their interest.

The second: taking from them what they offer of the obedience that is due from them.

The third: the people with him are of two kinds: one who agrees with him and supports him, and one who opposes him and stands against him. And upon him, in each of these, there is an obligation.

His obligation in their commanding and forbidding is to enjoin what is good (al-ma'ruf), which is that by which their welfare and the welfare of their affairs is achieved, and to forbid them from its opposite.

His obligation regarding what they offer him of obedience is to take from them what is easy for them, and what their souls are willing to give, out of generosity and by choice, and not to burden them with hardship and difficulty so that he corrupts them.

His obligation when the ignorant act ignorantly toward him is to turn away from them, and not to repay them in kind or seek revenge against them for himself.

So Allah, Exalted is He, said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Take what is easy and forgive, enjoin what is right, and turn away from the ignorant.﴾ [al-A'raf: 199]

'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "Allah commanded His Prophet to take the pardon (al-'afw) from the characters of the people."

Mujahid said: "It means: take the pardon from the characters and deeds of the people without causing them distress, such as accepting their excuses, pardoning and being lenient, and not being excessive in searching out and probing into the realities of their inner selves."

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "Take what is left over of their wealth." That is what is surplus beyond the needs of the family. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219]

Then He said: ﴿And enjoin what is right﴾ [al-A'raf: 199], and this is every act of goodness (ma'ruf). The best of it is tawhid (monotheism), then the rights of worship (huquq al-'ubudiyyah), then the rights of people (huquq al-'ibad).

Then He said: ﴿And turn away from the ignorant﴾ [al-A'raf: 199], meaning: if the ignorant person acts foolishly toward you, do not respond to him with foolishness. Like His saying: ﴿When the ignorant address them, they say: "Peace."﴾ [al-Furqan: 63] On this basis, the verse is not abrogated (mansukhah). Rather, he turns away from him while upholding Allah's right over him, and does not take revenge for himself.

Such was his (ﷺ) character. Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was the best of people in character." He also said: "I never touched silk brocade or silk softer than the palm of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Nor did I ever smell a scent better than the scent of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). I served the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for ten years, and he never said to me 'Uff' (an expression of displeasure). Nor did he ever say, regarding something I had done: 'Why did you do it?' Nor regarding something I had not done: 'Why did you not do it?'" Agreed upon by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) also informed that "righteousness (al-birr) is good character."

In Sahih Muslim, from al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about righteousness and sin. He said: 'Righteousness is good character, and sin is that which troubles your breast and you dislike that people should become aware of it.'"

So he (ﷺ) contrasted righteousness with sin, and informed that righteousness is good character, while sin is what wavers in the breasts.

This indicates that good character is the whole of the religion. It is the realities of faith and the laws of Islam. For this reason he contrasted it with sin.

(Benefit)

It has been said: The proofs of Allah do not contradict one another; rather, they are all truth, each confirming the others. If Allah, Glorified is He, has affirmed ignorance for the one who does evil, while he acknowledges Him, His messenger, and that He has forbidden that and threatened punishment for it, yet He judges him with the ignorance because of which he committed the evil, then how about the one who associates partners with Him, disbelieves in His signs, and opposes His messengers? Is that not the most ignorant of the ignorant? Allah, Exalted is He, called His enemies ignorant after establishing the proof against them, when He said: ﴿Take what is easy and forgive, enjoin what is right, and turn away from the ignorant.﴾ So He commanded him to turn away from them after establishing the proof against them and their knowing that he was truthful. And He said: ﴿When the ignorant address them, they say: "Peace."﴾ So "the ignorant" here are the disbelievers who knew that he was the Messenger of Allah. This knowledge does not preclude judging its possessor as ignorant. Rather, knowledge is affirmed for him, and negated for him in one respect, as Allah said about the Jewish magicians: ﴿And they had certainly known that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter. And wretched is that for which they sold themselves, if they had known.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102] So He affirmed for them the knowledge by which the proof is established against them, and negated from them the beneficial knowledge that necessitates abandoning harm. This is the crux of the matter and the secret of the answer. No one enters the Fire except a knower, and no one enters it except an ignorant one. This knowledge does not combine with ignorance in one man. To clarify this: desire, heedlessness, and aversion prevent one from its perfection, from keeping it present, and from knowing its requirement in detail, and they set up for its possessor doubts and interpretations that oppose it. So the motivating force keeps weakening, and the counter-force takes effect until it is as if it had never existed, and its possessor becomes in every respect like the ignorant. If Iblis had known that his refusal to prostrate to Adam would lead to what it led to, and that it would bring upon him the greatest punishment, and he had been certain of that, he would not have refrained from it. But Allah placed between him and this knowledge, so that His decree might be carried out and His judgment and destiny might take effect. And if Adam and Hawwa' had thought that if they ate from the tree they would be expelled from the Garden and that what befell them would befall them, they would not have approached it. And if the enemies of the messengers had known in detail what would happen to them and what would befall them on the Day of Resurrection, and had been certain of it, they would not have opposed them. Allah said of the people of Pharaoh: ﴿And he had certainly warned them of Our seizure, but they disputed the warnings.﴾ [al-Qamar: 36] And He said: ﴿And a barrier was placed between them and what they desired, as was done with their like before. Indeed, they were in disquieting doubt.﴾ [Saba': 54] And He said of the hypocrites, who had witnessed the signs of the Messenger and the proofs of his truthfulness with their own eyes: ﴿And their hearts were in doubt, so they wavered in their doubt.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 45] And He said: ﴿But you tempted yourselves and waited and doubted.﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1; al-Hadid: 14] And He said: ﴿In their hearts is a disease﴾ [al-Baqarah: 10], which is doubt. If this were due to the absence of the knowledge by which the proof is established against them, they would not be in the lowest level of the Fire. Rather, this was after the proof had been established against them and after their knowledge, which did not benefit them. Knowledge certainly weakens through heedlessness, aversion, following desire, and preferring appetites, and these matters produce doubts and interpretations that oppose it. So reflect carefully upon this point, for it is among the secrets of divine decree, the Sharia, and justice. Knowledge may refer to complete knowledge that necessarily produces its effect, and it may refer to the mere inclination (al-muqtada) toward it, even if it is not complete because its conditions are not fulfilled or its obstacles are not removed. The second can coexist with ignorance, but not the first. It is thus clear that the root of evil deeds is ignorance and the absence of knowledge. If that is so, then the absence of knowledge is not an existing thing. Rather, it is the absence of hearing, sight, power, and will, and an absence is not a thing that requires an agent who produces it. It suffices for it the absence of the willing of its opposite and the absence of the cause that necessitates its opposite. Pure absence is not attributed to Allah, for it is evil, and evil does not pertain to Him. So when this decisive knowledge is absent from the servant, and his soul by its nature is moving and willing, and that is among the requirements of its nature, it moves by the impulse of nature and appetite, and that prevails over the call of knowledge and recognition, so it falls into the causes of evil, inevitably.

[Section: On his (ﷺ) conduct toward his allies and his party]

So He commanded him to restrain himself with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face, and not to let his eyes turn away from them. He commanded him to pardon them, to ask forgiveness for them, to consult them in affairs, and to pray over them.

He commanded him to shun those who disobey him and stay away from him until they repent and return to obedience to him, just as he shunned the three who were left behind.

He commanded him to establish the prescribed punishments (hudud) upon those among them who committed what necessitates them, and that in this matter they should be equal before him, the noble and the lowly alike.

And in repelling his enemies from the devils of mankind, He commanded him to repel with what is better, so that he would meet the harm of one who harmed him with kindness, his ignorance with forbearance, his injustice with pardon, and his severing of ties with joining ties. He informed him that if he did so, his enemy would become as if he were an intimate friend.

And in repelling his enemies from the devils of the jinn, He commanded him to seek refuge in Allah from them. He combined these two commands for him in three places in the Qur'an: in Surat al-A'raf, al-Mu'minun, and Surat Ha Mim Fussilat. He said in Surat al-A'raf: ﴿Take what is easy and forgive, enjoin what is right, and turn away from the ignorant. And if an incitement from Satan incites you, then seek refuge in Allah; indeed, He is Hearing and Knowing.﴾ [al-A'raf: 199-200] So He commanded him to guard against the evil of the ignorant by turning away from them, and to guard against the evil of Satan by seeking refuge from him. In this verse He combined for him all the noble qualities of character and all dispositions. For the ruler with his subjects has three states. He necessarily has a right over them that they must fulfill, and a command he gives them, and there must be some neglect and transgression on their part toward his right. So he was commanded to take from the right that is due from them what their souls willingly and generously offer and what is easy for them, without hardship. This is the pardon, which does not cause them harm or hardship in giving it. He was commanded to command them with what is right (al-'urf), which is the good that sound minds and upright natures recognize and acknowledge as good and beneficial, and when he commands it, he should also command it with kindness, not with harshness and severity. And he was commanded to meet the ignorance of the ignorant among them by turning away from them, rather than responding in kind, and thereby their evil is averted.

And Allah, Exalted is He, said in Surat al-Mu'minun: ﴿Say: "My Lord, if You show me what they are promised, my Lord, do not place me among the wrongdoing people." And indeed, We are able to show you what We promise them. Repel with that which is better the evil; We are most knowing of what they describe. And say: "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the whisperings of the devils. And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, lest they be present with me."﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 93-98]

And Allah, Exalted is He, said in Surat Ha Mim Fussilat: ﴿And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel with that which is better, and thereupon the one between you and him is enmity as if he were an intimate friend. And none is granted it except those who are patient, and none is granted it except one of great fortune. And if an incitement from Satan incites you, then seek refuge in Allah; indeed, He is the Hearing, the Knowing.﴾ [Fussilat: 34-36] This is his conduct with the people of the earth, both mankind and jinn, believers and disbelievers.

He had gathered for him the noble qualities of character in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Take what is easy and forgive, enjoin what is right, and turn away from the ignorant.﴾ [al-A'raf: 199]

Ja'far ibn Muhammad said: "Allah commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) with the noble qualities of character. There is no verse in the Qur'an more comprehensive of the noble qualities of character than this verse." It has been mentioned that when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Jibril: "What is this?" He said: "I do not know until I ask." So he asked, then returned to him and said: "Allah commands you that you join ties with the one who cuts you off, give to the one who withholds from you, and pardon the one who wronged you."

There is no doubt that the one who is obeyed has three states with the people:

The first: commanding them and forbidding them in what is in their interest.

The second: taking from them what they offer of the obedience that is due from them.

The third: the people with him are of two kinds: one who agrees with him and supports him, and one who opposes him and stands against him. And upon him, in each of these, there is an obligation.

His obligation in their commanding and forbidding is to enjoin what is good (al-ma'ruf), which is that by which their welfare and the welfare of their affairs is achieved, and to forbid them from its opposite.

His obligation regarding what they offer him of obedience is to take from them what is easy for them, and what their souls are willing to give, out of generosity and by choice, and not to burden them with hardship and difficulty so that he corrupts them.

His obligation when the ignorant act ignorantly toward him is to turn away from them, and not to repay them in kind or seek revenge against them for himself.

So Allah, Exalted is He, said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Take what is easy and forgive, enjoin what is right, and turn away from the ignorant.﴾ [al-A'raf: 199]

'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "Allah commanded His Prophet to take the pardon (al-'afw) from the characters of the people."

Mujahid said: "It means: take the pardon from the characters and deeds of the people without causing them distress, such as accepting their excuses, pardoning and being lenient, and not being excessive in searching out and probing into the realities of their inner selves."

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "Take what is left over of their wealth." That is what is surplus beyond the needs of the family. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219]

Then He said: ﴿And enjoin what is right﴾ [al-A'raf: 199], and this is every act of goodness (ma'ruf). The best of it is tawhid (monotheism), then the rights of worship (huquq al-'ubudiyyah), then the rights of people (huquq al-'ibad).

Then He said: ﴿And turn away from the ignorant﴾ [al-A'raf: 199], meaning: if the ignorant person acts foolishly toward you, do not respond to him with foolishness. Like His saying: ﴿When the ignorant address them, they say: "Peace."﴾ [al-Furqan: 63] On this basis, the verse is not abrogated (mansukhah). Rather, he turns away from him while upholding Allah's right over him, and does not take revenge for himself.

Such was his (ﷺ) character. Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was the best of people in character." He also said: "I never touched silk brocade or silk softer than the palm of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Nor did I ever smell a scent better than the scent of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). I served the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for ten years, and he never said to me 'Uff' (an expression of displeasure). Nor did he ever say, regarding something I had done: 'Why did you do it?' Nor regarding something I had not done: 'Why did you not do it?'" Agreed upon by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) also informed that "righteousness (al-birr) is good character."

In Sahih Muslim, from al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about righteousness and sin. He said: 'Righteousness is good character, and sin is that which troubles your breast and you dislike that people should become aware of it.'"

So he (ﷺ) contrasted righteousness with sin, and informed that righteousness is good character, while sin is what wavers in the breasts.

This indicates that good character is the whole of the religion. It is the realities of faith and the laws of Islam. For this reason he contrasted it with sin.
